The Examiner, Saturday, August 27, 1904. FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
; C,pyriyht.

The holiday season is yet at its prime and all those who can afford it are recruiting out of town and are revelling in the pleasures of sea- side and country resorts. In regard to the former, it is quite noticeable how much smarter the women are nowadays in their dress and how much attention is given to the details of the toilette. It is not so many years ago since any old soiled finery was considered good enough for wearing out at the seaside, while hats and shoes were likewise pretty well worn out. Nowadays this style of toilette is only occasionally to be met with and is viewed with the horror it merits. A neat, trim skirt and blouse, however plain and inexpensive, will appear to greater advantage than a • gorgeous but soiled frock, however pretty it . may once have been and how elaborate its
,RETTY BODICE.

fashioning, and of what costly materials. In- deed a neatly cut and fitted skirt of navy blue serge for the mornings and another of a rather more elaborate nature of cream serge for the afternoons will, with a variety of 'blouses, prove most valuable. The skirts should be cut to clear the ground and be neatly fitted to the figure. Neat collars and silk stock ties and one or two belts of various degrees of smartness are of course necessary comple- ments. _ _

A bodice is often made of the same material as the skirt and forms a pleasant change from 'the perpetual blouse. In my first sketch is given a charming style for a simple and up-to- date bodice of fashionable cut trimmed with 'a quantity of guipure lace and displaying some admirable stitchery. The inner vest, as it were, is of the lace, while the outer is of cream satin stitched with a waistband to match. This, made 'in a light weight of cream serge, looks charming. Nearly every afternoon frock boasts a bodice to match the skirt, and these are generally liberally trimmed with piece lace of the coarser variety arranged as a deep yoke or in some style which defines the outlines of the shoulders and upper arms. The sleeves increase in elaborateness towards :the

return by the same vessel in which you will go out., you Will hand the package to the ship's purser. I Will meet you myself at the landing-stage on Ow vessel's return to England ; you will get the pack- :ige from the purser, hand it to me, and so we N4ill it, urn here, and your task will be at an end. 115.7 t ,nade matters quite plain to you ? " "Quite," I answered. Naturally, the directions given to me sounded stk-ange, but then, after all, that did not concern ; it was evidently something of value that was to be given to me to bring to England. My duty would be to carry out my charge carefully and honestly. _ .
'There were some further instructions which I received concerning ways and means, and I am 13,-.4ind to say-- my new employer treated me mos, liberally in all _respects.

beith was booked for me on the Ocean Queen, by telegraph, and in three days' tinie, being two days longer than I really required to be ready in, I was on board the vessel and leaving England for the first time in my life.

My journey to India was of the usual uneventful kind, but, being my first sea-voyage, I found much to amuse and interest me in my new surroundings on board ship. At the same time, I was careful to maintain my reserve, and, convinced that mine was more than an ordinary enterprise, I made few acquaintances on board and no friends. The general •belief among those passengers who conversed with me was that I was going to India to join some relatives, an opinion I did not trouble to 'contradict. .

Bombay was reached at last, and, after staying for a rest at an hotel for a day, I set out to fulfii the important part of my business. A slow, but interesting railway journey took me to my destina- tion which was a small railway station some forty miles from Bombay. On leaving the station I made my wv along a road which wound its way through some millet fields and, to my -great satisfaction, I found the ryot, to whose house I was directing my steps, at work in the fields. He accompanied me to his dwelling, and entertained by his wife, I spent a pleasant evening there. My business was explained to the ryot, who seemed more than ord-:nirily sericas concerning it.; indeed, he raised so many objections and mingled these with so many entreaties to me to return to my employer without carrying out my object, that I felt all the more determined to see the matter through to its termination. Finally the ryot ceased to object. He demanded from me one pledge, which was that I would not, under any consideration, mention his connection with the affair. I was further obliged to disguise myself in the garb of a Hindu woman, and thus attired, I was led at midnight front the -peasant's hut and conducted through a wood, by devious ways, to where, standing solitary and grand, there rose up the frowning front of a Hindu Temple. "The memsahib will pay me my reward for con- ducting her here," said the Hindu, and he held out his hand.

"My instructions were otherwise," I insisted. "You are to take me inside a Temple, there you are to see that a certain package is put into my•-hands ; after that you are to keep me safe in your house till morning. On leaving your house I am to give you this bag, which is full of rupees. I will not part with a rupee before you have carried out your agreement to the letter," I insisted. The Hindu seemed a little surprised at my deter- mined manner. No doubt be had expected to get the rupees from a woman without much trouble. • "There is danger, but the rupees are many," sai.t" the Hindu slowly. "Follow me, then, memsahib, and you shall have great Kali's gift.," Pondering the Hindu's words over, I followed the man. Every footstep falling on the stone stairs, which ran from one gent outer wall to that within, sounded heavily on my ears, tread as sgtly as I did. • Through one great gap, where once a' wall had stood, we passed to another. When five walls had thus been passed through we stood on the steps of the Temple itself. Still following my guide, and with the bag of rupees held tightly in my right hand, I went up the Temple steps which were lit with the faint -gleam of moonlight issuing from behind the edge •of a heavy storm-cloud. A few seconds after, I stood in the Temple of Kali, and there, in all the hideousness and horror that must ever surround the goddess, rose before me that huge idol. Up in front of great Kali rose a • long .:noky flame, and this at times was licked by a darting tongue of light brighter than itself, as someone in front of the great idol poured a liquid mass into a vessel placed upon a tripod. Before the idol were gathered several Hindus, making . supplication it seemed, and one of these, -hearing footsteps, rose and sharply faced myself and my guide. To a question which the worshipper pnt,. I could only make an answer which shewed my almost total ignorance of the language he spoke. The man was alarmed. He ran to a bell which hung beside the idol, and, catching at the long, brazen tongue which hung 'down, he swung it against the sides of the bell, till the sound seemed to Almost deafen me.

_ The ringing of this bell brought a number of Hindus into the Temple, and, had T been a man, I think a few minutes would have ended. my career. As it was, beyond crowding round toe and raising their hands threateningly, no harm was done to me. The Hindu who had guided me, made a hurried explanation, the effect of which was to cause the cries of the worshippers to become more frenzied than ever, while one of the latter, seeipg the bag I held, and at which my guide pointed as he spoke, made a snatch at it. I swung the l•ag of rupees threateningly, but before I was almost aware of it, a Hindu behind me snatched the bag and wrested it from my grasp. My efforts to regain it were of ile no avail, and then the crowd of Hindus, joining in a mad song, apparently invoking c with biirco"lesdanrdoririnndp c ti me,rer noevs out €nt' (11yrf ilrtls thig Ka n li's the Temple. I must confess that it was with a deep feeling of. relief that I found myself -outside the Temple, yet, at the same time, I was deeply chagrined to feel how easily I had been despoiled of the rupees, and how completely I had failed in the object for which I had been sent to India. The Hindu who had guided me did not leave the Temple for some hours after I was thrust, out, and I could hear, as I lingered on the Temple steps, the sounds of the wild orgies of Kali which were being carried on within the Temple. When day dawned I turned away dissatisfied, yet determined not to return to Bombay without, seeing the Hindu and making some attempt to regain time lost rupees. I wandered about for some hours watching for the Hindu's return, and tired of looking for his -rnoin,,, I then went once more to the hut where ad been by my false guide. entered the hut without ceremony. Imagine my surprise when I found the Hindu seated within. He rose, salaamed to me respectfully, and stopped my indignant torrent . of words with a gesture. "Memsahib," said the Hindu, "the Feringhee asked a great thing of the poor Hindu, greater, perhaps, than she can suppose. All the Hindu has left, now, since the Feringhees have come to his land, are his Temples and his gods. Yet the Hindu's word is his word. Come to my hut in three days and you shall have that for which the rupees pee were paid." 'I will wait for it here for three days," 1: answered ; "and if I do not get , that or the rupees back'oo will have good reason to remember the attacx of your cowardly countrymen upon an unarmed Englishwoman. You will find that the arm of the law of the Feringhees can reach von and all who were concerned in stealing tliose rupees." To my surprise the Hindu raised no objection to proposed. His wife was kind. to me, 'atie planithoilg I h she would not .converse with me. The man was absent from early morning fill late each night, but he spent his time elsewhere than working in the fields. On the third day, when he returned somewhat earlier than usual, he placed in my hands a package. "TO-morrow, memsahib, you may depart and take with you this. It is .what your rupees have purchated.'. hastily pulled the wrappings from the object, and saw, to my surprise, a beautifully-carved ivory box. "Yon lutist promise not, to open it, memsahib," said the Hindu.. "It has within it that which is Kali's gift to those wbo 9eek it. You will solle airietsntliyb fprgitiis,evitzt y )'Oil o•n t: lrizit ilgei?7, it, unopened, to ti I readily assented to this, and on the following morning, more pleased with the ultimate success of my jourtwy t han I can e,xnress. left the peasant's hut, travelled by train to .1 otobiy. and handed over to the parser before night, the singularly handsome carved ii,rry box for which my ein:4l.9yer had sent meFsivi),,T7s afterwards, the Ocean Qat:en left Bom- bay Olt hsr return voyage. .and it was with a feelino

div.head: USEFUL WRAP.
div.p: A USEFUL WRAP.

wrists and are sometimes finished by series ot frills of silk, fine lawn, or lace. The style is a pretty one and this fussiness tends towards reducing the apparent size of the hand, but it also has its inconveniences as the frills get quickly soiled and consequently must be re- newed. I recently saw a very striking three- quarter coat of apple green cloth trimmed round the neck with some very handsome embroidery, while the full sleeves concluded in a deep cuff filled in with innumerable soft white lawn frills bordered with a line of green. The effect was charming and unusual. The useful wrap shown in my second illus- tration is of tussore silk with a deep cape collar of silk embroidery which continues down the fronts. The sleeves are very loose, allowing the coat to be easily slipped on even over an elaborate gown, and are finished by a full frill of coffee coloured lace. This makes a charming dust cloak for driving or travelling, for it is durable and light and does not easily soil. Linen is, of course, a very fashionable material this year for the three-quarter coats so much worn, but it is thicker than silk and crushes more easily, although some of the newer makes are wovdn so as to do away with this fault as much as possible. White linen is very smart looking made with strappings of coarse lace and buttons Of an ornate descrip- tion, but it is only possible for those who have

div.head: SMART HAT,
div.p: A SMART HAT,

an extensive wardrobe as, of course, it shows any marks and quickly soils. I have also seen some coats of a bright geranium red, but these are too striking to prove very popular, al- though the colour is certainly very becoming. Waterproofs and dust cloaks are nowadays much more artistic and more decorative than in former years, and there is more fit and cut in their fashioning than half a century ago when the circular cloak represented all that was worn. . . _

The smart hat given in my third sketch is of white chip trimmed with a long curling black ostrich feather. The shape is very smart and becoming, with the gracefully curved brim and high crown, round which a piece of soft white Oriental satin ribbon is tightly drawn. It is devoid of the much worn streamers or ties and is guiltless of the ever present lace fall Which in itself confers distinction. Fine straws are much in vogue this season and feathers are very much worn. A beautiful pale blue straw hat had a long curling ostrich feather which shaded from white through an ever deepening range of shades of blue down to one which almost merged into violet. A small bunch of violets nestled under the brim on the coiffure. The hat was worn by a beautiful wide browec brunette whom it became to a marvellous degree. To my mind it is not every woman who can successfully wear these fashionablE plumes which shade from one colour tc another, as in many cases the effect is apt tc .be vulgar looking, and I would therefore ad- vise a self coloured plume to any other.
COQUETTE.

div.head: KALI AND HER BLUE DIAMOND.
div.p: KALI AND HER BLUE DIAMOND.
ET CIL.X.RLES J.
INIANSFORD,
Author of "Shafts from an Eastern Quiver,* "Under the Naga Banner," "A Bride's Experi• meat," "The Adventures of Mark Paton," &e.

anyone who knows Jndi t all, and has heard of Kali,will acknowledge tha The is a goddess who is not .to be trilled with.; least of all can any Western mind ex,.--)ect to get the better of the Orientals who guard her,scred temple. _ . .

To interfere with a Hindu goddes-s at any time is rash work; but Kali is more than a mere goddess, and her worshippers are proud of the fact. No doubt she has particularly good sight, for she has a third eye, which eye is in her forehead; and said to consist of a blue diamond of amazing size and rarity. Kali is further noted for her dexterity and strength, for she has four arms, two on each side, the upper ones bolding dangerous-looking 'knives clutched in their sinewy fingers, while the lower ones twine themselves in the hair of the heads of victims who have been decapitated. Round great Kali's neck is a chain of skulls ; nay, her very robe, covering a strange, misshapen body, is blood- coloured. _ .

.Yet it was this goddess whom a madman—for he could hardly have been less—chose as an object to despoil, and the instrument with which he hoped to carry out his plot was myself. . Instead of describing Kali as I have done, first and foremost, I ought, perhaps, instead, to have mentioned how it happened that I, a mere woman., at the age of twenty, came to be chosen as the chief actor in what may well be considered a re- markable affair, and one which, to the present day, has hitherto been shrouded in considerable mystery.

To begin, then, at the beginning. In these days when women are employed in so many walks of life, at one time considered the peculiar property of men, there was nothing surprising in the fact that, when I applied to Colonel Robertson, of the old Manor of Leahurst, for appointment as secretary, he wrote and fixed an interview .with me. • - The Manor of Leahurst, which has recently had so much publicity given .to it, stands in its own grounds, at some distance from the high road which runs through a part of Epping Forest. It is therefore in what some people would describe as a lonely situation, while • others, according to 'heir fancy, would call it merely retired front the ruck of life.

Leahurst had been empty for a number of years, so I learnt from a garrulous labourer with ivfiom I sntered into conversation previous to my interview with its owner. For one thing, -it was heavily rented ; and, for another, it. bore no very enviable reputation, for the occupant, previous to Colonel Robertson, -whom I was to interview; had been killed by some burglars who had entered the premises. Colonel Robertson, however, the labourer assured me, did not mind the evil reputation of the house, for he seemed to seek solitude. He had only two servants, and they were seldom seen. Besides, the house had recently been strongly fitted with shutters and bars and bolts, while Colonel Robertson's male servant, a Hindu, was said to pass the night ‘eated in a chair in the ball, with a revolver ready at hand, in case any further enterprising burglars were so foolish as to make an attempt upon the owner's privacy. Without sayini, that. I was disconcerted by all this news, I am (me to acknowledge that, had the salary offered not been a tempting one, I should have returned to •town n about seeking an interview. I had almost decided to do so at iirsc, and, indeed, had turned away from Lealmrst and taken a few steps towards the country station, when, reflecting that after all, my informant wag merely a local gossip, my common-sense came to my aid, and I made my way to the front gate, where I pulled vigorously at the bell. After a rather long interval, someone came down the neglected gravel drive. It.was the Hindu, who, whenever he was reputed to sleep, certainly was wide awake enough then. "Salaam, memsahib!" said the Hindu, making a sweeping bow, "and what name anckbusiness may it be ? " I gave the-Hindu my. card.[' He returned witlfit to the house, leaving- me out- side the gate which he did not unfasten. - "Salaam, metnsahib," said the Hindu once more. as he returned, and -proceeded to open the gate for me to pass through. "The Colonel will see you in the book-room—the library."

I followed my .guide, who had carefully closed the gate, and was soon across the threshold of tho house and then wa% ushered into the library. 1 had an opportunity of observing my surroundings. There was a.general.air of mustiness prevalent; the room seemed, however, to be in use, and although the month was June, a small fire was smouldering in the grate. Certainly the chilliness of the apart- ment seemed to require something to dispel it. What struck me most, however, was the strength A the iron bars across the windows. They were cioss to each other and formed quite a network, white inside, as well as out, there were heavy shutters hanging which were strengthened with large plates of iron. The room looked much more like a strong- room, or even a prison, than a library, in spite of row upon row of books which covered all the walls except one. Against this last wall was reared a large cabinet, heavy and solid-looking. Just as I was debating in my mind what the oontents of the cabinet might possibly be, the door opened and Colonel Robertson came in. I must confess I greeted him with an air of surprise at his appearance. I expected to see a querulous old man ; why, I can hardly say ; instead, I saw a man not more than forty-five or so, dressed in well- fitting clothes, and wearing a fez. lie was very dark, and had a heavy -beard his features were prominent, his chin being very square, thus giving his face an air of- massiveness. His fingers were covered with rings-, which fact stnick me as being rather odd, for the man had no other vestige of -effeminacy about him. "So you are Miss Forbes?" said the Colonel, smiling', as he held out his hand reassuringly. 'Please don't rise; I daresay you wonder why I live here like this. and whether I am to be trusted, and lots of other things, Miss Forbes? One at a

time, though. I own I' live very secluded, but I have my reason for that." I made no remark; it seemed wisest. not. Colonel Robertson should find discretion was one of my qualities, at all events, I thought. "My advertisement for a secretary was perhaps a little misleading ; what I want is a man or a woman who can keep their own counsel upon occasion, and be thoroughly trusted to carry out any little duty, England or elsewhere, that I may require of Lhem."

I bowed, but again made no reply. "For instance," said the Colonel, "the first duty of my new secretary will be to go to India for me, on a little private business." I had always had a desire, though not the means, to travel, and the vista which this remark set before me was distinctly pleasing. "Suppose, now, Miss Forbes, you and I come to terms, would you be willing to travel so far as fndia on my private business? " I explained that I liked the idea immensely. "Then, as that is really the only difficulty to oonsider, I shall offer you the appointment," said the Colonel. "I have had two secretaries before you, I wish you to understand ; both of them signally failed me in the first little duty given to them to carry out. They were men perhaps e lady -an be more discreet." The compliment to my sex pleased me. I was determined that, so far as I could help if, I would not lose my appointment through want of attention to detail, or lack of discretion. "When could you be. ready to start for India? " as the Colonel's next question. "In twenty-four hours," I anered. He ovidently liked my businesslike repls'.' "I think you are precisely the secretary I have Leen looking toy—precisely," he repeated. "The (tiny I wish you to perform is simply this: You will travel by steamer to Bombay, keeping the reason of your going entirely to yourself. On arrival you will take the train to B--, which is about forty miles distant from the city itself. There you will deliver a note for me to a ryot or peasant, whose-exact address I will give you. It will he necessary for you to go with him wherever he may vish you to '"0 ; You, in brief, are to place your. -self unreservedly in his hands and ask no quest:one. You understand that clearly ? You are, on no amount to question this Hindu! " I gave an assurance that I would not. over), .good ; the result of your journey- with the ryot will be that he will place a small package, your possession. You will Niefpe tahissinpaalcltaognee: n and on no account part with it. On .reachone the shin. for win will be able to

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Where the King is Staying.—The King always stays when at Marienbad,at the Weimar Hotel,which is a huge , building surrounded by pine trees. It is usually crowded ' at this time of the year with English and American visitors, but Marienbad can scarCely be called a gay or fashionable place. Its chief attraction for visitors— apart from the waters, which can be bought of any ! chemist—is its fsolitude and loneliness of environment... The King is no doubt sometimes unconvenienced by the • mobbing of foreign visito-rs, but the townspeople do all they can to afford his Majesty immunity from intro- , sion. Royalties after all, have this matter very much • in their own hands and they can do much to discourage all too flattering attention if they wish to do so. in 11 Denmark and in Italy,it is possible for the sovereign to i pass among the people and exchange informal salutations, without attracting a crowd or vulgar curiosity. The Motor Car on Deeside.—The motor car has • completely invaded Deeside, and the King and Queen,ll also the Duke and Duchess of Fife,now more frequently use cars, in place of the old familiarhorses and carriages when in the Highlands. The herseless carriage is also: making its appearance upon some of the old coaching routes, so much favoured by visitors to Scotland, and that between Ballater and Braemar is now served by motor omnibuses. The King has all along approved of the automobile, and is constantly having new cars built, embodying all • the latest improvements. They are all finished off in the Royal colours, purple lake with red edgings, and special pains are taken to make the police familiar with the Royal ears. It is no doubt owing to i this that they sometimes cover distances in a space of time which it would be more than a breakfast table problem to reconcile with recognised speed limits. Mr. Balfour's Sisters.—Mrs. Sidgwick, the Principal of Newnhatu College, with whom Mr. Balfour has been staying for the meeting of the British Association at Cambridge, is the Prime Minister's eldest sister. She is three years his senior, and is the widow of Prefessor I Henry Sidgwick, who died in 1900. Her husband took a prominent part in founding the most famous of women's colleg over which Mrs. Sidgwick has presided I for the past twelve years. Mr. Balfour has two other sisters—one the wife of Lord Rayleigh, and Miss Alice I Balfour, who acts as hostess for him both in London and at Whittinghame. Miss Balfour is an exception- ally capable woman, and though behind the scenes plays no small part in affairs relating to the government of the country. - Scarcity in the midst of Abundance.—Lord Rayleigh is known all the world over as a great scientist but he is also largely engaged in the milk trade. At first he took to keeping cows as a hobby, and sold the milk to his neighbours, but he is now trying to supply London with the pure article, and keeps over a thousand cows,with this laudable ooject in view. This sending of supplies to town seems however to afford further ground for the complaint now so often made, that it, is almost as diffi- cult to get milk in the country,as it is to get fish at the seaside. Only the other day a tourist wrote to the papers complaining that he could obtain nothing but condensed min at a country inn, and this too, in the midst of a grazina district. Valuables should not be left at Home.—The police authorities warn small householders against leaving their valuables at home, when starting out on a holiday. It is not much to ask some friend to take care of them, and this is much safer than the time honoured practice of hiding them on top of the wardrobe, in the coal scuttle, or fire grate, or between the bedding as fancy may dictate. The holiday season burglar is as well acquainted with all these little hiding tricks, that they generally present few difficulties to him, unless they are very elaborstely arranged. In that case there is some- times trouble in remembering where the valuables have been put, and the householder who placed them in the refuse box, and had them taken away by the ragman, was in the worst dilemma of all. Robberies would be far less frequent if people who go away and shut up their houses, would hand over their valuables to some friend, for the time being. Autumn Modes and Shopping.—The leading French firms have this year agreed upon an arrangement to pre- vent their autumn models from being copied by the cheaper houses. The new autumn styles are therefore likely to be a little later than usual in making their appearance. and it will probably not be until the end of next month that they will be much in evidence. For general shopping however, visitors to London will find this a very convenient time of the year, as in the dull season, whenthe shops are half-empty, it is •possible to obtain much better attention from the assistants. This is a matter which successful shoppers always bear in mind. If bent upon some difficult errand, they never go when the girls are tired with the day's work,but choose a time in the morning when they are likely to be more obliging, and whilst the place is free from the stress and -confusion of the more busy hours of the day. div.p: sirable ideas of that particular period, and are adding such pretty and artistic touches to it, that the result leaves little to be desired. One thing, however, the really well dressed woman is careful to see to is that exaggeration is left severelyZalone. She will, for ex- ample, have nothing to do with the gigantic sleeves, or over-full skirt, even though she can afford to patronise the best of modistes. For those who have to be satis- fied with third or fourth rate dressmakers,any attempted close following of the fashions is worse than foolish. Inexpensive fabrics often look extremely well when made up simply, but when exaggeration comes in, the effect is paltry and common to a degree. New Millinery.—The small, closely set clusters and wreaths of flowers, which adorned so much of the smart spring and early summer millinery, are among the modes of the past, and fashionable milliners are now shewing a preference for a more dashing and effective style. Huge single blooms of every possible and impossible colour, appear in the most modish and dressy headgear, and the idea does not make for economy, as they so quickly get out of order. A very little in the way of wind or rain, reduces them to an undesirable state of shabbiness. In travelling hats, a novelty is a fine felt, made in a round brimmed shape, a straw edge being laid on the brim, and a straw band round the crown, which finishes in a rosette, or small bow and ends. A couple of quills are run through the rosette, or how, which affords a smart finish to this useful, and altogether delightful travelling hat. The Undesirable Whalebone.—Evening gowns are no longer tailed; they are round in shape, and rest from ten to twelve inches only on the ground behind. One or two of our great modistes continue to place a hoop of whalebone, or one of its substitutes, in the hem of the underskirts of such gowns, but lesser lights are con- tenting themselves with an extra allowance of frills— tucked, gathered, and inserted with lace—and lace flounces with which they adorn the slip or underskirt. These have very much the same effect as the whalebone, and possess none of its inconveniences.

div.head: LANCASHIRE HEROES.
div.p: LANCASHIRE HEROES.
Gallant Rescues from Drowning.

The completed list of awards for bravery issued last night by the Royal Humane Society contains the following :—Lancashire cases: Bronze medal to Thomas E. Hailvvood, Bolton, for his gallant and plucky action there on July 16, An old man had thrown him- self into a mill reservoir, the water being foul and 10ft. deep. In an attempt to save him Hailwood dived in many times, and at last got him out, but life was then extinct. Testimonial to Ted •Heaton, professional diver, for jumping from the pier at Morecambe on July 11th, and saving a visitor from Bingley who had fallen over. Testimonial to G. H. Wilcocks, of Leigh, for his attempt to save a man who was drowned in the canal there on June 18th. Testimonial and £1 to John Wilding, of Rochdale, for his gallant rescue of two youths from ift, of water in the canal at Rochdale, on July 10th. Testimonial to William Clitheroe, draper, of St. Helens, for rescuing a girl named Holmes from the canal there on July 9th. Testimonial to George Fowler for his rescue of a boy front a filthy, stagnant pond at Radcliffe on July 24th. When got out the boy was apparently dead, but Fowler who is an ex-constable of the County Constabulary, succeeded in restoring him.
THE NEXT GENERAL ELECTION.

We believe (says the "London Sun") that an appeal will be made to the country in April next. if this informsition be correct, and we have every reason to believe that it is it means that the Government have decided to take the verdict of the country on their next Budget.

Ot ..thailaul,ness that 1. turned my lace towards Engtuid again. I was fortunate in having a good -eturn voyne, and when the vessel reached South- mpton, my first care was "•Lo get the ivory box from he purser and hand it ,to my .mployer, Colonel Robertson, who came to meet me and to learn the cesult of my mission.

div.head: fIL
div.p: fIL

-- - "I need not tell you, Miss Forbes, 7 Colonel Robertson was saying, "how much I appreciate the successful effort you have made to get possession for me, of this inestimable treasure. It is only right, now that your effort has met with such success, that you should learn the exact nature of the enterprise upon which you have beea engaged. I will acknowledge, frankly, that it was from -first to last a matter of life or death with you. That heing so, you will find me not unmindful of the fact in the reward which I intend to bestow upon you." I did not reply to this speech ; it struck me as callous and cruel in the extreme for a man to send a woman on such an enterprise while he remained safely at home shut up in a house which was barred and protected in the strange manner in which Lea- hurst was. Colonel Robertson rose, and unlocking the fold- ing doors of the cabinet, which stood in the library where we then were, he drew out in succession several drawers, which he placed upon a table standing in the middle of the room, and then he invited me to inspect the contents. On rising to look at them, I confess my astonishment was com- plete, for _every drawer seemed to be a blazeNof light. Precious gems of all kinds sparkled and scintillated before me, 'while the magnificent size of some of the diamonds, rubies and opals, roused my highest enthusiasm. Colonel Robertson was pleased at the el ident interest I took in his collection.

"You will understand, now, why this room is so . heavily shuttered and barred," he said. "A mil- lionaire may have expensive hobbies; mine has been to collect the most perfect gems that are to be had for money. Still, although I possessed all these rarities, one precious gem was beyond my reach ; there are but three pure blue diamonds of any size known to exist, and the greatest and purest was that gem which adorned the forehead of Kali, the Hindu goddess. Time after time I have tried by means of bribes and in other ways to get posses- sion of that wonderful stone. My messengers have hitherto failed, but you—you—a woman have suc- ceeded in getting this preoions gent for me. My collection is at last complete! Within this ivory box is the famous blue diamond of Kali!" Colonel Robertson opened the ivory box, and there I saw, held by golden claws, what appeared to be a shining blue stone. While Colonel Rotertson turned the box about,. trying to get the rays from the lamp to fall fully upon the blue diamond, I put back, at his request, the drawers into the cabinet. I was trying to push one of the drawers into its .place, when, Colonel Robertson ,stopped me. "Stay!" he exclaimed; "there is a vacant place ta that drawer for this famous stone:" Ile put the box down upon the table, and •taking hold of the blue stone, drew it from its setting, holding it towards me: . . A report like the crack of.a rifle reverberated upon the air, and Colonel Robeftson, with a wild cry, threw up his arms. The room was filled with smoke, while half- dazed by the noise, I was only conscious of one cart, the blue stone had exploded in the colonel's and ! _ _ _ _

, Kali. as I hay said, is a goddess who has many arms. When I was sitting in the library that same night, watching the spark of life gradually growing feebler and feebler in the man who had received fatal injuries by the ...terrible explosion of the blue stone, I saw lying on the floor a piece of paper. It was singed with the effect of the explosion which I had witnessed, yet upon it I could still see some words in tamil which the Hindu servant of the ng man afterwards translated to me: "Kali's arms reach ,far; they destroy all who dare to provoke her wrath." The Western mind cannot cope with the Eastern one, but the Eastern mind•learns at times how to in the subtlest ways the latest discoveries of Western science.

div.head: SEVERE POACHING AFFRAY AT ASTON.
div.p: SEVERE POACHING AFFRAY AT ASTON.

At Runcorn, on Tuesday, Joseph Oakes and Thomas Moores, both of Kingsley, near Frodsham, were charged with night poaching on the Aston 1-all estate of Mr. Hervey Talbot, J.P.—Mr. H. N. Linaker prosecuted, and Mr. J. Burton defended Moores. Mr. Linaker stated that on Sunday, the 14th inst., at ten p.m., William Jones, the head keeper, and four other keepers, while in Loft Wood, at Aston Grange Meadows, saw a number of men setting nets. When the nets were set and the men commenced to drive rabbits into the nets the keepers showed themselves. Nine or ten of the men came for them with long sticks, and a severe struggle took place. The keepers were severely assaulted, and the men got clear away. Mr. Linaker asked the magistrates to deal severely with the prisoners. He knew the chairman (Mr. Fred Norman) did not look upon poaching ls a serious offence. Mr. Norman: Why do you say that? Mr. Linaker: From remarks I have heard from the bench that you did not consider poaching a particularly serious offence unless followed by assault. The gentle- man who had the Aston shooting spent from.Cl,2oo to £1,400 upon it last year, and there was no doubt that rabbits were private property...protected by the Game Acts, and to take them:was pure stealing. Mr. Norman said he must disavow any sympathy with poaching. He had said from the bench, when men had been charged ,with seriously assaulting keeptrs, that whatever consideration might be shown to them for poaching alone, when they ptoceeded to dan-tole keepeis they put themselves beyond the pale of all consideration. Mr. Burton called William Jones, bootmaker ; Joseph Lloyd, butcher ; and Abram Lewis, farmer' who stated that at the time of the allay Moores under the influ- ence of drink, was at Kingsley, and an hour's walk from the scene of the poaching. The case against IVlootes was dismissed. Oakes was then charged with assaulting .Jones, the head keeper, who said he was struck on the shoulder's, ribs, and arms, and he was black from his shoulder to his hip on the left side. There were five men attacking him. Oakes struck at him. The prisoner exhibited a number of wounds on his head, and said he had a rib knocked in. He said his wife and child would have to go to the workhouse if , he were sent to prison. I The prisoner, who had been previously convicted for poaching and assault on the police, was fined 40s. or a j month for poaching, mid sentenced to a month's hard abour for the assault.

div.p: EVENTS OF THE WEEK,
THE WAR IN THE FAR EAST.
CHIEF OF THE JAPANESE ARMY STAFF.

The war in the Far East has undoubtedly after many rumours, reached a grave crisis, and it is certain that at the time of writing the grand and final assualt on Port Arthur, the " supreme effort," is in progress. This great attack, which has been carefully and Consistently worked up to for many weeks has been falsely reported as often as the fall of the fortress has been rumoured, and tne operations hitherto have only been spade work. Ring by ring the forts and preliminary positions have been taken in the face' of terrible loss of life, which has not yet been officially revealed, and the greatest pluck •and endurance have been shown on both *sides. And now the final moment has come, and upon it turns everything for the Japan- •ese. They are, however, cool and confident that a few days at the outside will see them masters of Port Arthur, but the Russians are equally determined and will fight to the death, so the contest will be a terribly bitter .and bloody one. Preparatory to the final
LIEUT.-GENERAL KODAMA.

.effcrt the Japanese, acting unner orders direct from the Mikado, made a formal de- mand for surrender and offered safe convoy to all non-combatants, but both were refused in unmistakable terms. But one sign of the approaching end was the withdrawal of the foreign attaches from the town. The latest news from inside Port Arthur is that it is well provisioned, free from disease, and in the best of spirits. Truly, whatever its ultimate fate, General Stoessel has proved himself a great commander and has made a splendid uphill fight in the teeth of dis- couragement. News from the main armies round Liaoyang is that all movements of any imsnsions have been stopped by the rains, • which have called a compulsory halt, and both the armies are marking time in torrents and deluges. At last the vanguard of the Baltic fleet is definitely reported to have sailed for the Far East by way of the Cape, and in a few days the admiral will follow on his flagship, but it must be at least two months before they reach their destination. And by then much may have happened.

div.head: BRITISH ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION.

The annual meeting of the British Associa- tion has been invested with peculiar interest this year owing to the fact that the Premier is its President, and, for the nonce. .forsook politics for science, addressing the, most <tminent scientists of the day on their own ground. The venue of the meeting wa s Cambridge, and Mr. Balfuur delivered hi s presidential ad- dress in the Corn Exchange. The proceedings were opened by Sir Norman Lockyer, the outgoing presi- dent who intro- duced Mr. Bal- four and at the same time read congratula- tory wire from the British Association of IR NORMAN LOCKYER. South Africa. This was hearti-

ly received, as next years meeting is to take place at Care Town, when Professor Darwin, son of the famous evolutionist, will preside. This .year there was no subject of absorbing interest, as there was last year in radium, and the Premier chose as the subject of his presidential address" Reflections Suggested by the New Theory of Matter." It is his belief that this new or electric theory of matter which holds that electricity is tlip reality of which matter is merely the expression, thust materially alter in many respects our conception of the universe. Each atom contains distributed force and power. Up to five years ago, he claimed, the human race without exception lived and died in a world of Minions, not only about things remote or abstract; transcendental or divine, but about things one sees and handles, about those "plain matters of fact" concerning which all were most self-satisfied. As it is, we are only living on the fringe of the vast question of the Kinetic energy stored in molecules, which greatly stirs the intellectual imagination. But however far back you probe and reconstruct a long-drawn sequence of causes and effects it will never give a satisfying explanation of knowledge itself.- In his address the Premier plainly revealed his faith in a great spiritual reality per- meating things temperal. It was a memorabls occasion, even in the annals of the British Association.

div.head: DURHAM PROFESSOR KILLED ON THE ALPS.
div.p: DURHAM PROFESSOR KILLED ON THE ALPS.

The new Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod in the room of the late Sir Michael Biddulph, G.C.8., is Admiral Sir Henry Frederick Stephenson, G.C.V.0., K.C.8., who, it can be freely stated, has had an active and distinguished career. Eetering the Navy in 1854, he servid, in the St. Jean d'Acre in the Black Sea during the Crimean War, and was present at the capture of Kertch and the fall of Sebastopol. On the outbreak of the Mutiny Sir Henry proceeded to India, and did admirable work with the naval brigade in quelling that formidable outbreak. After commanding the gunboat Heron on the Canadian lakes during the Fenian disturb- ances in 1866, and being thanked for his zealous and capable aid, the gallant admiral had further experience in the China seas, where, he acted as flag-lieutenant on the Rodney under his old friend the late Sir Harry Keppel. A. good deal of discussion and interest has been raised, together with not a little fun, at the projected "cruise of the coronets," as it has been nick-named. A few days ago certain chosen persons received a circular, surmounted by a coronet, which invited then in the name o the Earl of

There he was in- formed that Lord Muskerry's secretary called daily for letters, and this secretary proved to be a son of Dr. Lunn, of Continental tourist fame. "The Co-operative Cruising Com- pany," which had charge of the arrangements, was found to be under tile directorship of Dr. Lunn, who is organising everything for the committee. The Dominion Line steamer, " Canada," of io,ooo tons, is the vessel chartered, and the itinerary embraces visits to Marseilles, Naples, Capri, Palermo, Pirwus (for Athens), Constantinople, Smyna, Beyrrout (for Damascus), Hafia (for Nazareth), Jaffa (for Jerusalem), Alexandria (for the Nile), Malta, Tunis, and Algiers, starting from 'Liverpool. Considerable discussion was raised as to the exact position of the peers in question, and, to crown all, the _Earl of Tankerville advertised in the "Times" that the invitations had been issued without any know- ledge, understanding, or consent on his part. And so the matter stands at the time of writing.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

DEATH OF A ST. HELENS WORKS MANAGER. The death occurred at St. Helens on Thursday of Mr. W. H. Swim, for eighteen years manager at the Greenbank Chemical Works of the United Alkali Com- pany. Mr. Swim, who was forty-five years of age, and was unmarried, had been ailing since the early part of this year, and his decease was caused by pleurisy and i pneumonia. He was the son of a doctor n practice at Earlestown, a native of that town, and served his time as a chemist at Messrs. Muspratt's works, being after- wards for eight years assistant manager at Messrs. Hutchinson's' Widnes chemical works, when he was ap- pointed to the position at St. Helens, which he held until his death. He took but little share in the politi- cal or social life of the town, but was esteemed for his personal qualities by a large circle of friends. Tile funeral takes place at the St. Helens Cemetery on Saturday afternoon. DEATH OF A ST. HELENS WORTHY. The funeral took place on Tuesday afternoon of an old St. Helens lady who has beenclosely identified with Wesleyan Methodism in that town. She was eight y- seven years of age, having been born at Moss Rank near St. Helens, in 1817, and was the Wife of Mr. R. Hough- ton, the head of a well-known St. Helens Wesleyan family. She was a member of the first Wesleyan chapel erected in the b )rough, in Market street,a building now ued as excise and accountants' offices, and up to a week psior to her death she regularly walked down to the serrvices at the Central NN,rsleyan Church. Her intellec was remarkably keen, and she could tell many stories about the early history of the town and her own reli- gions denomination, In which she was -an active and striking personality. Three of her sons are circuit stew- ards, and one Mr. J. H. Houghton, is well-known in Rugby football circles, and is secretary of the North- ern League. A funeral service was held in the Wesley Church, and sympathetic references to the deceased lady's character and useful life were made by the Rev. George Parker, of St. Helens and the Rev. J.H. Doddrell of Fleetwood.

FAILURES IN ENGLAND AND WALES.—Aecordingi to I "Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, Aug. 19th, was 149, viz.:—New Bankruptcy Proceedings published in the London Gazette 67; Deeds of Arrangement registered. 82. The respective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were: Bankruptcies, 69 Deeds of Arrangement, 71—Total 40; being a net increase in Bankruptcies of 178. and a net increase in Deeds of Arrangement in 1904, to date, of 413.

div.head: COUNTY RATE CALL.
div.p: THE COUNTY RATE CALL.

The CLERK reported that he had not yet received the County rate call. It was later than usual and it was scarcely fair to the parishes that it should be so late. He telephoned to the County Offices and was told that the Clerk who had to submit the precepts was away and if he returned in the course of the afternoon he would send them. There was no reply this morning.
SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.
LIGHTNING CONDUCTORS TO BE USED

At a meeting of committee on the 2.3 rd August, a letter was read from the Vulcan Boiler and General Insurance Company,Limited,intimating acceptance of new boiler in replacement of old for insurance at an increased pressure of 701bs. It was agreed that the old policy be sent to the company for endorsement in accordance with the terms of the letter and recom- mended that the tender of Mr. Antrobus for the erection of a sample shed in the yard of one of the four homes at £4 15s. be accepted ; also that the tender of Mr. W. J. Hewitt for supplying and fitting lightning conductors at £2,9 10s. be accepted. Mr. BILLINGE asked what necessity there was for the new work. Was it due to a recommendation of the Local Government Board, the insurance company, or the ingenuity of the committee or its chairman. (Laughter). Mr. MATHER explained that it was not a personal question. Mr. S. Di.vrEs said it was very necessary for , the committee to care for the lives of the children of the institution, but in his experience this question had not been mentioned before. He imagined that owing to the screaming of the children during a resent thunderstorm the committee thought it better to take action. Personally he was not in favour of the expendi- ture, except in one place where the chimney was. Mr. THOMPSON said he would like to know whether this was the only tender received. Rev. Dr. MERCER said according to modern- ideas lightning conductors were necessary for the preserva- tion of life. (Hear. hear.) Tenders were invited and the committee chose the lowest. There was a difference of opinion on the committee as to whether lightning conductors were necessary or no, but the resolution was carried, Mr. Davies being against it. Mr. HICKMAN asked how many condustors were to be provided, and of what quality they were. Mr. MATHER. said there would be one to each build- ing—seven. The conductors would be of copper. Mr. HICKMA.N : At what price? Mr. 111 A.THER. : 103. Mr. EIECKM : It is a very reasonable price if the conductors are of copper. The minutes were passed.
FISH FOR THE OFFICERS.

- Mr. THOMPSON called attention to the two items for fish for the officers. He asked whether tenders were invited for fish. The OH kIRMAII said a tender was obtained for fish consumed in the house, but not for the officers. Mr. THONIPSON said no price was given on the account as to the price of the fish. The CHAIRMAN replied that qs a matter of fact the Board had nothing whatever to do with the officers' fish except to pay for it. That was part of their allow- ance, and they could spsnd it as they wished. .
- Mi.. A. J. JOLLEY said the Board 'made a monetary allowance each week for the officers.

TFIE TRAINING OF PROBATIONER NURSES. At a meeting of the House Committee on August 12th it was resolved to recommend to the Board that by way of experiment separate and distinct contracts for the Workhouse and the schools be diyidedly asked for; that both institutions keep new and separate samples accord- ing to requirements for trades:nen to tender to.—The committee considered the results of the probationer nurses examination in physiology and hygiene fairly satisfactory. At a meeting on August 19th, the Master reported a case of scarlet fever in the hospital, and Dr. Braide reported that the case had not been removed to the isolation hospital as the Corporation officials had refused to admit without an undertaking for payment of maintenance of the same. The matter was referred to the Clerk to take such steps as may be deemed neces- sary to have the case removed at once. Several mem- bers hoped that the deadlock would be finally settled between the two bodies.—ln respect to the better training of the probationer nurses, Dr. Braide offered to give supplementary lectures during the winter months,both on abnormal conditions of health and mid- wifery, and the offer was cordially accepted. Other features in connection with this question were deferred until certain negotiations had ripened. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY moved the confirmation of the minutes. • Mrs. CLAY seconded. Mr. HICKMAN asked what the fees were at the tz:ch- nical classes for nursing. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY : 7s. 6d. for the session. The minutes were passed. THE DEATH OF A. GUARDIAN. A VOTE OF CONDOLENCE.
The CRAInnA.N intimated that since the last meeting
of the Board they had lost one of their oldest and moit genial members by the death of Ur. Clarke. He was one of the oldest members as regarded - his length of

service on the Board and also as regarded the len'ith of his life. He was sure every member regretted exceed- ingly, Mr. Clarke's departure from them. He (the chair- man) always found him a very agreeable man to get on with, although he was a man of considerable strength of character and one holding some opinions which cer- tainly were not general. Mr. Clarke was, however, very amiable and very tolerant of the opinions of others. (Hear, hear.) He (*he Chairman) would move that a vote of condolence be passed to Mrs. Clarke and family in their bereavement.

M. Wthr,rAm Houoirromin seconding the resolution said thp Board had suffered a distinct loss by the death of Mr.,Clarke. As onelof his oldest colleagues, he (111 r. Houghton) could testify the more to the enthusiasm with which Ntr. Clarkealways discharged his duty as a Guardian. He was constant in his attendance and a very hardworking Guardian. His death was a distinct loss to the Newton ratepayers, and the Newton Relief Committee had also sustained a'great loss. His exten- sive knowledge of the district was of grett use to the Committee when transacting relief business. (Hear hear.) Mr. J. BILLINGE supported the resolution and it was carried unanimously.
A RESIGNATION.
The CLERK read a letter from Mrs. Holmes resigning her position of secretary to the Ladies' Visiting Com- mittee.
THE BOARD AND THE VALUATION BILL.

The CLERK read a communication from the Secretary of Representatives of Boards of Guardians and Union Assessment Committees convening a meeting of mem- bers of the Committee appointed re opposition to the Valuation Bill, to be held at the Westminster Palace Hotel, London, on Wednesday September 14th. Mr. ASHCROFT said he did not see the necesgity of sending a delegate to the meeting seeing that the Valua- tion Bill had been withdrawn.

The CFIAIRNISN said although it had been withdrawn it would Undoubtedly be brought up again whether there was a change of Government or not. He felt sure there would be an alteration made in our valuation methods. He thought it would ba very well-went money indeed if the Board took its part in moulding any future bill brought forward. Mr. THOMPSON, speaking as an overseer, said it was a very important matter. He proposed that Mr. A. J. Jolley attend the meeting. Mr. BILLINGE seconded, and the proposition was carried. The Clerk read a communication from the Hon. Secretary of the North Western Poor Law Conference that the'3oth Annual Conference will be held atLancaster on S litember 23rd and 21th. It was decided on the proposition of Mr. 131:LUNGE to appoint the Chairman and Vice-Chairman of the Board (who were appointed to represent the Board at the recent preliminary conference meeting) and Mr. George Mather to represent the Board at the Confer- ence, together with the Clerk, on the dates named.

div.head: VACANCY ON THE HOARD.
div.p: THE VACANCY ON THE HOARD.

Mr. Billinge and Dr. Patterson gave notice of the death of Mr. John Clarke, Guardian of the poor for the Viaduct Ward, Newton. Instruction was given for proceeding to the election of a Guardian for the said Ward in the place of Mr. Clarke, deceased.
THE ESTIMATES.

The CLERK presented -it—s-t:f&-;in-ent giving the esti- mated particulars of common charges for the half-year ending at Lady Day, 1905. The estimated expenditure totalled up to £16,921, compared with £16,507 9s. 10d. in the previous half year. The report was adopted. SUGGESTIONS BY MR. JENNER FCST. INTERESTING OBSERVATIONS, Mr. JENNER FUST, upon the invitation of the Chair- man, addressed the Board. On the previous day, he said, he visited Padgate Schools and he was very glad to say that he found it in a very prosperous condi- tion. The children seemed healthy and vigorous and with the one exception of a case of ringworm, they were free front disease. Ringworm seemed to linger at the schools but at the present time it seemed to be reduced to a single case and no doubt an end would be seen to that. Going through the differ- ent homes he found them in very goad order. lle noticed that the children were still without tooth brushes, and one could hardly go through a poor law institution without finding tooth-brushes provided. He was ex- amining the means of escape in case of fire and in go- ing round he could not help but think that the fasten- hags of the windows that gave access to the iron stair- case Were not easily dealt with. it Was all very well

when there was no hurry for someone to take a key and open the windows leisurely but the Guardians must re- member that these fastenings had to be dealt with in theory at all events in a great hurry and perhaps in case of panic. He did not think any harm would be done by removing the fastenings entirely, and allowing them to be opened in the ordinary way. If the Guardians found that trounle arose through this procedure then it would be time enough to adopt some easy means of fastening the windows. At present they were rather a danger. The number of , children in the schools had been for some time rather in excess of the ordinary number for which the homes had been built. No doubt the Guardians had this in• view and if the numbers increased to any great extent, they would take some steps to prevent any overcrowd- ing which would injure the health of the children. With regard to the clothing, he saw that the Board was adoptine tweed instead of corduroy and the cloth he saw was of excellent character. As regarded those children who were leaving the institution he noticed one omission. There was one omission of a Bible or some book of devotion. As regarded children belonging to the Church of England a Bible and the Book of. Common Prayer might be .given, as regarded Roman Catholic children of whom there was a considerable number, he believed the book valued was "The Garden of the Soul," and as regarded Non3onformist children, at all events a Bible would be acceptable. If the , Chairman of the Schools Committee would attend to , present them and give a few word of advice he did not Mr. DAVIES : Do they come out of his own pocket . Mr. MA.THER, Yes, the words of advice.

Dr. MERCER.: The Bible would be very acceptable I to the Roman Catholic children. Taey can be got very cheaply indeed. Mr. JENNER FUST said he also visited the Workhouse, and although he did not go through the whole of the buildings he was very pleased with what he saw. There ' were one or two things to which he wished to call atten- tion. The ward in the male hospital set apart for con- sumptive cases, and which were supposed to be treated by the op3n-air treatment hardly fulfilled its object. The windows were only open at the top, and the tem- perature of the ward at the time of his visit was 62. That was a reasonable temperature for any ward, and it seemed to him that a great deal more fresh air was zequired than the ward was receiving. He did not want to interfere with the Medical °leer's discretion in any way, • but he was inclined to think the Medical Officer would agree with him in what he had said. Throughout the infirmary the lower sashes had been blocked so that they could not be ; raised at all. He thought a change might be made in that direction. He believed the reason for it was a I certain amount of fear of any of the patients throwing I themselves out of the window, and also of a fear of articres being introduced into the infirmary of an un- desirable character. As regarded the danger of patients throwing themselves out of the window he believed a couple of bars outside,which would not give the idea of a prison, would prevent it. He did not &ink they could ventilate a ward as it ought to be ventilated without some .facilities for opening the windows at the bottom being provided. There were two or three points to which he was anxious to callithe attention of the Medical Officer. Theclassification book was not kept—a book prescribed by article ten in which the Medical Officer was to record his opinion as to the fitness for employment of that person. The book was kept up to two years ago but for some reason had been dropped. Another article of the dietaries order prescribed that the Medical (Meer should once at least in every four weeks revise the diet. He didnot feel quite sure how thathad been carried out There was no record of it. He would suggest that the Medical Officer be asked, when he revised it every four weeks, to make some kind of entry on the bed card or the book showing that the recommendations had been carried out. The order also directed that the in nates under the age of three years should be visited and direc- tions given as to diet. He unierstood it was not the practice of the Medical Offieer to visit the nursery at regular intervals, but only when his attend°. was called to a partictilar case. The idea of the order was that he should prescribe a diet for each child and should watch the effect of that diet in each individual case. With that view the medical Officer should pay regular visits to the nursery to see how each child WAS getting on. Among other improvements, he was very glad to see that the double bedsteads in the main building had been got rid of. As regarded escapes from the vagrant wards he understood that the cells might be regarded as safe. There was an I idea that the grids would be available for escape pur- poses, but from experiments made thet was not possible. They were in rather bad order and if the Board was going to renew them p3rhaps an arrangement could be made whereby the grids could be opened from the out- I side and thereby afford an additional means of escape in case of fire. The upstairs wards had no additional means of escape except the staircase. He was very glad to be able to speak in high terms of the general condition of things. Very considerable improvements had been carried out during the last few years. The house looked bright and clean. Particularly he would draw attention to the men's side which had just been painted through, and the additional brightness in the appearance of the wards by the substitution of nice colours in place of the everlasting Workhouse drab. It cost no more and looked very much better. He con- gratulated the Board on the success of their new laundry. He confessed it had turned nut as far as one could see on going through, better than he thought it would. He hoped it would answer its purpose for a considerable number of years. He understood the extension of the Workhouse was under consideration but he did not propose to say anything because he did not believe it had advanced to a stage that really any definite conclusion had been come to beyond the fact that the Board had decided to make an extension for a certain class. As time went on, if he could be of any assistance, he would be very glad to render it. (Applause.) The Cu aunt aN said the Board was very pleased at the remarks which had been made by Mr. Jenner Fast. The Chairman of the House Committee would be quite delighted at the pat on the back which he had got from Mr. Jenner Fast, because all the improvements seemed to be in the house. Mr. Al 4.THER. said he was vary pleased to hear the report in regard to, the schools. With regard to the little things recommended, they would be brought before the House Committee. Re quite agreed it would be very nice to present these children with books and bibles on their outward journey through life. (Hear, hear.) Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said the HOLM Committee would give careful att(lntion to the points which had been raised. There were one or two other matters hinted at which the members of the House Committee had hinted

at in the past. 111 r. Jenner Fast had alluded in very guarded terms to the question of interfering with the discretionary powers of some of the Board's officials. He (Mr. Jolley) would not say more at this stage beyond giving the assurance that the matter would receive care- ful attention from the committee.
MR. HICKNI iN ASKS A QUE3TION.

Mr. HICKMA.N inquired of the Inspector if he had been through the old infirmary block. He would like to know whether the Inspector had noticed that there was a number of persons sleeping immediately over the car- penter's shop, the paint shop and the stores iu which there were stored paraffin, turpentine and paigt. He would like the Inspector's opinion whether these work- *hops and these risks of fire to the inmates ought not to have immediate attention. On the men's side there were 55 beds and 24 were occupied each night. On the women's side there were 23 beds and 7 of them were used. • These inmates slept over the caspenter's shop where there wasa large quantity of shavings and loose timber and over the paint shop and other places where inflammable material was stored. Mr. JENNER. FUST said he did not go through the old infirmary on the'previons day, but he was there at an earlier period, and Mr. Moorsorn also reported upon it. The particular point did not attract his attention. He did not gather whether Mr. Hickman's idea was that the paint ecc,., should be removed, or whether the inmates should be removed. (Laughter.) He was quite sure that the House Committee would consider the matter. Mr. DAvrEs said he was rather surprised at Mr. Hick- man's statement. A short time ap Mr. Hickman brought forward a motion that the Board should make no further extension. Now he suggested something that would cause an extension. Mr. HICKMAN said he was suggesting an extension. He had asked for Mr. Jenner Fuses opinion upon the facts he had brought before him. At the last meeting he argued against the extension in the way proposed. He considered there ought to be an alteration, and that a corrugated iron building should be erected for these workshops. The premises already used for this purpose should be utilised for the additional accoin- modation re-paired. instead of building another expensive building such as suggested, especially con- sidering the present state of trade. The CIIkIRMAN : You are getting rather out of order. Mr. HICKMAN : I don't want to be misrepresented. The Board then rose.

An out-of-date excursion ticket from Leeds to Liver- pool was found in the possession of a Liverpool man named Morris Rosenberg, a tailor's machinist, who was travelling in a Leeds and Liverpool express on Wednes- day. His explanation at the Cit y Police Court to-day was that he had bought the ticket in Leeds for sixpence. A fine of ss. and costs was imposed.

div.head: WARRINGTON IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: WARRINGTON IMPROVEMENTS.
Private Street Works and Longford Boot Alterations.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY.

At the To:va lull, Warrington, on Thorsday morning, Mr. W. A. Dazat, Local Govarnment Biard Inspector, conducted an inquiry into the application of the Cor- poration to borrow .26,030 for private street works, and £1,327 for the extension of Longford dept in the township of Winwick-with-Elulme. Among those pre- sent were the Mayor (A lderman Bolton), Aldermen Evans and Smethurst, Councillor Pemberton, Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), T. Longdin (borough sur- veyor), S. Wilson (deputy town clerk), W. 1-1. Wood- cock (assistant overseer), A M. Ker (deputy borough surveyor), Wilson (manager of Longford depot), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk to the Rural District Council). The TOWN CLER,K said the application to borrow £6,000 was to carry out certain works under the Private Street Works Act. The Corporationallowed owners of property seven years within which they might pay their apportionments of paving expenses,and necessarily they had to borrow the money to carry out the work. Mr. WOODCOCK said the population of Warrington at the last CetallS srIS 64,241, and the estimated popula- tion at the present time was 67,000. The assessable value was £225,518, and thi d3bt U1213C tha Vlit3ry Act was £269,833.

Mr. LONGDIN stated that there were twenty-two streets and back passages which formed the subject of the application. They were in a very bad condition, and much had bean said in the pipers and by the Medical Officer of Health and others about the unpaved streets and passages. The committee were very anxious that these works should go on, not only these but a number of others, as soon as they could get the sanction of the Local Government Board. They had had great difficulty during the last twelve or eighteen months in getting materials for the streets as the prices had gone up. Now the prices had come down,the committee were in a position to carry out the works at the lowest rate possible to owners of property. The passages and streets would all have a concrete foundation. The passages would be paved with brick setts and the streets with syenite ,or granite. With regard to one item, a footpath in Hardy-street, the total cost of which was £lB 12s. 9c1., the committee wished it to be withdrawn, as a few years ago, the street was paved through, but the land was not built upon. Since the Corporation had taken the street over, the land had been built upon,and it was the duty of the ratepayers to put the footpath io order. The TOWN CLERK said this would reduce the applica- tion to £5,381 is. 3d. In reply to questions by the Inspector, Mr. STANLEY WiLsoN said one case of apportionment to which objec- tion had been made, had not yet been settled. This was in regard to a passage off Manchester-road. The objec- tion raised was that the proposed works would not benefit the owners, as their property was much lower than the passage and therefore they could not use it. With regard to Winmarleigh-street, the committee had only received information last week that the owners of property there preferred granite setts in lien of wood. The committee considered that as they had done all the streets around with wood blocks this street should be completed with wood paving. The owners objected on the ground of expenditure, as granite would cost £228 less. The committee had not decided whether they would accede to the owners' request, as the Council had I already decided on wood blocks._

The TOWN CLERK: A short length of the street is already paved with wood. We have anplied for seven years in which to repay the., loan, but the Finance Com- mittee would like about eight years to carry this out.

div.head: LONGFORD DEPOT.
div.p: LONGFORD DEPOT.

The Tows CLERK said that in regard to the Longford Depot extension he had to make a confession. They had already spent part of tiv money, but they had done it under pressure from the Warrington Rural District Council in whose district the works were situated. The Rural District Council had made all kinds of bitter complaints of the nuisance caused by the manufacture

div.head: of cOncentrated manure carried on there. The Cor-
div.p: of cOncentrated manure carried on there. The Cor-

poration had done everything in their power to abate what the rural authority contended was a nuisance. The works had been partly of an experimental nature with the object of putting a stop to the complaints. They had already purchased land for extension purposes, but that was done under the powers they possessed by the Act of 1899. The amount they wereauthorised to borrow was £14,400, of which they had spent £7,400 on Longford Depot and the rest on hospital extensions. They had acquired eleven acres of land,two of which they had appropriated, and the remainder they proposed to sell. They gave a trifle over £5O an acre for the land,and he had no doubt that they would get an enhanced price for the land they re-sold. The Town Clerk proceeded to give in detail the various items of expenditure included in the applir cation, and said there was a sum of £125 for a condens- ing tower whichhad already done much to abate the nuisance there. The total amount already spent upon work included in this application ins £2,569 14s. He regretted very much having done is, but the Corpora- tion had had to do it under pressure of the District Council. They estimated that £1,757 10s.. would be required to complete the works at Longford in addition to the sum he had already named. When the w•ork was carried out, he believed that there would be no cause for complaint. The character of the works themselves was very offensive, and he thought they had adopted the very best means of preventing any complaints. Mr. WiLsoN, the manager of the depot, then explained the plans. Councillor PEMBERTON asked if part of the works covered by this application had anything to do with the experiments which a certain firm was undertaking for 1 twelve months. The TOWN CLERK: They have nothing to do with it. Several other questions having been answered, the inquiry was closed.

Mr. Holcombe Ward has won the United States National Lawn Tennis Championship. Mr. H. L. Doherty, who won the championship last year, did not defend the title. Mr. Ward did not lose a single set throughout the tournament, and now holds the cham- pionship for the singles. Mr. Ward, in partnership with r. Wright, also won the doubles.
