div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
AUGUST 27th, 1904.

There is so much THE NATIONAL persistence in the STAMINA. r epr esentation that we are a race which is physically unfit that there may ba sus- pected to be some object in it that is not fully avowed. We shall not be far wrong, we imagine, if we assume it be a part of the great plan for frightening the nation into conscription. If the race is to be saved, the male portion of it must be exercised in military duties. That is really the contention that lurks out of sight under the quite false representation that the people of England are more or less rapidly going to the dogs. The report of the Committee on Physical D aterioration should have put an end once and for all to the idea that we are becoming weaker and smaller, and, as a nation, far less fit for the battle of life than we have been heretofore. Singularly enough however, the report is being employed as if the Committee had formed conclusions exactly the opposite of those at which it actually arrived. It is clear, therefore, that there are some people and'some organs of opinion that are determined not to be convinced on this matter. Offer them what proofs you will, and they still remain of the same opinien. It suits them to believe that the nation. is losing stamina, and they are determined to proclaim their belief from the housetops. If it were a fact that there has been of late years a gradual deterioration of physique among any large section of the people, we should be driven into enteitaining some exceedingly curious views. We should be justified in concluding that measures which have been adopted for the purpose of improving the general health are, in fact, destroy- ing it. Better food, shorter hours of work, less overcrowding, more holidays, more abundant means of recreation, would have to be condemned as tending to the national ruin. But anyone who crudely put these contentions forward would be regarded as a lunatic. We know tnat the British stock is not degenerating. It is not necessary for those who are reasonable and observant among us to be reassured on the subject by a Committee of Inquiry. We need merely to look around us for reassurance. We see everywhere signs of a healthy nation, increasing in stature—alike as to its men and its women—well-fed, welldressed, energetic, marching on to a higher plane of living. There are, of course, sections of the people which must be excluded from this description. They live in the slums; they do not make progress ; they pro- duce weedy and ancemic children. Even those, however, are growing fewer than they were in pro- portion to population; and they do not represent a new condition in the life of cities, but a sur- vival.

The cry of physical deterioration was raised in connection with the admitted difficulty of procur- ing healthy and well-grown men for the Army. It is impossible, it must be admitted, to contemplate a regiment of " Brodricles boys" with any swelling , feeling of national pride. Many thousands of them, though they are part of our Army, are not reckoned among the available forces of the country They would have to be set aside if we were sending out troops to encounter an enemy. Yet these are such examples of the youth of England as have managed to pass the regimental doctor. Far more have been set aside than have been admitted into the Army. Were we to draw conclusions as to the physical conditions of the people at large from the quality of the young men who nowadays offer themselves to the recruiting sergeant, we should undcubtedly have occasion for much reflection of a melancholy sort.

It happens, however, that the bulk of the young I men offering thQrnselves for the Army, and failing to medical examination, are the worst possible samples of the youth of England. The ppibalse s a military career does not draw the same proportion of stalwart young men as formerly. Its attrac- tions have not increased as have the attractions of civil life. There is no r3580n to alarm ourselves by deep and depressing speculations on such a topic. Nor are we wise in attempting to extract general conclusions as to the stamina of the nation from the successes and failures of the I recruiting sergeant. A young man who is doing fairly well, who has a prospect of regular wages before him, and who has no quarrel with his sweet- heart, prefers the workshop to the Army. No'

doubt such as be would crowd into the ranks in times of depression in trade and wide lack of employment. But as thicgs are,it is not patriotic to libel the nation by crying out that we are a people getting more and more enfeebled, and less fit year by year to maintain our place in thp world. It would be unfortunate if some of those nations which dislike us should take our national pessi- mists at their word.
A writer in one of THE GROWTH OF the current monthly BUREAUCRACY, magazines once more

draws attention to the very serious problem which is arising as bet- ween local and departmental government. The tendenzy to centralise more and more in Whitehall the control of local affairs has been marked of late years. It has been seen in the actions particularly of the Local Government Board and the Board of Trade, and to some extent it is fostered by the dissatisfaction which many people now feel, and which is growing, at the heavy burden which the conduct of municipal affairs is placing on the ratepayers all over the country. The cry which has gone up for some power to check excessive municipal expenditure is furnishing the pretext— and a very plausible pretext too—for an extension of a practice which those who have to do with local government cannot but view with grave con- cern and misgiving. Bureaucratic government is not a desirable thing, and in this country, where freedom to localities to manage their own affairs has always been held, within reasonable limits, to be an essential principle, it is quite certain that it would produce very unwelcome results. The straining after authority in Whitehall is a natural growth of increasing departmental activity, and as such is not perhaps in itself to be utterly condemned. But it is clear that the municipalities, looking at the matter through other glasses than those through which civil servants, and rerhaps even legislators, see it, must be pre- pared to resist to the utmost the organised attempt to extend the control of the departments. Nor is it entirely to be ignored, in considering the ques- tion, that jofficial, and officious pedantry is to a certain degree itself responsible for the heavy expenditure in which many municipalities have indulged, while it is evident that the ?ontrol at Whitehall has not so far proved any successful check upon the tendency to lay out money ex- travagantly.

Mr. James Ball, the elective auditor represent- ing the Labour party has so thoroughly fulfilled the trust reposed in him that the gratitude of the ratepayers generally will be assured. Elective auditors in Warrington have for so long contented themselves with. seeing that two and two make four and certifying the interesting fact, that the people of the town have almost lost sight of the necessity for taking a special and direct interest in those corporate accounts which show how their money has been spent. Mr. Ball, in a report which he presents to the public in another column, recognises the fact that recent events have aroused a legitimate and reasonable desire "for greater detail and fuller information as to municipal expenditure," and in well-chosen terms he reviews the municipal busi- ness which has been transacted during his year of office. There can be no doubt that a report such as Mr. Ball has favoured us with tends towards a feeling of confidence and security in the town's administration—and this has been conspicuously lacking in the paEt. We are glad to note that Mr. Ball has little fault to find, though he doubtless brought a critical mind to bear on the audit. The tone of his remarks is generally complimentary to the borough officials. He has taken the trouble to elucidate the mysteries of out- standing accounts and the perpetual gas annuities. Like Tennyson's brook these" go on for ever," and Mr. Ball very properly animadverts on the refusal of Parliament to grant powers to compel the sale of these awkward legacies from the past, thus proving itself "more concerned in safeguard- ing vested interest than in promoting the public weal." It is gratifying also to find that Mr. Ball recognises the burning necessity for enlarging the rateable sphere, and boldly advocates the taxation of land values. This is not a political question and the elective auditor very properly exhorts the muni!inality to press for such a reform in season and out of season. Unfortunately we know that his advice will be disregarded, but he has never- theless done good service is introducing a topic so vitally important to the ratepayers. On perusing his report they will, we are sure, hope much from Mr. Ball in the future.

Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P., makes no secret of hii being a follower of Mr. Chamberlain and a "whole. bagger." We are glad of the fact, for as Mr. Chamberlain's visionary schemes are losing what- ever trar.sient popularity they once won, the chances of Mr. Pierpoint's return for Warrington as a Protectionist and a retaliator become corres- pondingly and beautifully less. He may not re- member the fate of Mr. Bridgman at Oswestry—a one-time impregnable Tory stronghold which fell into the hands of the Liberal Free Traders as soon as the electors realised what Mr. Chamberlain's pro- posals really involved. If a whole-hogger could be so easily despatched at Oswestry, the similar pro- cess of pig-sticking should afford even less trouble at Warrington. There were some curious and specious definitions of Protection at the Conserva- tive garden fete on Saturday. Mr. Pierpoint said we"should not go on taking all goods from foreign countries whici refused to receive our manufac- tured goods except at a very high rate." Why not, if we want the goods? Mr. Draper thinks it is not in accordance with the fitness of things "that this country should indefinitely continue to concede to other nations opportunities and advan- tages which they did not reciprocate." Well it has suited us to carry on business on these lines for a long time and we are yet the most prosperous, best governed, and healthiest nation on the globe. By embarking on a tariff war in preference to Free Trade we might feel that we were "getting our own back," to some extent,but in the end we should punish ourselves most. The workingmen have shown at almost every bye-election that they are disinclined to follow Mr. Chamberlain into the thorny field of fiscalitis, and if Mr. Pierpoint chooses to do so they must exercise their option of forsaking Mr. Pierpoint.

It will be welcome news to many householders if not to property owners, that the Corporation is giving attention to some of the streets and back passages which are in such a bad condition as to be regarded as a menace to health. At the Local Government Board inquiry on Thursday, the Borough Surveyor stated that twenty-two streets and passages are to be taken in hand, and those townsmen who have supported the Medical Officer in his recent criticism will be. hopeful that this is but the beginning of a large and much-needed improvement. During the recent heavy rains, it has not been an uncommon sight to find many of the streets aud passages in the poorer parts of the town completely flooded, to the great discomfort of those unfortunate people who have been obliged to go to and fro. The measures re- ferred to by the Borough Surveyor may, we pre- sume be regarded in the light of a first instalment of a determined effArt to remedy the existing state of things. The list of unpaved streets and passages in the report of the Medical Officer of Health covers eight pages, so that there is many years steady work in front of the authorities and not much hope of them being able to relax their efforts for a considerable time.
The members of the Warrington Board of Guardians have every reason to congratulate themselves upon the excellent report which Mr. Jenner Fust give on Wednesday of his visit to the

institutions under the eare of the Board. Local Government Board officials are as a rule very sPar; ing in the use of compliments. It is more usual to expect officially-worded complaints and a long list of recommendations. Mr. Jenner Fust, how; ever, seems to have been very favourably impress' with the improvements which have been intro- duced at Padgat9 Schools and thoWorkhouse.l3°th institutions are under the superintendence of car able officials,and the Board has shown a coinmend- able disposition in recent years to aim at efficiency T all departments of poor law administration. has meant the expenditure of money but there is reason to believe that it has been money viTli" spent. Much remains to be done before the NS ar- rington poor law institutions can be regarded as models, but it is some satisfaction to know tha,b the methods already adopted have the approval oL so high an authority as the Local Government Board inspector.

There is good reason to hope that the agitation for the abolition of tolls on the old Warburton Bridge will soon be rewarded with success. The various authorities concerned have come te an arrangement to act in concert, and an appeal to the Ship Canal Company is t° be backed up by the Warrington Rural COIL eil, Warburton Parish Council, Bucklow Rtir4,l Council and the Lyrnm, Trlam and Cadisheau Urban Councils. Most of our readers will be aware that the toll is charged for crossing the small stone bridge over the disused river bed, and like the bridge the toll is a relic of nygone days. It sesele very absurd, coming from the Lancashire side, to cross the huge Ship Canal bridge free, and then be pilled up at the insignificant structure a f63W hundred yards further on. The absurdity of. tile thing does little to lessen the annoyance, eapecia!lY to motorists, who have to pay heavily for tnt.7 privilege of entering Cheshire via Warburton:Nl should imagine that the Ship Canal will be inclini to look at the matter reasonably when the aPnee reaches them.

Warrington made her obeisance to the veterau founder of the Salvation Army on Saturday, as " motor passed through the town on his memorable car tour from Land's End to AWrdeen. The General's stay was of brief duration,bat the recer tion which awaited him was spontaneous and thusiastic. The scene in front of the Town• I{3 was a memorable one, and was a striking tributef to the popularity of the General. But a few brig years ago the General and his army were the stv. ject of general sneers and obloquy, and now thef spectacle is witnessed at every town he visits e people turning out in their hundreds to welcorne and wish him God speed on his unique journt Ile has not yet silenced criticism, and probabll never will. But he has at any rate conquered Pre.. judlce, and even those who do not admire 111: methods are prepared to admit that the gelid religious movement which he has initiated has he, a widespread and wonderful influence for annd I° this and other lands. •

- Wednesday night's illumination: at St.Peteraburg, fallowing the august ceremony of christeniugtptlt cap on the popular rejoicings. Throughout the have been picturesque, and the most pictureel circumstance of all has been the hearty goodvil! of the populace. Everyone has welcomed thlas mite of humanity who is yet a future Czar a° the possible saviour of his people. We have be(!° charmed with the magnificent gilded coach ,ift which he went to christening,and with the fact the he wore pale blue robes and lay on a beautiful blOO cushion; and while he has moved in so much stet: he has lit it all with satire, and discovered tir touch of nature which makes the whole world lan' by crying lustily when he came in contact with th° uuplelsantness of the water. We are torced to errhne conclusion that there is sense in that baby. add to his other titles to popular admiration, !'" already weighs 1011 b. At such a time fo history it is pleasant to see a nation aft-ef‘ed ,:a thus by domestic sentiment. There has 0°.% in the past a wretched, undisciplined acqulsli tiveness, the nation's eyes being in the ends .fq, the earth ; she is concerned at home now more humane and inspiring emotions. R115.,5",„ will return spontaneously, as well as of neeesslive' to her domestic obligations in a political selle'r To a chastened people the ribbon:about the shot' nt of the young Knight of St. Andrew may represe',7 a better bond than the pride of conquest. If titiv,c*, are to be defeated on the other side of the go.- in positions morally and physically untenable, they must sup their gruel. A better sentimbnt and ! better work await them at home. They mu" return to their own house, and be content to do, like ordinary mortals, to the best of their powers, the work that lies nearest to their hand.

SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. - The George Hotel Licence. The George, Hotel licence was again under con- sideration at a meeting of the Finance Committee held this week.. The matter was deferred until the committee had ascertained what their position would be under the new Licensing Act. We understand that Councillor Maginn intends to move a motion at the next Council meeting that the tender of Messrs. P. Walker and Sons be accepted. • SUGAR is DEARER.—Advt. The Voters' Lists. The revising barrister (Mr. Foard) will hold a Court at the Town Hall on the Bth of September for the re- vision of the lists of votes. There are 171 claims and 92 objections whereas last year there were 214 claims and 93 objections. The reduced number of claims and objections is evidence of the great care which has been bestowed upon the -new list by the Assistant Overseer (Mr. W. H. Woodcock). The number this year is the lowest on record. The new list includes the names of 11,693 voters as compared with 11,593 last year. PUBLIC' BENEFIT. UNDER the CLOCK for B:3 BOOTSin LANCASHIRE.—Advt. On Sunday successful camp meetings were held by the workers at the Methodist Free .Church, Buckley- street. At the morning service, on the ground off Forster-street, Bro. Henry Bradford presided at the fortnightly, meeting of the, " Loyal Friendship" Lodge, (War- rington District), held on Monday night, at the Blue Bell Inn,Markeoplace. V.G. John Appleby was in the vice-chair, sopported by the following officers William Pennington; P.P.G.M., Thomas Knight ; James Bramhall, P.G-.; R. Rigby,J. Higham, - Oswald Peacock, T. Litton and Burgess Lee. After -the lodge had been duly opened, the Chairman called Upon D.G.M.W. Pennington to present an emblem of merit to P.G. Joseph Pennington, jun., for services rendered to his lodge. Bro. Pennington said it gave him much pleasure to do so, and he hoped the emblem would be an incentive to the younger members to follow the example of Bro. Pennington, who was quite a young member. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Horses and Cattle Shipped from Latchford. ?, On Saturday the second consignment of horses, cattle and sheep, left Latchford Locks for the River Plate, South America, on the Manchester Inventnor. They had been brought from many parts of the United Kingdom and are being sent for breeding purposes. Some ot the horses were from Cheshire. There were 116 prize sheep, 20 horses, several of which are race horses and 21 cattle,. Two of the horses had belonged to the late Sir Klandell Maple, namely, Kitawake and Mistic, while another animal which was sent away was sister to St. Amant, winner of this year's Derby. Three celebrated bulls were among the stock and were much admired, as well as a • number of very fine horses from Newmarket. Latch- ford is regarded as a more convenient place than Manchester for the shipment of the cattle and there is likely to be a very steady trade in this direction for some time. It is believed that supplies will be sent at least once a month. BEST BOOTS FOR ALL.—UNDER THE .CLOCK.—Advt ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINER& WATERS.—Advt. Cheshire Teachers and Nature Study. The Director of Education for Cheshire, in the course of a report to the Cheshire Higher Education Committee on :the subject of instruction in Nature study for teachers in elementary schools, suggests that centres for this class of work should be established at Altrincham, Chester, Crewe, Hyde and Macclesfield. The Director of Education points out the value of instruction in nature study, and says that the result of recent examinations show that a large number of teachers have profited greatly by classes hitherto held but that further opportunity °for obtaining instruction is necessary to make them able to turn their know- ledge to proper advantage in their schools. He further suggests that a special class shall be formed at •one centre in the county, to be held on Saturdays, for a higher course of study and built upon the course already taken, and that there shall be as much practi- cal work as possible in connection therewith. The Ffigher Education Committee have approved the scheme, and the Director of Education has been authorised to make the necessary arrangements at the 'various centres for the classes to be held. SUGAR is DEARER.—Advt. A Collier's Injury. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, Mr. Browne applied on behalf of William Baker, a collier, of 29, Fairclough street, Burtonwood for a declaration of liability or for a nominal award of compensation against the Collins Green Colliery Company.—Mr. Pearce, of Liverpool, represented the respondepts.— Alr. Browne said the applicant wanted a declaration under the Workmen's Compensation Act that the cora- Pany was liable for compensation on the ground that the applicant was permanently injured. The man had -lost his 'fourth finger absolutely and could not use one of the other fingers. If the applicant allowed six months to elapse before making the application he could not recover, and the company could discharge him from his work.. ,He merely asked for a declara- tion that the respondents were liable in default of his being able to earn the amount per week he was en- titled to under the Workmen's Compensation Act. The applicant told him that he knew of many eases where •after six months had elapsed, men who had been iajured and had not obtained a declaration of the Court, had been discharged and were unable to claim 'Forapensation.—Mr. Pearce contended that if a man lost a small member of his body he was not entitled .„.to. damages, nor was he entitled to a wage under the ,workmen's Compensation Act unless the result of that !oss partially incapacitated him from earning a liveli- tood. When a man, as was the case here, was working at his old job at the old rate of wages, how could it be /laid that he wasipartially incapacitated?—His Honour • ..;"id he appreciated the point exactly.He would adjourn 'no case sine die without any prejudice whatever to any action which Mr. Pearce might wish to take and the applicant must be bound by Mr. Browne's action. div.p: DEATH OF MR. EDWIN RICHARDSON. Funeral Yesterday. '

We deeply regret to announce the deah of Mr. Edwin Richardson, of Paddington House, Warrington, which took place a little before half-past seven on Tuesday morning. He had been in failinghealth for some months and had not been at business Since Christmas, but his long and tedious illness was borne with the utmost resignation and patience. He was attended from the first by Dr. Bennett of Padgate. At an early stage, Dr. Graham Steele, of Manchester, a noted specialist, was consulted, and subsequently Dr. Joseph, and all of them were unremitting in their attentions, but unfortunately without avail. With possibly one exception, we believe that• Mr. Richardson was the oldest tradesman in War- rington. He was the youngest sou of the late Mr. John Richardson, farmer, of Booth-lane, Elworth,Cheshire, where he was barn on the 29th September. 1835. He was educated at Mr. Herring's Academy, Sandbach ; and came to Warrington in the year 1850 as an apprentice to Mr. William Sanderson, of Bridge-street, whole- sale and family grocer, with whom he subse- quently entered into partnership, continuing the business, on the death of Mr. Sanderson in 1867, for over twenty years in his own name, and afterwards in partnership with his son, Mr. J. E. Richardson. It may be worth while to note that a portion of the pre- mises occupied by the firm is famous as the house in which John Howard lodged whilst printing his great " Prison " works, and that Mr. Richardson always took the deepest interest in Warrington, its history, and its affairs, as well as in all national events, an interest which he maintained almost to the day of his death. When he came to Warrington. then a small country town, the farmers were in the habit of bringing their butter, eggs, and poultry to Buttermarket-street, where the goods were regularly exposed for sale. Mr. Richar- dson had many vivid recollections of his early days, and used to narrate with obvious pleasure now the shops in ' Bridge-street were, at that time, under the supervision of one of the old night watchmen, who regularly- ' patrolled the .street to see if everything was safe and periodically call the hour. There was scarcely an event or a personality in the local annals of the lastfifty years with which he was not familiar, and. although he never took an active part in public affairs, his public spirit I was evident in many ways throughout his busy life. A prominent member of the Wesleyan Church, the deceased, in his younger days, was greatly interested in Sunday school work, and, whilst residing in Warrington, officiated for some years as secretary,and afterwards as superintendent, of the old Buttermarket-street School; indeed, there is scarcely an office in the Warrington Circuit which is open to laymen which has not been held byhim. In politics he was a Liberal Unionist,but, in that respect, as in everything else, he always exer- cised an independent judgment, tempered by a deep and intelligent patriotism. Mr. Richardson 's principal hobby was gardening, and he spent some of the happiest hours of his life inhis pleasant grounds. His favourite flowers were roses and chrysanthemums, both of which he grew with great success. Mr. Richardson leaves a wife and three children to mourn his loss. Among his fellow-tradesmen he was held in much esteem, and a large circle of relatives and friends remains to tenderly respect his memory. THE FUNERAL.

Amid many ma,nifestations of tegret and esteem, the grave closed over the remains of the deceased gentleman yesterday. Pior to the cortege leaving Paddington House, a brief service was conducted in the house by the Rev. G. H. Carnson (superintendent), Rev. W. C. J. Neville, and the Rev. John Gunnell (Penketh). The cortege then proceeded to the Wesleyan Church at Pad- gate, where the funeral service wsi held. The residents of the village drew down their blinds as a mark of res- pect, A fairly, large congregation assembled, and pend- ing the arrival of the funeral party, Miss .J. Bennett, the organist, played as voluntaries I know that my Redeemer liveth ' and "0 rest in the Lord." As the coffin was borne into the church by four of the deceased gentleman's employees. the Rev. W, C. J. N6ville recited the words of St. John "I am the Resurrection and the Life" &c. Thecoffin was covered with beautiful wreaths and rested in one of the aisles during the service. Mr. Neville read the ninetienth psalm and then the congregation joined in singing the hymn commencing "Lord it belongs not to my care." The Rev. John Gunnell read the lesson from Paul's first epistle to the Corinthians. xv. chapter, and a brief address was delivered by Mr. Neville. The hymn "On the Resurrection morning" was sung, and the R V. G. H. Carnson then engaged in prayer. The impressive service was brought to a close by the playing on the organ of the "Dead March" in " Saul." The chief mourners present were Mr. John E. Richardson (son), Mr. Arthur Bennett (son-in-law), Mr. 'John Richardson of Warmingham (brother), Mr. Thomas Richardson of Elworth (brother), Mr. W. Moreton (brother-in-law), Mr. Charles Richardson, Mr. E. Richardson, Mr. Edward Jackson, Mr. John Jackson and Mr. Robert Heywood (nephews). The friends present included Mr. R. G. Henshall, Mr. William Silcock, Mr. Thomas Grime, Mr. A. H. Dunn, Mr. R. Corbett, Mr. G. H. Meldrum and Dr. Bennett All the employes of the late Mr. Richardson were present. Amongst those who attended the service at the church were: Miss B. Dutton, Councillor Brough Messrs. Percy Bennett, William Ford,James Ford. James Urmson, James Gandy, J. Critchley,F. Dixon,F.Wright, Joseph Mason, George WeaVer, G. Bayley,J. Bailey,John Bennett. J.G Withenshaw,W. E. Plinston,Henry Ward, Frank Harris,Joseph Grounds, F. Taylor, Joseph Spruce (Preston Brook), T. Appleton (Statham), J. Appleton, Samuel Moss and Isaac Johnson.

div.head: ADDRESS.
div.p: THE ADDRESS.

The Rev. W. C. J. Neville said he had the pain- ful privilege of addressing to them a few words concerning their brother who had passed hence to be ''for ever with the Lord. John Wesley said, when referring to some of the members of the early Methodist societies, " our people die well." The passing from them of Mr. Richardson had been no exception to that statement which Wesley made con- cerning the Methodists. I n these later days there were those—and Mr. Richardson had certainly been amongst the number—who"died well"and justified their founders boast. But in order to die well, one must live well. He might say without exaggeration that Mr. Richardson wore '• the white flower of a blameless life." Coming to Warrington when he was fourteen years of age to become an apprentice of the late Mr. Sanderson, he formed many acquaintances that helped him to become a Christian—a Methodist Christian. Mr. Sanderson was himself a leading Wesleyan in Warrington and Mr. Richardson always felt very grateful to Mr. Edwin Brown, a man in Mr. Sanderson's employ, who introduced him to Buttermarket street Sunday school, where he found a sphere of work. Mr. Richardson put on record that he joined the Wesleyan Methodist Church at the age of 18, and began to attend the class meetings. One of the classes attended by Mr. Richardson was conducted by the Rev. J. Agar Beet. When Mr. Richardson came to live at Paddington House he transferred his membership to Padgate Church. Ho Mr. Neville) had known Mr. Richardson for the last three years, and it gave him a sad sort of satisfac- tion to be able to take part in that service at a time when ho was about to leave the circuit. He was drawn towards the late Mr. Richardson by the charm of his gentleness and unfailing courtesy. His chief character- istics might be said to be his humility and tranquility. He was a man who did not seek a prominent public position. He loved his home and family and flowers and the quietness of the life of a country gentleman. He saw life steadily and as a whole and from the stand- point of the eternal. When it was borne in upon him that he would probably not recover from his illness he was not unduly perturbed in spirit. There was not the bustle to make preparation that characterised some people. He already lived in the presence of the eternal and he appreciated the importance of eternal things.He lived the eternal life—the life which was in touch with eternal things here and now and which but awaited the complete unfolding of the eternal in the bright and full light, which now came to us only in part and spasmodi- cally. Now he had "awakened from the dream of life." He had passed into +he light of God by way of death. We used that word for want of a better name. There was no death. What seemed so to us was merely a transition. The soul had awakened in a great and true sense and was in touch with all that was eternal and all that was true.

WARRINGTON POLICE SPORTS. A SUCCESSFUL MEETING. Not only to the members of the Borough Police Force but to the to'wnspeople in general was it a source of satisfaction that the annual police sports were carried through on Thursday under favourable conditions. The large-heartedness which prompts the "men in blue" to make this yearly effort on behalf of local charities always excites a ready res- ponse from the public, and only fine weather is needed to ensure success. After the unfortunate experience of last year when the Pparts had to be postponed and then held in heavy rain, the promoters were relieved when Thursday opened with every prospect of sunshine. Happily their hopes were realized, and although there was a slight shower late in the afternoon, the complete programme was submitted and iirovided some excellent sport. For some days the policemen had been busy disposing of tickets, and it is anticipated that the proceeds will allow of welcome donations to the Infir- mary, District Nursing A.ssociation,and Police Athletic Club. The last named institution, it may be stated, fulfils an extremely useful purpose in helping the members of the force to spend their leisure in a con- genial and profitable way. For a mid-week meeting the attendance was very encouraging, about 3,000 persons lining the Wilderspol enclosure. So admir- able were the arrangements that the seventeen events were decided without a hitch, and very little time was lost between the races. By shortly after six o'clock the sports were at an end. Some exceptionally keen contests aroused interest to a high pitch. The fit-bit of the afternoon was the two Miles bicycle handicap, T. Sherratt, of Sankey Harriers, being loudly cheered for the splendid riding which gained him premier honours. A.. E. Howard, of Sankey 'Harriers, who was so badly hurt at Liverpool a short time ago, rode in the mile and two mile contests, but although he won his heat in the longer race he failed to take a prize. C. Berry, the well-known Warrington cyclist, added to his laurels in the mile handicap, but had to admit defeat in:the big event. Not the least interesting feature of the sports was the military tournament by eighteen soldiers from Orford Barracks, under the direction of Sergeant-Instructors Stamford and Sweeney. The men went through exercises with an ability and skill which did them credit, the boxing and cockade fight- ing proving popular items. The Warrington Blue Coat School band and Miss Turner's mandoline band were in attendance, and rendered enjoyable pro- grammes. The Athletic Club had been fortunate in securing the services of capable and energetic officials and a special word of praise is due to Sergeant Evans upon whom, as secretary, much of the work of preparation had devolved. The complete list of officials is as follows :—President, Mr. Luke Talbot, Chief Constable ; Vice - President, Detective Superintendent Monaghan ; judges, Councillor D. Tinnion, J.P., Messrs. Stanley Wilson, Harvey, Rabbit, and Pickavance, N.C.I.T. ; referee, Mr. Thomas Locker; marksmen, Messrs. A. Booth, F. Crabtree, D. Wylie, • P.C. Robinson, and F. Whittaker; stewards, Inspectors Taylor and Rowbottom, Sergeants Williamson and Barlow, Detectives Ifeacock: and Clough, P.C.'s Newey, Hayes, Stewart, Edwards and Wyse; clerks of the course. Chief Ihspector Phillips and P.C.'s Hoigkiss and Dennett ; starter, Mr. T. Wainwright, Salford Harriers ; secretary, Sergeant W. Evans ; assistant secretary, Sergeant S. Smith. 100 YARDS FIAT ACE (CONFINED TO WARRINGTON POLICE). As usual the opening event gave our bail " peelers " an opportunity of displaying their sprinting 'me contest showed that the force is not without men who are fleet of foot, althoggh the entries were low. There were only two heats, and as four prizes were offered all the finalists secured awards. P.C. Houghton, from the eight yards mark,ran in first,and he was closely followed by P.C. Holland, (2 yards). Sergeant Evans (14) showed that he is still a sprinter to be reckoned with, and captured the third award, P.C. N'ewey (5) being fourth. The prizes were :-Ist, time piece and bronzes; 2nd. case of cutlery; 3rd, silver plated teapot; 4th, case of Carvers. 100 YARDS FLAT RACE (OPEN). There was a close struggle in this race, F. Sager, of Rochdale, breasting the tape first. Half a yard separated him from J. Guy, of Preston, and the third prizewinner, P. MacKinley, of Sefton, was only a few inches behind. The winners of heats were :—C. Sinclair, Warrington, 9+; F. Yates, Tone, 8; J. Guy, Preston' 7,2; J. Moran, Warrington, 6_?; W. Dilley, Kettering, 44; A. Cowap, Little Leigh, 10: J. The awards were :—ist, marble clock and ornaments; 2nd, dessert combination; 3rd, silver-plated egg tray.

Massey, of Chelford, had just got going when he col- lided with a young man who had been starting another competitor and was leafing the track. Fortunately he ' was travelling slowly and neither the rider nor the pedestrian were much hurt. The heat was re-contested, and when racing at a good speed W. Effingham, of Darlington, fell heavily to the ground. G. Graham, of Workington, also came off,but was not much the worse .for the accident. This race proved interesting, D. Carroll, of Man- chester, winning by about a yard. H. Stephens, of Liverpool, gained second place, but there were only inches between him and J. A protest was entered against Carroll's running, on the ground that as he is an officer employed by the Ship Canal Company he cannot be considered a bona fide member of a police force. Consequently the prizes were withheld until the matter has been decided. 'Winners cf heats :-Ist heat, 1, H. Stephens, Liverpool,l9 ; 2, W. Carroll, Manchester, 12; 3, J. C. Nadin, Manchegter, 15; 2nd heat, 1, J. Riley, Nianchester, 18 ; 2, J. Davidson, Manchester, 17; 3, J. Bacon, Manchester, 18. Prizes :-Ist, silver-nlated tea urn; 2nd. silver-plated cheese dish: 3rd, silver-plated inkstand.

220 YARDS FLAT RACE (OPEN). With a capital numbee of entries, this race was keenly contested, and the sprinting of local competitors was watched with interest. E. Harris, the popular foot- baller, again turned out and was successful in his heat, but had to admit defeat in the final. F. Sager,of Roch- dale, again acquitted himself well and carried off the first prize with only half a yard to spare. W. Bryan,of Prescot, ran in second. and the third prize went to W. Postings, of West C. H. Winners of heats :—E.Harris, Warrington, 9 ; W. Bryan, Prescot.ls; W. Dilley,Ketter- ing, 7; F. Sager, Rochdale. 14; S. Flurdsfleld, Salford, scratch; J. Hughes. Sankey, 151: F. Yates, Tonge, 13i; W. Postings, West C.H., 10; A. Cowap, Little Leigh, 16. Prizes:-Ist, combination cabinet; 2nd, six bottle cruet. 3rd, silver-plated biscuit barrel.

TWO MILES BICYCLE HANDICAP. Exceptionally good riding made this bylfar the most exciting event of the afternoon. Keener finishes have seldom been witnessed on the Wilderspool enclosure, and the prize-winners thoroughly deserved the honour. T. Sherratt, of Sankey Harriers, from the 45 yards mark, is to be complimented upon a remarkable per- formance. He stuck to his task manfully, and gradually forging ahead, not only came in first in his heat, but gained premier honours in the final. His victory was by no means a scrape through, for he was two lengths in advance of R. Dutton of Rainford, who started from the 215 yards peg. E. Massey, of Chelford was an excellent third. C. Berry began promisingly but eventually withdrew. Winners of heats :-Ist heat, 1, G. Boyden, Salford, 230; 2, H. Critchley, Bold, 290: 2nd heat, 1, T. Sherratt, Sankey, 45; 2 J. Dolman, Ashton-on-Ribble, 275 3rd heat, 1. A. Guildford, Man- chester, 245; 1 A. A. Howard, Sinkey, 225; 4th heat, 1, J. Houghton, Warrington, 240; 1 E. Massey. Chelford, 105; sth heat. 1, C. Berry, Warrington, 150; 2, R. Dutton, Rainford, 215. Prizes:-Ist., silver and cut glass table centre-piece; 2nd, salad bowl; 3rd, sardine dish.

div.head: TEIE PRIZES DISTRIBUTED.
div.p: TEIE PRIZES DISTRIBUTED.

At the close of the sports the su3cessful competitors received their awards at the hands of the Mayoress (Mrs. Bolton), who was cordially thanked on the proposition of the Chief Constable. Mr. Talbot remarked that the Mayoress had done them the honour of watching the sports for several hours—and that must have been a tedious duty for a lady to perform. He also expressed indebtedness to the Mayor,who had lent his kind patron- age, and said it was a good sign when they saw the chief magistrate of the town and his worthy consort patronizing the sports promoted by the police for the benefit of charities. He hoped they would be able to hand over to the institu- tions this year, more than ever they had done in the past. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Talbot concluded by thanking the officials and bands. He wanted the public to understand that the police were their friends and servants and not "bogy men. (Applause.) Alderman aUTCHINSON se3onded, and the motion was carried with cheers. The Ma.vou briefly responded.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Legh Street Primitive Methodist Church.

• At this church on Sunday, the Rev. L. Stowe, the newly-appointed minister, occupied the pulpit, morning and evening. The church had been re-decorated, and presented a beautiful appearance. Large congregations assembled,and at the evening service the choir rendered with effect." God so loved the world "(Stainer). Miss Woodland sang "I know that my Redeemer liveth." A reception tea was held on ..londay evening.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

Mr. B. Farrar (hon. secretary of the society) presided at the meeting held on Sunday. He spoke upon "Work and effort." He reviewed the work of the P.S.A. Society and urged the members to personal effort on its behalf, with the object of increasing the society's numbers and usefulness. Mr. C. Rose, of Droylesden, spoke upon the value of little things, basing his remarks on the text "How great a matter a little fire kindleth." There was a good attendance and the meeting was characterised with great earnestness, the singing being very hearty. Mr. A. Healey and Mr. H. Gray also took part in the meeting. Master Pearse presided at the organ.

div.head: Baptist Church, Golborne Street.
div.p: Baptist Church, Golborne Street.

The services on Sunday, last were taken by Mr. W. E. Jones of Warrington, whose evening sermon Was based on the text" Then Agrippa said unto Paul: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." (Acts 25.18). Agrippa's position was not a unique one; there were multitudes to-day who, like him, were convinced concerning the things of God, but not converted. Salvation was not a matter of mere intellect. Men were saved, not by believing in Christianity as a system, but by believing in Christ as a personal and divine Saviopr. 'Then there was the class of intellectually and morally convinced, but hesitating ones, and these the preacher urged to take the important step of accepting the Saviour. Others were kept out of the Kingdom on account of some special thing, and were by delaying, putting in jeopardy their soul's s tivation. In closing, the preacher urged all to make the decision and thus become, not "almost," but "altogether" Christians.

div.head: Choir Sermons at Hill Chile.
div.p: Choir Sermons at Hill Chile.

At Hill Cliffe Baptist Church on Sunday. the choir services were held, and large congregations assembled. In the morning the Rev. J. S. Hughes p reached upon "The music of life, or making music out of life's miseries," basing his remarks upon Psalm iii. In the afternoon there was a musical service, Mr. Hughes pre- siding, and an interesting programme ivas submitted. Mr. C. Whitehouse, Warrington, gave "Calvary," and Glory to Thee," very effectively, and Miss Bertha, Bouchier gave two solos on the violin in highly credit- able style. Mr. Levi Richardson sang" Come unto me," and " Where'er you walk," with feeling, while Miss Allen sang very sweetly," Children's Voices." • A duet was also given by the Misses Allen, entitled "0 Lovely Peace," and Miss Wilson sang "The Mission of the Rose" in a pleasing manner. The choir gave a good rendering of the anthem, "Therefore with Angels" (Novello). Mr. Huthes spoke on "The power of music in home life, church' worship and Christian work." Mr. J. M. Muir, A.R.C.0., directed the service throughout. In the evening the chapel was fall. The Pastor, the Rev.J. S. Hughes preached,and took for his theme" The New Song," mentioned in the Book of Revelation, explaining its mystic meaning, and the qualifications of those who would take part in it. Hetook occasion to. urge a greater spirit of unworldliness and other world- liness to guide and inspire and colour our present life The choir sang an anthem in good style. Mr. James Strange, jun., presided at the organ morning and evening.

div.head: New Organ at Stockton Heath.
div.p: A New Organ at Stockton Heath.

A handsome new organ presented to the Independent Methodist Church, Stockton Heath, by Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Mounthid, was dedicated at special services on Sunday by Mr.G.Hunter, (president of the Connexion) and Mr. J. Whitley. There were large congrega- tions. In the afternoon, Mr. Whitley give an address on "The organ, its origin and use in divine worship." The organ was, he said, the largest, most noble, and most harmonious instrument of all wind instruments in general use in church services. How much the organ had done in the improvement of divine service eternity alone would reveal, as it put additional strength and feeling into it. Music had held a very prominent place in religious worship since the creation of the world, and the organ which they opened that day, with its keys, its stops, and all other appliances, they now dedicated and set apart to the service of God and that church. He woqld not give much for the spiritual life of any church where there was no singing and music, which were among the chief delights of heaven. They might not receive much good from the lessons of the day, or from the sermons, but if they heartily joined in the true spirit of the singing they would always be benefited and blessed. _ _

_ The organ, which was built by Messrs. W. and E. Richardson,llalme, Manchester, and at which Mr. W. H. Payton, :Ans. Bac., presided, is a splendid instrumene, and was greatly admired by the congregation, who warmly appreciate Mr. and MN. Monnfield's generosity. Mr. W. Brayshaw conducted the choir, and the soloists were Mr. A. Griffiths, who rendered "If with all your hearts" and "My hope is in the everlasting ", Mr. E. Pownall, who gave "Sun of my soul"; and Miss Moun- field, who contributed " Abide with me." Tho col lee- Mons. which were in aid of the fund to wipe off the church debt, amounted to £2l.

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.

REV. W. C. J. NEVILLE'S FAREWELL SERMON.—On Sunday evening the Rev. W. C. J. Neville.preached his farewell sermon at Penketh Wesleyan Church to a good congregation. After the sermon, the Rev. John Gunnell and Mr. C. E. Parker wished Mr. Neville "God-speed" on behalf of the people of the Church. The service concluded with the singing of "God be with you till we meet again," and the Benediction. Tam ANNUAL FLOWER SHOW.—The annual show pro- moted by the Penketh and Sankey Cottage and Window .Gardening, and Cage Bird Society was held on Saturday list. The show was held in the SAM 3 field as last year. The entries were rather more nutne,•ous than usual, and a very creditable variety of frait. flowers, &Z.., was shown. Two largl tents, one for the Horticultural exhibits and the other for the cage birds, were erected, and the exhibits in each were set out to the best advan- tage. The show this year, was under new management, and the president, Dr. T. A. Murray addressed the numerous gathering, on matters partaininz to the ex- hibition. Outside attractions were Maypole dancing by the village children, items by the Warrington Male Voice Choir, and music by the Penkeith Tannery Prize Band which played for dancing until dusk. The fine weather brought a large crowd to •the field, and the show this year was one of the most successful that has been held,

div.head: INTERESTING EDUCATIONAL POINT.
div.p: INTERESTING EDUCATIONAL POINT.

A question has arisen in connection with the Cheshira Education Committee with regard to company owned schools. One of these was recently offered to the .county Council if it would accept its liabilities and assets. The Board of Education, however, decided that in future schools owned or connected by a company will only be eligible for recognition if the company fis wound up and its property vested in trustees or secondary educational purposes.

div.head: TWO SEPARATE PLATFORMS.
div.p: TWO SEPARATE PLATFORMS.
The Conservative Association and Public Debate.
"NO REASON FOR THE NEW DEPARTURE."
Mr. Howes Discusses the Political Situation.

When the political debate stood adjourned last Friday evening it was understood that it was to be continued by representatives of the two political parties on Thurs- day evening at Bridge Foot. It was found on Thursday evening, however, that the Tories had taken possession of the land on which the debate was to be continued,for the purpose of holding an open-air meetingin connection with the COnservative Labour party. Consequently the Liberals withdrew to a place near Arpley Station and there held a meeting. There was a very large attendance it being computed that there were between 2,000 and 3,000 present. Mr. Wilkinson Haigh presided, and he was accompanied on the lurry by Mr. Joseph Howes, Mr. J. Elwell, Mr. J. Willett and Mr. W. Nightingale. The CIIVRIIAN said he greatly regretted the turn of affairs. They were under the impression when they ad- journed the meeting on Friday evening that it stood ad- journed to carry on the debate between Mr. Howes and Mr. Fearnley. Somehow the Conservatives did not seem to understand the adjourned meeting or they would never have altered the position in the way they had done. He (the chairman) consulted Mr. Howes,and some of the leading men of theparty and it was thought advisable in the circumstances to withdraw themselves and hold a meeting of their own, although he (the chairman) would rather have faced the meeting and tested it whether it had to be an adjourned meeting or whether the Tories should rule the roost. (Hear, hear). The meeting he believed would have stuck to the ad journment and the meeting would have gone on. (Hear, hear). __

Mr. HOWES, who was heartily received;said his object had been to try and get this political question discussed thoroughly, intelligently and in a gentlemanly. manner. They did not want to stoop to anything mean or under- hand neither did they want to play tricks on the plat- form or to snatch a momentary victory. The ca,usethey represented would bear investigation,and if it was found not to be sound, the cause ought to go by default. He had been associated with public work for 25 years and he was prepared to meet in debate any representative man, if proper conditions could be laid down. There was nothing like political controversy because it enabled the people to get a lean of the true state of things and inlthese exciting times when we were rapidly approach- ing a general. election it was impossible Ifor people to know too much of the true Icondition of things politically. (Hear, hear.) The hon. secretary of the Liberal Association wrote a , letter to the Conservative Association asking them if they were prepared to put a speaker forward as their representative to meet an accredited representative of the Liberal party in this town to discuss, under proper conditions, the question of whether the present Govern- ment was worthy of the confidence of the people. I ' (Hear, hear.) The following replY was'received : Warrington Conservative Association, Sankey-street. 24th August, 1904. Charles Jackson Holmes, Esq-, hon. secretary of the Warrington Liberal Association. Dear S:r,—l have received your letter of the 22nd inst. I see no reason for adopting the new departure which.you suggest. When the time arrives in due course we shall be ready to discuss political questions in the usual way.—Yours truly, THOS. H. SUTTON, hon. secretary Warrington Con- servative Association. That means, continued Mr. Howes, that the Conserva- tive Association repudiate their representative over the way. (Hear, hear.) They refused to put them forward. If the Conservative Association would have nothing to to with them neither would the Liberals. (Hear, hear.) As representatives of an association they had a position so maintain. Any time that the Warrington Conserva- tive Association chose to put forth a representative man to properly and intelligently discuss under proper rules of debate the question of whether the Govern- ment was worthy of the confidence of the people, the Liberal Association would find a representa- tive to meet them. They need not go out of their way to say more than that. They did not want confusion or disturbance, but they wanted information and intelligent discussion of the great political questions of the day. There was -never a time more important when these great questions should be reasonably considered. He did not think it would be possible to find a man who would stand up in public and defend the present Government.(Hear,hear.)Mr. Howes proceeded to review the speeches made at Bridge Foot by the representa- tives of the Conservative Labour party. The chairman of the meeting (Councillor Wilson) told the audience that "English manufacturers found it utterly impossible to make and sell their goods at a profit in foreign markets." That was a peculiar statement to make in face of the fact that we were a great commercial country. We manufactured to , a greater extent than any other manufacturing country with thesame population. If we did not sell our goods I then we must be giving them away. (Laughter.) For Councillor Wilson to say that we could not sell them was to show that he had not sufficiently studied the question or he was making a statement that was not true. It was also stated that America was building more ships than we were. (Laughter.) What were the facts of the case? .Last year according to the Govern- ment Blue Book—produced by the Government as a re- ; suit of their enthuaiasm for protection.—this little i country beat all the world in shipbuilding. The total number of ships built by all the nations outside Eng- I land was less than the number built in this "tight little island" (Hear, hear.) Why were we able to do that? That brought him to the question of dumping. Some of the speakers at the Tory meeting were very severe on dumping. He would read them the I testimony of a trades union leader.—Mr. Cox (secretary of the Iron and Steel Workers' Association). Mr. Cox pointed out that the dumping of foreign steel and iron in this country had made it possible to keep some of our large works going, whereas they would have been closed if this dumping had not taken place. Mr. Cox stated that we had taken the German steel which had been dumped here and made it into ships and sold Germany the ships because their own shipbuilders could not compete with us. (Hear, hear). Owing to protec- tion in Germany,the price of material was so high, that on the testimony of the Blue Book the masters had to cut wages in order to compete with competitors. ZHear, hear). We did not want any cutting of wages in this country. (Hear. hear). It was better to work in the country where the dumped goods came than in the , country where the dumped goods were sent in a manufactured form. (Hear, hear). Dealing with the statement that every foreign country made us pay a tariff before admitting our goods, Mr. Howes said this was a protectionist fallacy. It was not the person who sold the goods that paid the tariff but the person who bought. (Hear, hear.) To speak of tariff reform was a misnomer. By reforpi, Liberals meant improvement—a going forward. By reform, the Tories meant retrogression—a going backward. (Hear, hear.) As Liberals they desired more Free Trade, but the Tories desired to restrict it. He was aware that.it, was popular to speak of striking back at the foreigner. but this policy of retaliation would strike a blow at our iron trade and other industries. It , would be a fatal mistake to keep out food coming from abroad until we had altered our land laws. (Hear, hear.) Under protec- tion the workers would give' the landlords a third of their income 'under the existing land laws. That was where the great conspiracy came in. What was the conspiracy? If protection were adopted in this country rents would 'increase', all round. If rents went up the purehasing power of the people would go down. (Hear, hear). It was said at the Tory meeting that a great many of our trades had been put out of existence because they could not live here, and that other trades 'employed fewer work- people than formerly. A document was published four days ago, giving statistics on this very point, and con- trasting the position of to-day with that of tetr‘years ago. From this paper it appeared that the bulk of our trade had been increasing all that time. There were one or two industries in which the total number of employed was less to-day than before. The point was that the number of people employed in the large industries in the country was much larger than it was ten years ago. (Hear, hear.) A larger'number of boys and women was employed as well as men. (Hear, hear.) When Pro- tectionists spoke of industries leaving the country, they always forgot to mention the large number which were introduced as a result of -our Free Trade policy. There vere many industries in this country which had been brought from pro- tected countries entirely owing to our free markets. Messrs. Wheeler and Wilson. and Messrs. Singer's were both sewing machine manufacturing firms which had come from protected countries and established themselves here.not for the purpose of trading with English people but for the purpose of trading with all the world through 'our open door. (Hear, hear.) Then there was the great Westinghouse firm which came from protected America and established itself in Trafford Park in order to take advantage of our Free Trade markets. That firm alone was employing 10,000 werkpeople. Tariffs were a hind- rance to trade. They placed the custom house officer between the purchaser and the buyer. Not only was delay caused in delivery owing to the examination of gools but the custem house official's salary had to be paid. (Hear, hear.) It was stated at the Tory meeting that food stiffs_and raw material would not be taxed: but. Mr. Chamberlain's whole scheme of preferential tariffs was based on a tax on food. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Balfour had said that the finished article was to be taxed. The finished article of one rninufacturer, con- tinued Mr. Howes. was but the raw material of another manufacturer. (Hear, hear.) The whole world was in a process of evolution and change. Ont-of one thing that existed to-day something else was bound to come forth to-morrow. If Mr. Balfour was only going to tax the finished article, there could be no tax, for it would be impossible to find the finished article. The steam- 'ships and steam engines of to-day were but scrap in a J rick sx-ar z woufr

short time and became the raw material of the manu- facturer. (Hear, hear.) The Liberal party represented the trade and industry and commerce of the nation, whereas the Tory party was representative of the land owning monopolists. It was quite true that the Liberal party when in office was not in power. Why? Because of the existence of the House of Lords. The Tory Labour party said it was satisfied with the House of Lords. (Laugh- ter.) By being satisfied with the House of Lords, the Tory Labour Party was opposed to Representative Government because you could not have Representative Government when one legislative chamber was not elected by the people. Representative Government could only be obtained when both Houses went out of existence at the same time and came into existence I again as the result of °, General Election. The question was asked, "Why had not the Liberals ended the Hormel of Lords"? They had been very near doing so once or twice, but unfortunately the Lords surrendered theirl point when the country was prepared to deal with them.' (Laughter.) Some day the Liberals would have to grapple- with the question again. At present they could not concentrate the attention of the people upon anyone question because tha Tory Government had brought forward so many retrograde measures. In to-day's papers they could see what was happening in South Africa. The Chinaman they were told,was onlyfgoing to work at the bottom of the mine.and white men occupy the positions of overseers. The Colonial Secretary had now discovered that the Chinaman was to be an overseer and he had also started trading. The people of South Africa were protest- ing against it and were threatening that they would separate themselves from Great Britain altogether and become a South African Republic unless we could sup- press the nuisance. And yet the people of this country were told that the South African people were in favour of the Chinese. There was a terrible reckoning on that question. (Hear, hear.) The Tory Labour party was supposed to be a trade union party,but there was only one question that need be put to the members on that point, and it was" As a trade unionist, do you think it is the duty of a Government to find cheap labour for any em- ployer at any time ? " (Cries of" No.") If the Govern- ment had a right to find cheap labour for employers in South Africa. they had a right to find it for employers in thit country. (A voice: They will do, if they have the chance). It was strange to find trade unionists de- fending a state of things like that. It was the greatest curse that could be inflicted on a nation. The yellow peril was a real peril. The very fact of getting the Chinese in the compounds, having their photographs taken andhanded over to the police, and taking impressions of their finger nails and finger tips, the very fact of one or two escaping and being re-captured and brought back, showed them—he was going to say the damnable state of slavery that existed In South Africa under the operation of the present Government. He spoke strongly, but the man who feeling strongly did not speak strongly was a traitor to his conscience. At the next election they might forget even the House of Lords or the land question. They would concentrate their attention, perhaps, on that one point of Chinese labour, and every workingman who was worthy of himself would avenge himself upon the Government that brought in the yellow man to push out the white man. They in Warrington had a good Radical candidate who before very long would be amongst them,—a man who took the entire Radical pro- gramme. On any of those points they would be prepared to meet their opponents and discuss with them. He believed that when the contest came, Warrington would do as other places had already done—that it would get in touch with reform and help to bring the Government to their knees and bring into office, to say the very least, a safer and sounder set of politicians. (Cheers.) The CHAIRMAN remarked that that was one of the finest open-air meetings that had ever taken place in Warrington. He believed there were not less than 2,000 or 3,000 people present. Mr. HOWES then intimated his willingness to answer any questions. . A MEMBER of the audience asked if it were not a fact that the Liberal party first introduced the principle of indentured labour in British Guiana and Trinidad?

Mr. HOWES replied that it was not the fact that the Liberal party first introduced the principle of inden- tured labour, but they did sanction indentured labour in the two places referred to. A large portion of the Liberal party opposed it at the time. but the indentured labour was nothing at ell like that of the Chinese in South Africa. First of all, the men who were indentured were brought into the country as free men of the country, and were allowed to enter into their indentures •apprentices did in this country. After their indentured period was over they could remain in the country, belome citizens, acquire the rights of citizenship, and the powel to own land. All that was prohibited in the case of the Chinese. There were no compounds in British Guiana and Trinidad. The wages the workers received they were at, liberty to spend where they liked and how they liked, and there was no police surveillance. No photographs were taken and no arrest was possible if they left work. Another question was "If we were to buy more food from the Colonies, would it really benefit the growers of this country ? " Mr. Howes's answer was: Of course not. He explained that if we bought less food from the Colonies it might benefit some growers in this country, because it would enable them to get a higher price for their goods from the people of this country. The people who bought would have to pay a higher price for their food than they did at the present time. The low price of things grown at home was kept down by the influx of goods from other lands. As there was no peasant proprietary in this countiy, increased Prices would not benefit the cultivators of land, but the landlords. Some countries sent us food stuffs cheaper than the colonies. Mr. Chamberlain proposed to tax the people who sent the goods cheap in order that the colonies might send us the goods dear. That was not the game our people should play at. Mr. NIGHTINGALE proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Howes for his address. He contrasted the state of things in this country with the conditions in America, Germany, and Russia. He said Liberals had been called little Englanders, but the real little Englanders were the people who were belittling them. The very men who were talking about dumping were the biggest users of the dumped article. The very men who were crying out loudest Ntere those who sent their capital abroad to establish mills to compete with British workingmen, and to grind them down. The idea in taxing food was to bring them on a level with the Chinamen who lived even upon dogs or rats, if need be, so that their masters might get a great profit at the least expense. They were compelled at such a crisis to take their stand for life or death, and to him the Tory Government meant death to all liberty. The so-called strongest Govern- ment of modern times had been so weak as to cringe to bloated millionaires. The white men wanted too much wages, se Chinese labour was introduced in South Africa. Mr. Chamberlain said he could not win his I fight without the workingmen. The Liberals could not 1 win without them, and he (Mr. Nightingale) asked his hearers if they were going to sell their birth-right. If they had the land free as it ought to be and could work it for the Use of humanity, they would have no poverty. (Applause.) - „ Mr. ELWELL seconded. He asked the audience to compaie their position with that of the workingmen of America which, he supposed, was one of the most pro- tected countries upon the globe. In America they were suffering from the effects of bad trade like we in Eng- land were. But what was the result? The ironmasters of America were not running their mills three or four days per week as would be done in this country. They were protected and had the privilege of combining and getting the whole of the iron or steel trade into their hands. Consequently when depression came, they closed down the mills they did not want. so as to run the other places at full spied. Men were thus thrown out of employment altogether Protection would bring into existence in England the great combines which were now seen in America. If Free Trade had been the evil that Mr. Chamberlain would have them believe, how was it that the country had prospered for so long, when we were working under disadvantages which no other country in the world was working under N In France and Germany thelroyalties were V; per cent, on the profits, and in Belgium 2 per cent. The royalties in this country were about ss. per ton on pig iron and steel. Another point was that the railway rates in Germany and Belgium were only one-third of wtheearhseienut.halcotountry. How had .tbocoutm oenal; hold our own under such conditions, if it was not thronghFree Trade? I If we had had the burden of a tariff as well as the heavy 1 railway rates and royalties, he was afraid we should ' have to have gone out of existence almost as an iron and steel producing nation. The speaker pointed out that many of the imports were absolutely necessary for lus to produce our iron and steel, and if there had been a tariff upon such imports the probability was that we would have been unable to make goods to export to foreign markets. 1 The vote was carried with enthusiasm. In respondinc• Mr.' HOWES gave his hearers the advice to "vote sober." If anyone wanted to treat them, let them de 'so after they had voted and not before. He concluded: Vote with a clear head and a warm heart, and we know what will be the result. (Applause.) 1 The Chairman having been thanked for presiding, the ; meeting concluded.

div.head: TORY MEETING.
div.p: THE TORY MEETING.
Fighting " The Demon of Free Trade."

Councillor WILSON presided at the meeting held at Bridge Foot under the auspices of the Conservative Labour party. There was a large attendance, and the Chairman in the course of his remarks spoke of fighting against "the demon of Free Trade." Mr. FERNLEY of Manchester said on Friday night Mr. Howes made a very lame effort to prove three things. First, he claimed to prove that the Tories were in a minority in 1867, although in office, and secondly that they could not carry the Reform Bill. Mr. Howes next stated that when the Tories introduced the Bill, they allowed their opponents to knock every clause away and nut fresh ones in. Mr. Howes, stated that, but he did not prove it nor did he produce any documentary evidence to prove it. All he

ens did was to produce a Radical historylnd quote some- thing which referred to a period sonre months prior to the Bill being introduced into Parliament and also from a book -.,hich was a rabidlßadical distinction of Disraeli's life. Moreover,Mr,Howes on,e;vpry extraordinary , statement, and that was that every one of the amend- ments of the Bill was introduced.by Mr. Gladstone himself, but he brought no evidence whatever to prove that assertion. Mr. Fearniey then proceeded to read various quotations from Cassell's history of England to show that only one amendment to the clauses of the Reform Bill of 1867 which referred to House- hold Suffrage was drawn up at a meeting at Mr. Gladstone's house, and owing to the defection of 48 Liberals who were in favour of Government proposal, it was defeated by 21 votes. This amendment, however, was not moved by Mr. Gladstone, but by one of his supporters, Mr. Coleridge. After it was defeated. Mr. Gladstone, in a declaration of policy, stated that h 3 fel& it useless to proceed personally with the other amendments standing in his name. The result was that Mr. Gladstone did not move a single amendment to the Bill. (Applause.) Moreover, in a celebrated cartoon published at the time by" Punch," Mr. Disraeli was given the position of honour as being- the leader who passed the Bill—not Mr. Gladstone.

Mr. 3'IA.CARTNEV of Manchester,addressed the meeting at some length on the fiscal question.He contended that anyone who was conversant with the history of England • would know that in respect of social legislation and measures devised for the purpose of improving the con- dition of labour, the Conservative party had practically a monopoly. Mr. W. L. WILTJA.MS moved a vote of thanks to the speakers, and contended that it was for the Liberals to prove that Mr. Fearnley was wrong, but they had not done so.

A VOICE: Slr. Howes wanted to come here and you would not let him. Mr. WILLIAMS, continuing his speech met with con- siderable interrnption and exclamations of "Rats." There was mach laughter when he expressed pleasure that Mr. Pierpoint would endeavour to induce Mr. Chamberlain to address a Warrington meeting. Mr. HANDS seconded, and the motion was put to the meeting and declared carried.
Mr. .FEIRNLEY responded and proceeded to reply to questions which had been handed lip in writing. The first was "Are you in favour of the taxation of food stuffs?" -

Mr. FEARNLEY replied that he was in favour of the rearrangement of the taxation of foodstuffs. This answer was greeted with groans and cries of "That is not the fiscal policy." "Answer yes or no." Mr. FEARNLEr then stated that he was in favour of the imposition of a tax upon corn coming here from the United States or from any other tariff-imposing country. He was in favour of corn stuffs coming in free from Canada, South Africa, Australia, India or Egypt, on con- dition that those coloaies gave us in return for that freedom an open market and encouragement in the shape of a preferential rate for our manufactured articles. He was also in favour of the tax being taken off tea, coffee, tobacco, dried fruit, cocoa and such articles as we now paid taxes on in what "these folks" 'called a Free Trade country. Another qiiestion was" Do you appreciate the agents who obtain Chinese labour?" 7 Mr. FEA.RNLEY replied that he; did not appreciate any such agents. He would, however, give a whole night to the Chinese labour question next week or the week after, and they would thrash it out thoroughly. The question which had previously been put to Mr. Howes as to whether it was a fact that the Ciberal party first introduced the principle of indentured labour in British Guiana and Trinidad was then asked. Mr. FEARNLFX : I will not deal with this to-night because it is on the Chinese labour matter. A VOICE: Answer the question. Mr. Fearnley : I will simply answer the question by saying yes. The Liberal party in 1895 introduced into British Guiana indentured, compounded, Coolie labour. (Cries of" not compounded.") The next finery was " How is it you did not meet Mr. Howes to-night as promised ?" Mr. FEARNLEY said he stated where• they were to meet, and he had been there that night. (Hear, hear.) In the second place if Mr. Howes had been kind enough to send him an invitation to go to the Liberal meeting he would have accepted it. A vote of thanks to the Chairman, which on being put to the audience had a mixed reception, concluded the meeting.

div.head: Liberal Association's Offer.
div.p: The Liberal Association's Offer.
The following is a copy of the letter sent to tha Secretary of the Conservative Asiociation:—

August 22nd The Hon. Sec., Warrington Conservative Association. Dear Sir,—l write to ask if your Association will be willing to name a Conservative Labour speaker to meet one of ours in a public debate to discuss the question "Is the present Government worthy of the support or confidence of the people ? " If you agree I should be pleased to suggest dates, and would propose that the meeting take place in the Parr Hall, the expense to be shared by the two Associations. Details to be arranged later.—Yours truly
C. JACKSON HOLIVES. (Hon. Sec., Warrington Liberal Association.)

div.head: GRAPPENHALL
div.p: GRAPPENHALL

THE CRICKET CUM.—The first eleven had as visitors the Hough Green Club and fell victims to them, thus recording the second defeat. Hough Green took first knock, and put together 49. As a rule a score like this is looked upon by the first as anything but fearfu', but on Saturday it proved too formidable for them. Hallam, for the winners, collected 16, Cole 9, and Linaker S runs. Warburton claimed 7 of the visitors' wickets for 17 runs. Grappenhalls response was very feeble—perhaps the holiday spirit is in some degree accountable—only 33 being recorded. Cor helped in no small measure towards this result, taking no less than? wickets. The second eleven also lost at Stretton by 23, Stretton scoring 67 to their opponents' 44.

WARRINGTON.
ENDING AUGUST 2kb, 1964.— Daring the week. the following births and' deaths were registered :—Warrington Registration District births, 47 ; deaths, 27. The excess of births over deaths- was 20.

The birth-rate was equal to 35.8. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 205 per 1,000, against 18.2 the average of the previous 4 weeks and against 193 the corresponding period of last year. The death-rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal t0'13•7 per 1,000, against 51 the average rate of the previous 4 weeks and against 6•9 the correspond- ing period of 1903. The an-es of mortality were 0-1 11-5 5-15 15-25 25-65 65—up. Total 11 G 3 4 3 27 _
The deaths included-3 from scarlet fever, /5 from diarrhoea, 1 from phthisis, 2 from accidents, C from all other causes.
The following cases of infectious disease have been reported during ete Wee:: :—Small-pox, 1 case, scarlet fever, 20 cases. Total number otpatients in hospital, week ending August 20th, 100. ___

METEOROLOGY.—The mean temperture Was 55 Fah. and therefore 3 deg. lower than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 67 F., was recorded on the 20th inst., and the minimum temperature 44 F., on the 17th inst.
The rainfall measured 118 inch. The general direction was W.N.W.

EARLESTOWN OCCASIONAL COURT.

He dropped one pair under the window and the other pair was found under his coat.—A remand until Thursday was granted. ,

In each place they were fighting with oneanother.—The I Chief Constable said they were "a gang of young I scuttlers." They/ were too friendly with each other to I fight in earnest, but pretended to do so in order to get respectable people around them and then rob them.— Defendants were each fined 10s. and costs.
