RAILWAY OFFICIALS AND DRUNKEN MEN.—Bernard Lyons last from Urmstcn, was charged with having I been drunk and disorderly on Bank Quay Station at 9.40 on Monday night.—The evidence of John Gordon, stationmaster, showed that prisoner was found drunk in a compartment. He had interfered with the passengers I and had in his possession an umbrella of which he could I give no satisfactory account—Mr. J. Rymer Young said he was glad to find the Railway Company taking notice of these drunken cases. His impression was that the . laxity of railway companies in this matter led up to cases like the present. He had himself seen drunken I men being assisted into the carriages by railway officials He was, therefore, glad the London and North-Western Railway Company were taking the present action against the prisoner.—The magistrates remanded prisoner until Friday. DRIVER ASSAULTED.—Joseph Daley, last from Chester, was charged with assaulting George Douth- waite, a cab driver in the employ of Mr. Edward Connor, living in King-street, on July 7th.—Complain- ant stated that at midnight prisoner came into the cab I yard and as he had no right there witness told him to leave.An altercation ensued,and prisoner struck witness in the eye with his fist.—Prisoner stated that he was drunk and complainant provoked him.—A fine of ss. and costs (El 45.) with the option of seven days' imprison- ment was imposed. FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillors Roberts and Thornton, Messrs. H. Roberts, Reynolds, Hepherd, Pilling and Jolley. THEFT OF BOOTS.—Thomas Carey, Dakin's Court, was charged with stealing or receiving knowing them to have been Stolen, a pair of boots value 4s. 11d, the property of Scales and Sons, Bridge Street. The Chief Constable said Mrs. Little, wife of the manager for Messrs. Scales, saw the boots hanging outside the shop door at eleven o'clock on Tuesday morning, August 4th. In the course of the evening she missed them. It ap- peared that during the afternoon prisoner went to Mr. Leslie's second-hand shop and offered for sale a pair of boots which he was wearing, stating that they hurt his feet.He added that he bought them from a shop inßridge street for 75. 6d. Mrs. Leslie bought them for 2s. 6d. and also gave prisoner a pair of old boots. The police were informed of the theft, and when the boots were shown to Mrs. Little she identified them as the stolen ones. Prisoner was arrested '.ty Superintendent Monaghan but said he had bought them irom a man he did not know for 3s. 4d.—Prisoner now stated that he purchased the boots for 35., but as they hurt, his feet he sold them.—This was his tenth appearance, and he was sentenced to two months' hard labour. Bstevrries.—James Arthur Emson, 49, Watkin-street, O was summoned for assaulting Mary Emson 49, Watkin- street, and was ordered to find a surety f£s to keep the peace for six months.—Mary Harris, 15, Pierpoint- street, was summoned at the instance of Amelia Howie, 25. Pierpoint-street, for making use of obscene language. A fine of 10s. was imposed.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr. J. Spruce presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. S. Woodward, T. Wright, J. B. Chadwick, A. H. Talbot, C. E. Linaker, C. E. Linaker, jun., J. Douglas, J. Whitley, J. T. Collier, A. G. Guest, G. Pilling, A. Broome, J. L. Jones, J. Stokes, J. W. Antwis, J. Bolshaw, H. Eyes, P. Mounfleld, H. M. Davies, J. H. Davies, J. Smith, H. Mawdsley, J. Fryer. W. Turner, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (deputy clerk), J. Cunnah (master), T. Cooke, T. Riley and W. R. de Prez (relieving officers).

div.head: PAITPERIS3,I AND ITS COST.
div.p: PAITPERIS3,I AND ITS COST.

A statement of pauperism and expenditure exclusive of common charges; lunatics in asylum and vagrants, prepared by Mr. Dansey,was submitted showing the cost per head on the number of paupers in the various unions in the district to be as follows:—Birkenhead,£7 14s. 5d.; Bucklow, £7 6s. 6d.; Chester, £9 3s. 4d.; Congleton, £6 9s. 4d. ; Macclesfield, £8 9s. lid.; Nantwich, £6 15s. 6d.; Northwich, £6,165. Bd.; Runcorn, £6 ss. 11d.; ockport, £7 10s. Bd.; Tarvin, £6 19s. id. ; Wirral, 27 ss. The Clerk pointed out that Runcorn Union had the lowest expenditure per head in the whole county. (Hear, hear.) Chester headed the list. In regard to the ave rage cost per head of the population, the amount for the Runcorn union was is. 3d. Chester was the highest with 2s. 7d. In several unions the average worked out lower than in Runcorn. Mr. Linaker said that Mr. Dansey gave the Chester Guardians a lecture on their extravagance at their last meeting. The extravagance was in one direction—that was out-relief. The cost of the out-relief in Chester Union was £4 Bs.4d.,per head whereas inNorthwich which had about the same rateable value and population the expenditure was only £2 13s. 4d. In Runcorn it was £2 us. A writer in a local journal had described him (Mr. Linaker) as a lecturer on economy. If there were more lecturers on economy and more people who would follow their advice on public bodies it would be a great deal better for the ratepayers. THE ACCOMMODATION QUESTION. Mr. Spruce moved that Messrs. W. and S. Owen, architects, Warrington be requested to report on the accommodation at the Workhouse. He said the matter had been fully gone into at a special committee meet- ing, and his motion would not commit the Board to any- thing except the architects report which would be submitted for consideration. The motion was carried and a committee consisting of Messrs. Fletcher, Spruce, Pilling, Morris, Baxter and Linaker was appointed to confer with Messrs. Owen. ' . SUPPLIES TO THE WORKHOUSE. The Clerk .was instructed to advertise for tenders for the usual supplies to the Workhouse during tLe ensuing half year.

THE WATER. MAIN EXTENSION. The Board accepted a scheme submitted by Mr. Walter Timmins for the further extension of the water mainat the Workhouse to be available in case of fire. The expenditure will be £33. FINANCIAL.

Mr. Woodward spbmitted the financial statement from which it appeared that the balance in hand at the last meeting was .£159 14s. Id. The total payments that day were £3864 9s. 6d., and the receipts during the fortnight £2846 lls. 11d., leaving an adverse balance of £159 14s. id. Twenty-three of the forty-one townships had not yet paid the call which was due on August 12th.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

A RUFFIAN WELL PUNISHED. James Quigley, 25, Naylor-street, was charged at the Borough Police Court on Monday, with having been drunk and disorderly in James-street, in the early hours of Sunday morning, and also with assa.ulting P.C. Frank Cooper.—The Chief Constable said Cooper was on duty on the day named, when he heard Quigley shouting to someone, but the constable could not sea who it was. He went up to Quigley and told him to be quiet, but he became abusive and threatened "what he would do" for Cooper. The officer was about to arrest the prisoner, when the latter commenced thumping him in the face and chest. A struggle then ensued and both fell to the ground. They were struggling for a considerable time until the constable managed to blow his whistle. P.C.'s Metcalf and Reynolds were near to and hearing the sound of the whistle they went to Ills assistance. The prisoner was mad drunk and when the handcuffs were put on him, he said it was a good job the other two officers had come, as he" intended to finish Cooper off this time."—P.C. Cooper bore out the Chief Constable's statement. During the struggle,he said,one of his arms was pushectthrough a window. His head also came in contact with the footpath, and his face, chest, head and' knees were seriously injured.—P.C. Metcalf said he went to the assistance of Cooper. who was rolling in -the gutter, Quigley having hold of him by the throat. When they got the prisoner up, he said he was Very glad they had come for he would have finished Cooper. He added that he would rather be in gaol in winter.— The Chief Constable observed that this was Quigley's 25th appearance. He would have a very bad end if he was not careful. He was a dangerous character and he always liked to pick a quarral with the police. He intended to do serious injury to Cooper.—The magis- trates sent him to gaol for six months. ALLEGED FURIOUS DRIVING.—A Boy's RECITATION. A carter named Michael Kenney, 34, Gee-street, was charged at the Borough Police Court on Monday, with furiously driving a horse attached to a lurry, to the danger of passengers in Haydock-street and Winwick- street on the 13th inst.—Mr. Steel represented the defendant.—James Fleming said he was driving a bread van for Mr. Stringer of Mersey-street in the vicinity of Haydock-street, when the defendant's horse and lurry dashed into his horse, which fell to the ground The defendant had lost control of his horse. Wit- ness's horse was knocked down and a shaft smashed. The defendant, who was driving furiously was ." laying on his horse."—A boy named Walter Stringer, who could just see over the ledge of the witness box, gave his evidence as though he were reciting a recitation at school. "At 2-15 on Saturday, August 13th, I was in Winwick-street," he cammenced, and proceeded to the end with his version of the story.—Mr. Steel: Vhere did you learn all this? Who taught you that? (Laughter.)—There was no answer.—Mr. Steel: Have you talked to anyone about the matter ?—Witness: No sir.—Mr. Steel: Who taught you to give your evidence by saying "At 2-15 on Saturday. August 13th? " and so on.—Witness: No one.—Mr. Steel: 'Where did you get that phrase from—" lost control of his horse?" Who taught you the recitation?—Witness: No one.— Further evidence was called in support of the complain- ant's case.—Sergeant Evans stated that the defendant denied having driven furiously and alleged that the complainant ran into him.—Mr. Steel, for the defence, said that the horse did not belong to Mr. Stringer, and it had to be returned to the owner. The object in bring- ing the prosecution was to get defendant convicted, if possible of furious driving, in order if at any time the owner Of the horse made a claim for compensation against Stringer he could say: "It was not my man who caused the accident, but the furious driving of Kenny." Kenny, continued Mr. Steel was a very respectable man, and had been in the employ of Messrs. W. and J. Richardson for about two years. The horse he drove was 15 or 16 years of age, and he contended that a coal horse was not capable of being furiously driven. If there had been no acci- dent there would have been no charge of furious dtiv- ing. So far as the collision with the bread van was concerned it was a pure accident. The defendant's 'explanation was that he was not driving furiously, but that he simply whipped up the horse to get across before Midland Railway Company's lurry passed. Unfor- tunately there was a misjudgment. In the circum- stances the case ought to be dismissed.—The defendant gave evidence bearing out Mr. Steel's statement.—The . Chief Constable: There seems to have been a mutual inclination to avoid a collision, but it seems to have been too late.—Peter Carey, Patrick Owen, and Samuel Burdett, manager for Messrs. W. and J. Richardson gave -evidence.— Ile magistrates retired to consider their decision' and after an absence of about ten minutes, returned, when the Mayor said the decision of the majority of the magistrates was that the case should be dismissed, but they thought the defendant ought to be more careful in driving round corners. LIVELY SCENE IN A RAILWAY COMPARTMENT— PASSENGER ROBBED OF HIS UMBRELLA AND ASSAULTED. Bernard Lyons, who has only recently come into this district, was charged at the Borough Police Court yesterday, with having been drunk and disorderly on Bank Quay Station at 9.40 on Monday night; also with stealing an umbrella value 25., the property of Edward Grooms, of Earlestown, and with assaulting Grooms— Mr. W. J. Bland, solicitor, prosecuted on behalf of the London and North Western Railway Company, and stated that at 9.15 on Monday evening Grooms joined a train to Earlestown. He had not been in the compart- ment very long when prisoner entered and behaved in a very disorderly and disgraceful way. Grooms wanted to leive the carriage when prisoner struck him a very violent blow on the nose, causing it to bleed. He then picked up Grooms' umbrella and leaving the compart- ment by the off-side door, walked along the railway. He was handed over to P.S. Barnett who took him to the lock-up. There was no doubt these cases were in- creasing and the travelling public were suffering trouble ,and inconvenience. He asked the Bench to make an ,example of the prisoner.—The magistrates fined prisoner who made his first appearance, 20s. and costs with the option of a month's imprisonment. 'TIRED OF MARRIED LIFE"AFTER FIVE MONTII3.—A SAD STORY. After five months' married life, William James Legg, 22, Clifton-street, appeared before the Mayor and other magistrates at the Warrington Police Court yesterday charged with persistent cruelty to his wife, Mary ,Ann Legg, 3, rove-street.—Mr. Steel appeared for the complainsi t, and said the parties were young and had only been !tarried five months. Defendant seemed, to, be of a very jealous frame of mind, and kept alleging that his wife was in love with certain men employed at the Cable Works. He had from time to time assaulted her. Very shortly after they were married he threw her out of bed one night, and she was compelled to sleep on a hearthrug in the room. On two occasions he had turned her out of the house and thrashed her,and she only returned on his promising he would not touch her again. Another time defendant threw his wife on a sofa, thumped her in the face, twisted her wrists, and otherwise assaulted her. GREATER THAN SHAKESPEARE.

A. YOUNG Hindoo, fresh from the examina- tion-room, was talking the other day to an Vnglish gentleman, an educational authority, who used to assist such students in India as he thought promising. Being asked if he intended to continue his studies, he answered in the negative, saying that though some might consider his decision foolish, he had more important work on hand. _ _

"Indeed; what is that ?" queried the Englishman. "Sir, you can assist me," was the reply; "I am writing an epic poem, and I wish to ask you to help me in publishing it." The other coughed to hide emotion, and then proceeded to "give auditor sense." He pointed out that in these busy days people have little leisure to read long poems, especially epics and instanced some late ventures that had fallen flat on the world.

" Yes ; but if the poem is really good ?" This from a lad who could hardly speak six consecutive words of idiomatic English, and whose peculiarities of speech could not be reproduced, was nearly too much for the Englishman. Wishing to clinch the matter, he said: _ _ _

"Well, good as your poem doubtless would be, remember that even Milton is slarcely read nowadays except by students, and epic- writers of less note not at all." "Sir," was the reply given in perfect good faith. "I have read the Milton and the Shakespeare with care, and have avoided the errors of both."

PENALTIES OF ARTIFICIAL CHARMS. • WHAT LADIES WILL SUFFER FOR BFAUTY. "THERE is no limit to the suffering a woman will voluntarily undergo in order to improve her good looks. The tortures of the Inquisi- tion are cheerfully sought by not a few ladies in society, provided such infliction encts the heightening of their attractions. The gentleman who made this startling statement 'was himself a specialist well qualified to speak upon the subiect. Further particul.rs were promptly asked for. "Teeth," he contieued. "are the most frequent rack upon which the fair one suffers. Any amount of pain is well warranted by the great benefit to the system derived from haying bad teeth put in order. But many women have teeth put in by methods the result of which is pleasing to the eye, 'out of no benefit whateyer to the digestive organs. A lady patient whom I recently attended lived, I found, solely on liquid nourishment. I asked the reason of this when good solid food had been prescribed. "' My teeth, she said. But you had as many as twelve put in at one tree I per. , sisted '\es: but I cannot use them,' came the unexppctel reply. "For the mere reason that they looked -- well, she had had the teeth fixed in a manner that rendered them useless for all prac- tical purposes. "A swelling of the veins of the arms in another society ornament greatly plit.led her medical attendant. She had to wear el ,stic bandages to remedy the evil. At last the cause of the trouble was revealed. The lady took great pride in the white ess of her bands I 'ming the season,' on retiring to rest. she slung her wrists up in two slings fixed to the curtain suspended above her head, in order to keep the blood out of her palms and fingers. "Of the agonies of waist compression everyone has read. All sorts of p -inful expedients are employed for the purpose, from steel bands to crocodile-hide waist-belts. One lady wore, for as long as she could every day, aleatber corset several inches too small. which could only be forcibly fastened' round her when she Was hanging from a bar fixed in her dressing room. "Would you believe that a young woman would mak:, a, incision at the outside corners of her eyes in order to make them larger It is quite a common practice with parents in foreign countries where daughters, if beauti- ful, can be sold for substantial sums. .And it has been done over here by women them- selves. "Though not exactly painful. various devices for altering the features are worn with not a little inconvenience. There is quite an important trade done in nose - machines, cheek and lip plumpers, ear caps and so on. One lady permanently injured her nose by an attempt with a home made appliance to alter the form of her nostrils. "Another of pallid complexion caused a painful swelling on her cheek-bone by con- stantly pinching the flesh there in order to create a little colour. A dame of high de- gree forces her feet into such tight shoes that directly she is in her carriage, driving to or from a friend's house, she is obliged to take them off for a short respite from paln. This was discovered when, on the occasion of het hroneham being run into by a railway-van. in her fright she leapt into the roadway in - her stockings. " Arsen;e and chalk eating; putting bella- donna in the eyes ; removing superfluous hairs by plucking them out and stabbing poison into the roots • dimple-making; sew- ing in artificial eyebrows and lashes; back straightening an figure promoting—all these supply additional tortures that ale nevertheless eagerly seized upon provided they, in even the remotest degree, add to the sufierer's good looks "Of the harm that is done one very seldom hears; but occasionally on my rounds 1 en- counter—if I chance to catch her by day- light—some gaunt, worn, faded, human butterfly, prematurely aged and wrinkled, whom I know to be a victim of this senseless , tampering with Nature."

A CELEBRATED writer, being caught in a shower, took shelter under a portico. A very pretty girl soon lifted the window, and after looking at him attentively for a moment, sent out a servant to him with an umbrella. The next day the delighted author got him- self up in his most fascinating style, and, as the umbrella was an old one, he laid it aside as a souvenir, purchased a new one of the costliest taste, and called on the lady to return the loan. She received the new umbrella, evidently without remarking the 'change and, after listening with curious gravity to the rather pressing tenderness of the acknowledgments, she suddenly comprehended that he was enamoured of her, and forthwith naively explained that, as he had stood in the way of a gentleman who wished to come and see her unobserved, she had sent him the umbrella to get him off the front steps!

IN a small village in Worcestershire there lives a farmer who is famous for making the best cider in the neighbourhood, and is equally famous for keeping it ; and as yet no person but himself and family has ever been permitted to taste it. At last one of his near neighbours said he was determined to taste it. Accordingly, he went to the farmer's house and entered into conversation with him concerning his crops, ctc., and by degrees led him to speak of his cider. He then said— "l understand you make very good cider ?" "Yes," replied the farmer. William, my boy, go bring a mugful." William soon returned with a mug brim- ming full, and handed it to the farmer, who drained it to the bottom at one draught. REFERENCE BY THE REV. JOHN YONGE. Preaching in Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday morning, the Rev. John Yonge made allusion to the visit of General Booth. Some of them, he said, were privileged on the previous day to see and hear that remarkable man who was at the head of the most remarkable religious movement of modern days. The spectacle struck him as infinitely pathetic and equally inspiring. It was the spectacle of a man who 39 years ago struck out a line of Christian service for himself, and who began and pursued it for years amid opposition, suspicion, obloquy, and even persecu- tion. But he had been sustained in it as no fanaticism or obstinacy could have sustained him. He had made his saving and uplifting mark upon hundreds and thousands of people throughout the world. Still he pursued his course, even amid the infirmities of advanced age, and despite all the heavy sorrows that ! had fallen upon his home and heart. He had outlived: opposition; he had conquered prejudice. He had won ; the favoui of all ranks from the poorest and the worst to the best and richest and highest. And he spoke to them at Warrington yesterday morning in all the un- affected simplicity of a rejoicing servant of Christ. ,How came it ? There could be only one explanation. He had believed and still believed with deeper faith than lever that God had been and ever would be with him. And so, amid an unresting career, he dwelt in inward peace and spiritual rest.

div.p: THE WORKMAN'S TOBACCO.
Effect oflthe Chancellor's "Amateur Finance."

Sir John Willox, M.P., presiding at the annual meet- ing this week of Messrs. Cope, Brothers, and Co., Limited, tobacco manufacturers, Liverpool, complained of the gratuitous and indiscreet meddling of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. "For many years past," • he said" Chancellors of the Exchequer had made tobacco 1 duties the plaything of their amateur finance, and there I had been a wide variety of changes which had worked I nothing but harm to the trade and injury to the revenue. I "The practical result of Mr. Austen Chamberlain's ; of experiment would probably be that the new lineitishworking man would find more wood and water lin his tobacco, and the British exchequer less money ' in the Imperial till." i

div.head: CHARMING HILLS AND VALLEYS
div.p: THE CHARMING HILLS AND VALLEYS

In one of the motor papers, attention is called to the exceedingly lax manner in which the final examination of anengine seems to be made before it is dispatched from the factory. The indictment is, unfortunately, only too true ; and worse still is the fact that adjust- ments which should be made at the works frequently cannot be done by the purchaser because the very spanners included in the tool equipment fit none of the nuts they are supposed to move. Both with a cycle and also with a car, it should be proved that the motor not only runs, but runs well, befOre it is despatched. Even when it is sent out properly adjusted, the pur- chaser will be wise to go over all the nuts and bolts after the first one hundred miles have been covered, for by that time they will usually have worked a little loose. But he does not expect to do this before running the engine at all, and a little care and management at the works would remove the necessity. And if he should be compelled to do it it is sarely not too much to expect that the spanners supplied will be of some assist- ance to him.

One of those indignant individuals, who add con- siderably to the gaiety of nations by the publica- tion of various schemes for the suppression and ulti- mate extermination of motorists, has just written to a daily paper to explain that the recent Act is a great mistake. Here we ale inaccordance with him although it is possible that, paradoxical as it may seem, we agree upon a point whereon we differ. In other words, we all think the Act an egregrious mistake, but from opposite points of view. But this is by the way. The corres- pondent goes on to show us what Parliament really should have done. The correct move, says this luminary, would have been to have enacted it a penal offence for any maker to construct a motor vehicle which could by any means travel more than fourteen miles an hour, down hill, and can be guaranteed to climb any ascent with a gradient of more than one in forty. Otherwise its virtues are painfully reminiscent of the recently advertised bazaar car: Can be driven down any bill. Can be pushed up any gradient. Three speeds and several reverses."

A useful tip in connection with tyre repairing is given by the motor contributor to the "Newcastle Chronicle." He says that, when it is necessary to remove an old patch from an inner tube, he finds that,instead of follow- ing the time-honoured plan of applying benzine, it is better to heat an ordinary flat iron in boiling water and then to apoly it to the patch which is to be removed. The heat of the iron so loosens the patch that it can easily be pulled off with the fingers without incurring any risk of tearing the tube.

The recent case heard at Greenwich, in which a pro- I fessional driver was summoned on three distinct charges under the Motor Car Act, draws attention once more to the general disposition on the part of the paid chauffeur to disregard one of the most important fitments in con- nection with a car. If a manufacturer's employee were not so ready to take out cars upon which the brakes are either badly fitted or are sometimes even taken off entirely for the purpose of repair, there would be fewer accidents, arising, as we are told, through the failure of the brakes. The most sanguine person living cannot expect the depression of the foot pedal to do much towards retarding the pace of the machine when the brake itself is in the workshop miles away, for, more often than not, it is the actual absence and not the failure of the brakes, which leads to disaster. Of course, if this were to be known, the driver would be liable to a fine of £2O for taking out a motor car upon which two independent brakes are not fitted.

We have, before now, drawn attention to the fact that the side brake is intended for and should only be used in an emergency. It is, therefore, all the more necessary that, when that emergency arises, no trouble whatever is experienced in grasping the lever and push- ing it backwards or forwards according to its action. Yet on how many cars is this overlooked, and the brake lever placed outside that controlling the speeds, although handling the latter need never be done in any hurry or under pressure.

div.head: THREE 'MONTHS FOR WIFE DESERTION.
div.p: THREE 'MONTHS FOR WIFE DESERTION.

lAt the Newton-le-Willows Police Court, on Thursday, James Wild, a collier, was charged with having deserted his wife and five children at Golborne three years ago, leaving them chargeablo to the Leigh Union for ten weeks, at a cost of £lo.—Mr. J. W. Unsworth, Kreliev- ing officer, stated that prisoner was apprehended at Durham, and had refused to support his family. He asked that prisoner should be made an example of and sent to gaol.—The bench committed prisoner for three months with hard labour.—Wild was further charged by his wife with having failed to comply with a mainten- ance order made in October, 1901, which carried with it alimony to the extent of 20s. a week. Mrs. Wild stated that her husband owed her £159, and had not paid a Ipenny towards reducing it.—On prisoner promising to pay his wife 108. per week regularly, the order was amended.

div.p: UNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. I THE FREE CHURCHES.

This Council held its fortnightly meeting at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr. S. Woodward presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. G. Piling (vice- chairman), J. Stokes, A. H. Talbot, T. Wright, J. B. Chadwick, C. E. Linaker, C. E. Linaker jun...l. Whitley, a. T. Collier, A. G. Guest, A. Broome, J. L. Jones, T. Antwis, J. Bolshaw, H. Eyes, P. Mounfield, H. M. Davies, J. H. Davies, J. Smith, H. Mawdsley, J. Fryer, W. Turner, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (deputy Clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer of health),J. Swinton and IV. Diggle (surveyors), andJ. Farrington (inspector 01 nuisances.)
N-VESTON MORTUARY QUESTION.

NIT.. J. Evans, agent at Runcorn for the Manchester Ship Canal Company, wrote stating that he had sub- mitted the Council's letter with regard to the provision Of a mortuary at Weston Point to his head office and ilad received a reply to the effect that the company intended to recommence using the building suggested for the purpose, in connection with the carrying trade and that it would not therefore beavailable for renting. The matter was referred to the Weston Parochial Committee.
ANTROBES WATER S PLY..

_ Messrs. Eaton, Son and Williamson, solicitors to Mr. Gerald Eaton, wrote as follows with regard to the i taking over by the Council of a pump in Pole-lane End, Antrobus: Before giving consent to the terms named: i.n your letter Mr. Eaton must be satisfied (1) that there ! la a sufficient quantity of water for his tenants first and the public afterwards (2) that he is put to no expense in the alteration (3) that the Council be responsible in the future for the maintenance and up-keep of the well , Said pump (4) that Jue provision is made when the alteration is effected that the road sweepings do not get into the well as they did before the removal of the Pump (5) that a proper agreement is entered into to be approved of by us on his behalf and that a plan of the I land proposed to be taken is approved of by us (6) that Our costs are paid by the Council. -1 Mr. Bolshaw thought Mr. Eaton ought to be satisfied without costs. Mr. Farrington said he doubted whether sufficient Water could be obtained at the well to supply both the tenants and the public. Before any agreement was entered into, he suggested that the well should be examined.

Mr. Bolshaw said the well had supplied all require- ments for years before the present" squabble"occurred. The Chairman said the well was a public one, and he considered Mr. Eaton's tenants had no greater claim uPon the water than the public. The vital question Was whether the water was worth getting. It was decided that Mr. Farrington should obtain details as to the water available. RESIGNATION AND REQUEST TO RECONSIDER. -Arr. W. Fletcher wrote tendering his resignation as a. Member of the Council as with present business engage- ments he could not attend the meetings regularly. On the motion of Mr. Linaker, seconded by Mr. Antwis, the Clerk was instructed to write expressing the Board's regret at the resignation,and requesting Mr. tletcher to reconsider his decision.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT,
div.p: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT,

Dr. Adams reported that two cases of diphtheria had ; Occurred at Weston Point, the disease having evidently I been imported from Runcorn. Measles had become • epidemic at Dutton, and he recommended that the w achools be closed for three weeks. The Council approved the recommendation. S IJG GESTED FRODSTIAM IMPROVEM ENTf

FheConncil then considered the suggested improve- I Merit in Church-street, Frodsham. The clerk pointed out that Mr. H. M., Davies had offered to cart away all , surplus soil and to pay £lO towards the improvement.l and the Frodsham Parochial Committee strongly mom, Mended the acceptance of the offer. The Council, how- ever, thought that Mr. Davies should contribute £2O. The Surveyor's estimate of the expense was .£57 17s. exclusive of carting away the surplus soil which it was estimated would entail an additional cost of .£4 Os. to £4los. _ _ _ _ _
A depatation consisting of Messrs. Samuel Davies, Percy Jones and \V. Shaw, waited upon the Council on behalf of the Parochial Committee to urge the accept- ance of Mr. H. M. Davies's offer of £lO.

_ It was argued that if the improvement was not made now, the work would have to be done eventually and Probably at a much larger cost. A member of the deputation contended that the Surveyor's estimate was too high. The Chairmlln pointed out that they could not charge the improvement on the locality alone. The whole tiis- I trict would have to contribute. Seeing there was a Strong feeling in Frodsham that the work should be done, he thought the position of the parish with refer- ence to similar places in the district might be considered, aS to whether the Council had expended as much money according to the rateable value and circumstances of the locality as they had spent in other places. Mr. Collier said Frodsham was growing and a great number of excursionists visited the village at holiday times. If the street could be widened, it wouldlbe benefit to the public all round. He understood that if Prodsham people were allowed to contribute directly, they would be pleased to do so rather than forego the improvement. He proposed that Mr. Davies's offer be accepted. Mr. .1. H. Davies seconded.

It wss ascertained that rile total assessable value of Prodsham was £12,349, and the amount expended on highway work during the past three years was £756 S. 9d„ ior equal to 3d. n the 2 per annum. Gd., or nearly 7d. in the g. _ .

, We. Choi rmrzn remarked that on those figures Frodsham atood in the position of having something due to her. The Clerk pointed out that Nit.. Collier's proposition could not he adopted without notice of motion. Mr. Collier gave notice that he would move the resolu- tion at the next meel ing. The Surveyor was instructed to obtain tenders for the tarrying out of the work.
THE NEW HOSPITAL. The Chairman reported that the Isolation Hospital Committee visited the site that day, and they had every reason to believe that the work was going on satisfac- torily.

HELSBY WATER SUPPLY. On the recommendation of the Helsby Sewerage and Water Committee it was resolved that the minutes of the 18th July with regard to the supply of water to the Cable Company's works be referred back to Helsby Parochial Committee for re-consideration with the sug- pstion that in the opinion of the District Council the Helsby water supply should be an independent one and 'under the entire control of the ratepayers..

div.head: UNLABELLED MARGARINE CHEESE.
div.p: UNLABELLED MARGARINE CHEESE.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday before the Mayor (Alderman Bolton) and other magis- trates, Margaret Ann :NlcKeon, a provision dealer, carrying on business at 18, Lovely-lane, and until recently at 30. Fennel-street, was charged under the Sale of Foods Act of 1899 with having exposed for sale a Piece of margarine cheese without branding and label- ling it as required, and also with neglecting to wrap it, in a piece of paper labelled " Margarine Cheese."—Mr.- Wilson (deputy town clerk) prosecuted, and stated that on Wednesday, July 13th, Inspector Flood went to the defendant's premises at Fennel-street and there saw in the window a piece of cheese marked Id. a pound. He asked to be supplied with half-a-pound of cheese. The young lady assistant on taking it out of the window Mid "It is margarine cheese." The Inspector asked where the label was and she commenced to search for it but did not succeed in finding it. She supplied the inspector with half a pound of the cheese and it had been analysed by Mr. Rnddock who certified that it,con- tained' ten pen cent. of milk fat and 90 per cent. of fat derived from sources other than milk. Provision dealers and others anxious to carry out the provisions of the net were at a disadvantage when people unfairly competed with them in this way. It was a frand'on the public to sell margarine cheese for cheese.—lnspector Flood gave evidence bearing out Mr. Wilson's statement. —Cross-examined by Mr. Browne, who represented the defendant, witness said there was nd intention to defraud, except that the cheese was exposed without a label.—Mr. Browne said the defendant had two shops— one she mt,naged herself at Lovely-lane and a branch shop in •Found-street. The branch shop did not pay 41's well as she anticipated and she sold the business to Mr. Clayton. Mr. Clayton could not take over the business at once. but he paid a deposit, and out of pure kindness; Mrs. McKeon allowed her sister to remain at the shop until Mr. Clayton obtained possession. Having sold the business, the defendant did not go down to the shop and see the cheese. There was no intention to defraud. 'rhe question arose whether she could be held legally respon.ible. She had sold the business and was not deriving any profit from the business, but merely allowing her sister to keep it going until Mr. Clayton took possession. He was prepared, however, to waive any objection on the ground he had stated. The defen- lant had committed a purely technical offence, and he would ask the magistrates to dismiss the case on pay- ment of cote.—The magistrates under the circumstances acted on the suggestion and dismissed the case on pay- ment of thp costs 9s.

div.head: NEW FREE CHURCH DEVELOPMENTS.
div.p: NEW FREE CHURCH DEVELOPMENTS.

Although the past month is supposed to be a slack time in the religious world, there are many features of interest to chronicle. Notably there are new developments in connection with National Free Church Council work which are being quietly matured at the Memorial Hall, London. Two important schemes likely to have far-reaching effects on the Free Churches of the nation are in course of formation, and will be launched in the near future. The first of these is a scheme for social service on a national scale. It is felt that social work instead of being a spasmodic and local affair should be taken up in an organised way, and a special Committee has been appointed by the National Council to direct and control the work. Dr. Paton has put in pamphlet form a number of suggestions pre- pared by the Committee and these will be sent to the 800 Councils affiliated with the National organisation. The suggestions cover many sides of social service. One proposal is that all prisoners, at the expiration of their sentences, should be met by a deputation of Christian workers and brought into touch with the Churches. It is also urged that special arrangements should be made for Christian workers to visit workhouses, and other public institutions for the purpose of holding religious meetings, 61-,c. Special work in garrison towns amongst soldiers, weekly gatherings of crippled children, concerted at i organised action for the suppression of impurity, the organisation of institutes in connection with the Churches for keeping in touch with young people after leaving the Sunday School, and the circulation of suitable literature on Christian social topics, are some of the important suggestions for united action by the Councils.

div.head: WORK FOR YOUNG MEN.
div.p: WORK FOR YOUNG MEN.

Another scheme which is in preparation by the National Free Church Council is of quite different a character. This is an age for young men, and they are more and more ''taking part in the social and political affairs of the nation. It is thought that they should take an even greater share in the work of the Free Churches, now that we live in such critical times. The National Free Church Council proposes to enlarge its borders and form Young Men's Branches. The work of Free Church Councils has greatly enlargt d of recent years, and it is felt that Free Church workers should have some assistance in their many undertakings. The Young Men's Branch is to be formed as a sort of reserve force for the Councils, to assist in Parochial Visitaticn, United Missions, Village Work, Electoral Work, &c. Thus far it concerns the Councils. To the young men themselves the idea presents a splendid scope for service. They are first to be trained with a thorough ground-work of Free Church Princi- ples and History, and aro to be assisted by speakers' classes, reading circles, and other aids. The National Council's Circulating Library, which pow includes many thousands of the best books, and which is being thoroughly re- vised, is to be adopted for the use of these Branches. Undoubtedly there are great possi- bilities in the work, and it is anticipated that in a short time these Young Men's Branches or Leagues will be in full swing in connection with many of the Free Church Councils. Full information as to their formation can be ob- tained of the Rev. Thomas Law, Memorial Hall, E.C.

div.head: DR. MACLAREN AND PREACHING.
div.p: DR. MACLAREN AND PREACHING.

A writer in the Free Church Chronicle says that according to latest information Dr. Maclaren is keeping well in health and spirits, but he is becoming more and more afraid of a return to pulpit work. If the doctor could speak to a normal congregation he might often appear; but his great reputation makes every appearance now a special occasion, and the call to a corresponding effort, which always comes to a great preacher from a great expectant congregation, is too strong for the doctor to resist. To preach in his old pulpit to his old congregation is an irresistible temptation to an emotional and intellectual effort which is now beyond his strength. So the prudent old doctor refrains.
RELIGIOUS CONVENTIONS.

Summer gatherings of Christian workers are coming more and more into vogue. Last month a very successful convention was held at Hexham in connection with the Durham and Northum- berland Federation. At the time of writing great interest is being shown in two conventions at Scarborough and Blackpool respectively from August ‘._)9th to September Ist. Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., President of the National Council, is presiding at each of these, and a diverse programme of meetings has been arranged, including a Sunrise Prayer, Meeting and other new features.
GIPSY SMITH AND SOUTH AFRICA.

Continuing his" Gospel Experiences in South Africa," Gipsy Smith gives in this month's Free Church C'hronicle an account of his work at Bloemfontein. "About six hundred," he says, "passed through the inquiry-rooms, Pearly three hundred I.ledges were taken on ihe Satur- day night; and this is not all. The b ssin,r realised by those who have been separated by the war, who are together again in fellowship, is to know that God is indeed amongst the children of men. Remember this: all took place close to the new-made graves of shout three thousand men who died by wounds or fever, or were killed in those terrible days of bloodshed which have so recently passed over this sad and devastated country." Gipsy Smith has since conducted missions at Johannesburg and Pretoria. At both places huge preparations were made for the visit. including the erection of special buildings. and the results have been extraordinary. This eminent missioner of the National Free Church Council is due to leave South Africa on September 21st, arriving in England on October Bth. Et is expected that a great Welcome Home will be arranged for him soon after his arrival.
PROGRESS OF FREE CHURCH FEDERATION.

An account of the National Free Church Council movement appears in this month's Free Chitrehman, and gives some interesting views of the work and workers at the Memorial Hall. London. It is difficult to realise to what extent the movement has grown in the short time in which it has been in existence. "Great as the work already is," says the Rev. Thomas Law to the writer of the article in question. "there is every indication that it will develop i all alor g the line in the near future. More mission rs have been employed, and there is likely t 4 be a large increase in evangelical work. I am more and more convineed of the vast possibilities of the National Free Church Council Movement."

div.head: PRINCIPAL RAINY DELINEATED.
div.p: PRINCIPAL RAINY DELINEATED.

In . Scotland, at least, the House of Lords decision in the United Free Church case has made Principal Rainy the man of the hour. A writer in the Free Church Chronicle gives an interesting character-sketch of this remarkable leader. " His genius as a master of Assemblies is unrivalled. His power of divining the feeling of an excited, tumultuous gathering of ecclesiastics, and of giving it expression, amounts to perfect instinct. He is never hitter, never discourteous to an opponent, though his speeches are occssionally .marked by some gentle, excellent irony. Th6re is little doubt that now that this crisis has come upon his Church, Dr. Rainy will rise to the occasion, and will be as conspicuous in the hour of trial as he was in the time of success."

div.head: TRAGIC WEEK-END AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: TRAGIC WEEK-END AT ST. HELENS.
BODY EXHUMED: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.
Fatal Midnight Fracas. POLICE PROCEEDINGS AND INQUESTS OPENED.

St. Helens has th's week been the scene of sensational developments in connection with two mysterious deaths —that of a girl named Jones, 14 years of age, whose body was exhumed on Saturday night, after a fortnight's burial, and the other the case of a man named Duffy, who was found dead on some waste land in Warrington road early on Sunday morning. Years have elapsed since such general interest in tragic occurrences was aroused as that which was manifested on Monday, and notwithstanding a continuous heavy downpour of rain,a crowd of some hundreds of people gathered in the square near the Town Hall and police office, where it was known the county coroner (Mr. S. Brighouse) was conducting inquiries into the two cases,,,vhile the police authorities had instituted proceedings against a man named Hackett for causing the death of the man Duffy, and a woman named Burikdred, at whose house the girl Jones, whose body had been exhumed, had lived for some years, had been arrested on a charge of attempting to commit suicide.

div.head: EXHUMATION OF A BODY.
div.p: THE EXHUMATION OF A BODY.
CORONER'S STATEMENT.

The county coroner (Mr. S. Brighouse) on Monday morning opened an inquest, at the Town Hall, on the body of Sarah Ann Jones, 14 years of age, who died on the 7th inst., and whose remains, interred at St. Helens Cemetery on the 11th inst., were exhumed on Saturday night. Chief-Constable Wood was in attendance, and a jury of 16 gentlemen was sworn, Mr. Thomas Shaw being the foreman.

The Coroner, addressing the jury, said :—Before we proceed to the mortuary to view this body perhaps it is now the right time to explain to you shortly what has been done in this matter. This Sarah Ann Jones was aged 13 years; she was born on the 17th August, 1890. She was the child of Edward Jones, of 97, Clock Face-road, and early in her life—l think she was about five years old—on the 19th December, 1895, she was admitted to the Whiston Work- house, and so far as we can find out at present she had neither father nor mother alive. She was under the care of the Guardians until the 29th of August, 1901, when she was entrusted to the care of a woman named Ellen Burndred, wife of Joseph Burndred. and they are now living at 39, South John-street, St. Helens. For some reason or other—it was on the 29th August she went to these people—on the 2nd September, four days afterwards, her life was insured, the result of which was that the sum of £2O 12s. was receivable at her death. On the 21st April this year she went back to the workhouse, but on the 2nd June she again re- turned to the Burndreds. On the 29th July— last month—Dr. Bellew was called in to see this child, and the death occurred on the 7th of this month, the burial taking place on the 11th. In consequence of information received,Chief-Constable Wood placed him- self in communication with me, and after bearing what, he had to say I felt it my duty to have this body dis- interred. I consequently issued an order, and the body was exhumed on Saturday night. Yesterday morning Dr. Unsworth, of North-road. St. Helens, made a post- mortem examination; Dr. Bellew, Dr. O'Keefe, and Dr. Bassett also being present. The object of the post- mortem was to take out the organs of the body and place them in the necessary vessels so that they might be sent to the county analyst for analysis. That will take some considerable time, most likely a fortnight or three weeks, so that this morning, after you have seen the body, I shall simply take evidence of identity so as to enable me to issue an order by which the body can be reinterred. Then at the end of three weeks you will have to come here again and bear the result of the analysis and any other evidence which Chief-Constable Wood may place before you. You quite understand you must not condemn anybody at the present time. This is only an inquiry to see whether death has come about in a natural way or whether the suspicions that the police have,are well founded. I think that is all I need tell you at; present, and you will now go to the mortuary , with me to view the body.

The coroner, jurors, &C., then proceeded to the mort- uary, where the body was lying, and on their return, Detective Inspector William Strong said:—The disinter- ment of the body took place at 8.30 on Saturday night, at St.Helens cemetery.l assisted in the disinterment. The body was in a coffin, and on the coffin plate was—" Sarah Jones, died August 7, 1904, aged 14 years." I removed the coffin and body to the mortuary, and yesterday morning, I opened the coffin in your (the coroner's) presence. Dr. Unsworth, Dr. Basnett, Dr. O'Keefe, Dr Bellew, Mr. Cooper (relieving officer), and Chief-Con- stable Wood also attended. They were all there under your orders ; Dr. Basnett representing Mrs. Burndred ; Dr. O'Keefe representing the guardians of the poor, and Mr. Cooper also attending as their official. I saw the body taken out of the coffin, and the post-mortem ex- amination made by Dr. Unsworth, and the jury have all seen the body. I have ascertained that this girl was born on the 17th August, 1890, and that her father was Edward Jones, a collier, and when last heard of he lived at 97, Clock Face Road. Chief-Constable Wood, in reply to the coroner, said he wanted an adjournment for about three weeks, so that the organs of the body might be sent to the county analyst for analysis.
-7171ie--6roner than intimated that the inquiry was adjourned until Tuesday, the 13th September, and the jurors were bound over to attend on that day.
SENSATIONAL DEVELOPMENT.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OF MRS. BURNDRED. At the Police Court on Monday forenoon, Ellen Burndred a respectably-dressed, middle-aged woman, wife of Joseph Burndred, collier, of 38, South John-street, and at whose house the girl Sarah Ann Jones had lived for some time, was charged with attempting to commit suicide. The magistrates en the bench were Messrs. R. A. Pilkington (chairman), T. Glover and W. J.Cook. 11Tr. H. L. Riley, solicitor,appeared for Mrs. Burndred. Chief-Constable Wood said :—This prisoner, Ellen Burndred, is charged with having, at 20 minutes past six on Monday morning, attempted to commit suicide by throwing herself into a pit of water in a field off Fleet- lane, Parr. She was seen by a man named Thomas Wilson, who works at Tickle's Brick works, and he was only 30 or 40 yards off. He saw her throw something into the water, and he turned round for a moment. Just then he heard a boy shout, and on looking round he saw the prisoner in the water. He ran to her and succeeded in getting hold of her and pulling her out of the water. Evidence in support of Chief-Constable Wood's state- ment was given by Thomas Wilson, of 88, Chancery. lane, who added that after he had dragged Mrs.Burnd red out of the water he asked her why she had tried to drown herself, and she replied "Trouble." She added that she threw her slippers into the water before she jumped in herself.—Chief-constable Wood said that upon that evidence he asked for prisoner's remand for a week.

Mr. Riley,in applying for his client to be allowed out on bail,said there was no doubt she had reasonably sus- tained a very great shock in the fact that the body of the child who had lived with her had been exhumed by the police,and an inquiry opene4 by the county coroner. There must be some suspicion in the matter with which Mrs. Burndred was connected,and he (Mr. Riley thought the bench would understand it was necessary in her in- terests that, in such a grave matter, her legal adviser should be able to have access to her and coin nunicate with her very often,and frequently at very short notice. Her husband was a most respectable man, and would undertake to look well after her, if the bench exercised their discretion snd granted her reasonable bail during the period of adjournment. Joseph Burndred. prisoner's husband, said that the imputation that she was in some way responsible for the death of the girl Jones had been a great shock to his wife. It had distressed her very much, and she could not help herself. If she was allowed out on bail he would look carefully after her. Chief-Constable Wood said he most strongly objected to bail in that case, and asked for prisoner to be remanded in custody.
The Chairman, after consulting with the Bench,said:— You will be remanded in custody until this day week.

div.head: DESPERATE MIDNIGHT STRUGGLE. Man's Skull Fractured : Charge of Murder.
div.p: DESPERATE MIDNIGHT STRUGGLE. Man's Skull Fractured : Charge of Murder.

The details which came to Het on Sunday afternoon and Monday with regard to the death of Thomas Duffy, 27 years of age, a colliery labourer, of 11, Francis-stieet Sutton, whose body was found on some waste land near to Hardshaw Brook Chemical Works, on Saturday mid- night, show that the occurrence was the sequel to a desperate fight,in which eight or nine men were involved. A party of five men were returning from St. Helens to Sutton when in Warrington New road they met another party of five coming from Sutton to St. Helens. The parties were apparently strangers to each other, but some words passed, and in the words of Chief-Constable Wood, " all of a sudden a general row struck up. Blows were given in all directions,the men knocking each other down, and when down some of them were kicked." The man Duffy was left unconscious with a fractured skull, and half an hour later he succumbed to his injuries.

Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, appeared for the prisoner. Chief-Constable Wood said : This prisoner, Patrick Hackett, is charged with having caused the death of a man named Thomas Duffy, 27 years of age, by striking

him and knockinc, him to the ground, causing his skull to be fractured. *lt appears that on Saturday night last the deceased min Duffy and four companions were at a beerhouse in Sandfleld-crescent, and remained there until about eleven o'clock. They all came out, and after some delay they commenced to go home. The deceased man lived at Sutton, and his four companions lived at Burtonwood. The prisoner and four companions were in a beerhouse in Ellbess-lane, Peasley Cross, and they remained their until eleven o'clock,and after some delay they also started for home—all the men living in St. Helens. In Warrington New-road, near to the Baths Hotel, the two parties met. They did nct know each other. I think it was the prisoner's party who went to the deceased's party and asked one of them for a match. Something was said about them being a match for one another, but all of a sudden a general row struck up. Blows were given in all directions, the men knocking each other down, and when down some of them were kicked, and amongst others the prisoner was knocked down. Half-an-hour later Duffy was found to be dead. Information was given to the police, and inquiries were made. The four men who were with the deceased and the four men who were with the prisoner were all brought to the police station on Sunday afternoon and inter- rogated. One of the men, who was in the company of deceased,said that he saw Duff y struck and knocked down but he did not know who it was that struck him; while two of the prisoner's party said that they saw the prisoner knock two or three down, but did not know whether the deceased was one of them. A third man of the prisoner's party said he saw Hackett knock down two or three men, and strike the man who was lying unconscious on the ground. He afterwards partially withdrew that statement. On hcaring those statements, he (Chief-Constable Wood) thought fit to charge the prisoner with causing the death of this man Duffy, and, in answer to the charge, be said—" I only did it in self- defence." He asked for Hackett's remand for a week.
Detective Curran gave formal evidence of Hackett's arrest, and said that in answer to the charge of haying caused Daffs death, he replied—" I only did it in self- defence."

Mr. Riley, on prisoner's behalf,said the case was one requiring very careful investigation, but there was nothing disclosed why his client should not be allowed out on reasonable bail. The chief-constable had shown it was a general melee. and in such an affair it was not, the hand that struck the blow that was individually re- sponsible, if there was any responsibility at all, and there was no reas.,u at all why they should differentiate at the expense of one and give others their liberty. They had the prisoner's own words, "What I did, I did in self-defence," which was not only his privilege but his right in an encounter of that kind. Prisoner was a townsman, and he asked the bench to grant reasonable bail. On the facts stated, ' he did not think any man would hesitate in surrendering hi nselr for trial. Chief-Constable Wood said he did not object to reasonable bail under all the circumstances.
The Chairman said the bench had decided to remand the prisoner to the 2nd September, and he would be granted bail, himself in £2O, and two sureties of £lO each.
MR. SEDDON'S SOLDIER SON.
Colonial M.P. Says he is a Coward.

The libel action that has been instituted by Captain Richard Seddon,eldest son of the New Zealand Premier, against Mr. T. E. Taylor one of the Opposition mem- bers of the New Zealand House of Representatives, is the gossip of the islands.l Mr. Taylor alleged that Captain Seddon, who went to South Africa with one of the contingents, was there disrated for cowardice in the face of the enemy, and that, on one occasion, he left his men in a hot corner' and two of them were shot, while the rest were helped by a timely rescue made by another officer. Premier Seddon fell badly when, on his son's return, he appointed the lad—for he is nothing more—to a high military position in the Auckland district, over the heads of hundreds more capable. Auckland protested so loudly that Captain Seddon was brought back to Wellington. Even then paternal blindness prevented Mr. Seddon seeing things. He appointed his noy military adviser to the Defence Department, and Mr. Taylor rose up in the House to demand explanations. it was known that he intended to make a personal attack on the Premier,And the latter asked and obtained the protection of the Speaker, so that the exposure was burked. _ _ _
Since then Mr. Taylor has made a speech outside the House, and the libel action is the result.

div.head: OPENING OF INQUEST.
div.p: OPENING OF INQUEST.
The inquest on the body of the man Duffy was opened before the County Coroner (Mr. S. Brighouse) at the Town Hall on Monday night, and was adjourned until Wednesday in next week.

SPRIGHTLY WARRINGTON. The Blind Walker's Interesting Impressions. Writing to the 'Daily Mail" Mr. J. C. Snap?, the blind man who is walking from Blackpool to Margate, gives the following interesting impressions of War- rington:— Warrington is by no means the dull and uninteresting town I had thought it. Sprightly, though not great, prosperity is the impression. Here I had the good fortune to be teken round the Orford Barracks, and to be initiated into some of the mysteries of soldier life. You pass by the sentry at the gate into a spacious en- closure. Men are walking about with smart, even step, and now and again a bugle rings out, quite close to your elbow. Children are playing here and there upon the hard parade ground—and quarrelling, too, just like other people's children. The canteen is a place of .much interest both- to ' visitors and also to those stationed here. This particular spot is well ordered—and well attended. There is the din of many voices, but the merry chink of glasses is pre- dominant. The birrack ropm is much quieter, the only sound 'being that of a 'thouth organ—a melancholy instrument at best. The beds here are not particularly soft, neither are the pillows. • The head of the bed is not open work, but a thin iron sheet. Above the head of the bed is a shelf, whereon is laid all Tommy's worldly belongings. The room adjoining this is sacred to the performance of his ablutions—and I may add in confidence that Tommy uses scented soaps. Here I had the honour of being introduced to the one V.C.• at Orford. The gnat d-roont is a species of a prison house, and sounds like it. From the barracks I went to listen to a variety entertainment. There were four in the orchestra—fiddle, piccolo, cornet and piano. A contor- tionist was giving a thrilling performance—there is music peculiarly characteristic of such. At the very apex of his performar,co, when even the quar- tet itself • was too much affected to play, and while the audience hold its breath a baby in the gallery howled a most lusty disapproval. From here I made my mly to the drama, and there listened to dis- tressed virtue and secrecy revealed by dying repentance. This town is alive with innumerable children. Waggon- ette after waggonette passes you laden with happy children, shouting, singing and whistling. Also I heard the strange sound of a traction engine towing along three or four heavy vehicles full of laughing boys and girls. Clogs are almost as common here as at Preston. but the wearers have a springier step. About Warring- ton there is an alertness you never dreamt of—a wide- awake feeling in the air which undoes the impressions ;of a lifetime. You had looked for rough brevvery*men WRITE FOR PAMPHLETS: ' and wire-workers—and you get no little degree of in- 111 telligent respectability. Let me, therefore, publicly MERRYWEATHER & SONS, apologize to the citizens of this most ancient and loyal town, a town that once had near it an insignificant vil- 13, LONG ACRE, LONDON, W.C. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible, not later than Thursday.

Moonshine Mysteries. Sir,—lt is perhaps too much to look for the attributes of the poet and file characteristics of the scientist in the same individual. For this reason, it is, lithink,to be regretted that Mr. Clindinning thought it necessary to prelude his verses on " The Moon" in your last issue with some references to what maybe supposed to be the present state of knowledge of our satellite. Not that auch an intrcduetory statement is inappropriate. My objection is that the resume offered Is so weak and ill-informca as to be a travesty of what was probably intended. Wherever did :qr. Clindinning gather " facts " -so ludicrous? We are told that 'from the nights in Eden when Adam first surveyed lunar phenomena until now . . . little more than theories have been brought to light." Really, this is enough to take one's breath away! I wai under the impression that we had left far behind us the nonsense about the aun's effulgence putting the fire out and the moon's rays causing fish and fruit to putrefy. But the reviving of such old women's tales in order to found upon them the deduction that" one finds it impossible to reconcile these simple facts (sic) with astronomical teaching that the moon is not a Great Light' as the Bible says it is, but only reflects the light of the sun" is surely a climax of psuedo-science ! The italicising of the word "only" is mine. Are we right then in assuming that Mr. Clindinning has his doubts about moonshine being merely a mirroring of the sun's rays? Evidently this must be so, else how are we to reconcile with the accepted astronomical teaching the fervid outburst "Hail, lovely Orb, so mild, serene, That shin'st in thine ow* virgin rays"? No. If we are to have a scientific preface let it he at least of an up-to-date character. Moonshine mysteries as a poetic theme need very delicate handling, bad science inevitably leading to Worse verse. 'Let me recommend Mr. Clindinning to consult a modern encyclopedia in 'moments when the Muse moves him to deal with matters rastronomical.—Yours

div.head: SCRUTATOR
div.p: SCRUTATOR
" Gorgonzola."—A Faulty Bye-law.

Sir,—A story is told of a certain railway company who advertised that if a Gorgonzola cheese which had been left on one of their platforms was not called for it would be killed, and they would. not be responsible for the death thereof. Now I have another story with refer- ence to the adventure of 2lbs of best Cheshire, which was purchased in town on Saturday last. A lady friend (Amine was bringing home the cheose in the tramcar to the cemetery end of the town when by some mis- adventure it was left in the car. Application was forth- with made at the Tramway Office,but the 21bs of cheese at 9d. per lb., could not be obtained until payment of 6d., which applicant was informed was the recognized fee under a certain section of the tramway bye-laws. Now sir, I contend that this bye-law is unjust. Tramways are built by public money and are therefore public property and it is very unfair that a shareholder should be fined for having left something on his own property. Had the fee of 6d. been addedto the conductor's wages, no one I think would grumble, but as the present bye- law stands it is most unfair and unreasonable. This incident would not have occurred under the old system of omnibuses and although the tramways hold the monopoly it is not right that-they should become tyran- nical. They evidently work on the principal that the more losses other people sailer the.greater will be their return and gain. I have never noticed in the tramway returns credit given for fees for 'lost cheese Sm. Have there been many? I would suggest that a much smaller fee would amply repay the Corporation for any trouble in- curred through an absent minded passenger. I might add that the lady in question is not simply a " strag " picked up on wet,days but a regular patron of the cars. Now budding councillors who come out in November next, here is an opportunity for making your maiden speechif you have not already done so and proving to theelectorate that you are,capable- of dealing with municipal matters. Might I ask what becomes of the articles that are valued under , the amount of the fee charged by the tramway authorities? Thanking you Mr. Editor for the insertion.—Vours &c., DEAR CHEESE."

div.head: • WARRINGTON MAN'S FEARFUL END. FOUND WITH BROKEN LIMBS IN AN OPEN TRUCK.
div.p: • WARRINGTON MAN'S FEARFUL END. FOUND WITH BROKEN LIMBS IN AN OPEN TRUCK.
Sequel to a Drinking Bout.

A Warrington man named Frederick Worrell, 30 years of age who had been employed as a head waiter at the City liestaurant, Birmingham„. met with a fearful end on the railway between Chester and Hereford. On the arrival of a Manchester goods train at Hereford at 4.58 on Wednesday morning fast week, Worrell was dis- covered in an open truck,sufferingfrom terrible injuries iconsisting of fractures of both legs and arms. The injured man must have been in the truck for about six hours' with his injuries exposed to-the weather. He awes admitted to the Herefordshire • General Hospital, but succumbed to the effect of shock from his injuries About seven o'clock on Friday morning. The deceased man has a father living in Winwick-road, and his sister, 'Mrs. Seymour lives at 105, School-brow. The deceased ivas formerly a barman in the service of Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons. He left to go to Birmingham some years ago where he had a situation at the City ReStanr- Ant. It was while on his way to Warrington that he I *net with the injuries" which terminated fatally. • I A A distressing feature in connection with the case is tthat he was about to be married. He was buried at Hereford on Wednesday. . The inquest was held at the Herefordshire General Hospital on Monday, before the City Coroner, Mr. J. Lambe. The principal witness was Mr. Samuel Smith, of the 'City Restaurant, Birmingham, deceased's employer, who stated that Worrell had been betting and losing money, and was engaged to marry a girl with whonrhe had been keeping company. To show that deceased had a motive for committing auicide, witness might tell‘the coroner that there had, been numerous applications for money, from him by creditors. When he went away deceased intended to go to Warrington, but got out at Chester. I 'Witness heard nothing of him frpm the ;time he left the '-restaurant on Saturday until the &lowing Wednesday when he received a telegram from the stationmaster at Hereford saying that Worrell had been found there ma truck with both arms and legs broken. Witness at once went to Hereford and saw 'Worrell at the hospital. 'Worrell was then quite rational, and as witness approached his bedside in the ward he said. "Hullo, tioss ; I am in a fine mess. Lost a good job. Both arms broken, both legs broken." Witness said to Worrall-"Novi, Fred, tell me all that has happened, and I will be a friend to you." Deceased replied" I will, if you won't tell anyone else." " The Coroner: Why should he say that? Witness,: He told me as a matter of fact that he was drunk. He told me that he was ashamed to come I back on duty on the Saturday night drunk. He wandered I about Birmingham for an hour or so drunk, and went towards .Snow Hill Station, where he took a ticket for Warrington. He said he was going to Chester, where he had uncles, aunts, and Cousins. : ttectititiedll sentences were disjointed, but he also;toldl him that he went to Chester to see some relatives with ' the intention of borrowing money to take him back to' Birmingham. I was on the drink for three days," 'he stated. "On the Tuesday I took a ticket at Chester for Birmingham, and when at the station went into the , refreshment room and had more drink with a friend.l When I came out of the refreshment room the train had I gone, and I wandered back into the town and had more drink. I wandered about till eleven o'clock. It was raining hard. I had no money. I saw the train coming and I tried to throw myself in front of it. I struck my chin on the parapet of the bridge. I fell into the truck and I, temember 110 more." As witness was leaving said to Worrall " Good-bye Fred, come and see You again; hope you will get better," to which deceased responded "I wish T had finiehell the, job." Dr. Eric C. Lindsay, house surgeon at th-e hospital said deceased was brought in on the 17th about G a.m. by men from the Great Western Railway. He was conscious but very much collapsed. He could speak,and could understand what was said to him. He had a fracture of the bones of both upper arms. Both the bones of both legs were also fractured, and on the left side the fracture was compound. He bad also a fracture of the left knee-eap. There were no internal injuries, so far as he could tell, and no fractured ribs. A juror asked were there any marks or cuts on his clothes.

The Chief Constable said that there '‘N'as blood on his shirt and underclothing. There was considerable blood on his underlinen and pants, but no cuts. The outer garments were not soiled, indicating in no way that he had been run over.

John Jones, a Great Western guard, said that on Tuesday, the 16th last, he had charge of the Manchester goods train due to leave Chester at 10.10. After leaving Chester there were two bridges over the line and under the bridge from which deceased was supposed to have fallen the train would be travelling fifteen or twenty miles an hour. Witness sawno object fall from the bridge. ft was only on arrival at Hereford that his attention was called to deceased who was lying in the fifth truck from the, engine. Deceased was conscious but could not give a clear account of how he got into the .truck. A juror expressed the opinion that deetitsed had attempted to commit suicide by trying to throw him.. self under the 'engine, but the train was going to

rclickiywand he fell into one of the trucks instead of on the rail road. ' Deceased's dying dispositions wereproduced in which it was stated :—How I received my injuries I don't re- collect, neither do I remember how I got into the goods heavy waggon; it was open. After the inquiry lasting three hours and a half the jury returned an open verdict.

div.head: LOCAL STUDENTS' SUCCESSES. Results of the Oxford Local Examinations.
div.p: LOCAL STUDENTS' SUCCESSES. Results of the Oxford Local Examinations.

Numerous local successes appear in the division lists announcing the results of the Oxford local examinations which were issued on Monday morning by the secretary of the delegacy. Boys were examined at 180 and girls at 203 centres. The total number of candidates examined Was 14,149, as compared with 12,674 last year, and 9,805 certificates were awarded, as against 9,683 in 1903. The senior candidates numbered 3,200, the junior 6,720, and the preliminary 4,229. Of these 2,011 seniors passed, 4,541 juniors, and 3,253 preliminary. Amongst the senior candidates 14 girls are placed in the first class, 40 in the second, and 133 in the third. Of the juniors 13 girls are placed in the first class, 75 in the second, and 302 th the third. Of the preliminary candidates two girls are placed in the first class, 18 in the second, land 32 in the third.
