div.head: FATE OF THE ALIENS BILL.
div.p: THE FATE OF THE ALIENS BILL.

"The Governrueat have dropped their Aliens Bill. At a meeting of the House of,Commons Grand Com- mittee on Law,-the Home Secretary moved that the consideration .of the measure should not be continued, on the ground that it is impossible to entry it through the committee .in the face of the determined opposi- tion which was being offered to it.—Daity Papers. The fate of the Aliens Bill is a good example of the perils and pitfalls that lie in the way of labour legisla- tion and social reform. This Bill was mentioned in the King's Speech at the opening of Parliament. It was introduced early in the session and referred to the Grand Committee on Law. It was backed by the promises and pledges of the Government. Yet with all these advan- tages in its favour, it has come to grief, and we shall hear no more of it till Mr. Balfour is hard up for some more bait for catching fools. i.—TILE ALIENS BILL WAS A PROTECTIONIST

div.head: MEASURE.
div.p: MEASURE.

It raised the battle cry," Down with the foreigner— Britain for the British." Among people who never think, thisis a very papular election card to play, and the Tories have played it for all it is worth. But people who use their brains sometimes knew very well that if you begin to chivy and harass the subjects of any othercountry, you only invite foreign nations to be rude and unkind to your own people. The Aliens Bill was undoubtedly aimed at the Jews, and its chief backers and supporters were men favourable to anti- Semetic agitation. The Jews have no country of their own, and no army or navy to protect them, so Jew baiting is a. safe and popular amusement. Our fathers welcomed them to this country, picked their brains, and profited by their business ability eight or nine centuries ago. But our Plantaganet kings plundered them, per- Fsecuted them, and murdered them for the sake of their wealth, and banished the remnant of them from the country. No Jew was allowed to set foot on our shores or carry on any trade,or possess any property after that, till the days of Cromwell. Other nations followed our evil example, and to this day Russia, Turkey, and other nations impose civil dis- abilities on the Jews, and persecute them with fiendish cruelties. A Russian Jew naturally tries to disguise his Hebrew origin. Instead of calling himself Abraham, or Levi, or some other Jewish name, his imitates his Russian neighbours, and calls himself Kaskowhiski or Kickern4lloff, till he settles in this country,and then he is content to be called Jones or Robinson.

The Anglicised Jew who settles in this country and prospers, becomes a naturalised citizen, ad6pts our manners and customs, and in two or three generations you would not know that his children had a -drop of Russian or Jewish blood in their veins, and they would be offended with you if you called them aliens or hinted at their foreign origin. It is from these respectable, prosperous children of men, who were aliens a few years ago, that we have the noisiest demand for the exclusion of the foreigner. They have done very well by coming to this country, and they do not want to spoil the trade by allowing too many foroign Jews to oome and compete with them: So in the East end of Londdn there are tens of thousands of electors, whose votes can be won by cry- ing "down with 'the foreigner," and " exclude the aliens." On the other hand, thereare Jews'of enormous wealth, and social power, to be reckoned with. Bankers, mer- chants, and financiers, like the Rothohilds, the Gold- smiths, and Goschens, are a power in this country, and no ministry can afford to quarrel with them. These rich Jews are bitterly opposed to the exclusion of their poor countrymen, and wken I heard that Lord Roths- child had registered a protest against the Aliens Bill I said it would never become law. The Prime Minister had to choose whether he would offend the Anglicised Jews in the East End of London, or the Jewish money- lenders and bankers in the City : he took the lesser ' evil of the two.
IL-THE ALIENS BILL EXPOSED US TO THE RISK OF REPRISALS.

Jew hunting and Jew baiting have their perils, as well as their pleasures. If the Jew has no army or navy or government to protect him, he has only to button up his pockets, and shut his banks, and he can bring all nations to submission. No government can float any great loan without his assistance, and when nations are hard up and stoneybroke, he is master of the situation, and he can dictate his own terms. So it is not wise to quarrel with him, or needlessly to offend him. If the Aliens Bill had been passed it would have got us into serious trouble with nearly all civilized nations. We have always treated aliens in this country as they treated our people when they landed on foreign shores. Ever since Englishmen began to travel abroad, and I settle in foreign lands, we have treated tho subjects of other nations as they treated our subjects in like cir- cumstances. If they were kind, and hospitable, and considerate to Englishmen, we repaid their kindness to their subjects here. If they fined, or persecuted, or banished our people we paid them back in their own eoin. The Aliens Bill would have brought us bank to these old methods, and if foreign nations were to send back all the criminals and undesirables that have fled from this country, because we closed our doors against their subjects, we should have a nice crop of difficulties to settle very soon. All civilised nations now keep a sharp eye on their own citizens in foreign countries, and if one of them should get killed or injured they send a big bill for damages to the rulers of that country, and they make them pay. An American war 'correspondent got shot recently in the Chinese sea by mistake, and that unlucky shot cost £5,000. The Sultan of Turkey has "rot let in for ever so many claims of that sort, and the Chinese Government has paid millions of money as coMpensation for the loss of the lives and property of aliens in that country. If the Aliens Bill- had passed and its administration had been left in the hands of zealous and unscrupulous agents, we should have been lanced in quarrels and misunderstandings with foreign Governments- every week, and we should have had to pay millions of money for their short-sighted and reckless meddling with foreigners. But the fiercest battle against the Aliens Bill raged round the principle of the right of asylum. Our fathers used tci boast that England was the home of freedom, and a sanctuary for the oppressed and the persecuted. We told every slave in the. world that the moment he set his foot on British soil his chains would fall off, and he would be free. We flung wide our door to wel- come the French Huguenots after the massacre of St. Bartholomew, and these men brought us the art and craft of the silk industry. We invited the persecuted Flemings to settle here when-the Duke of Alva was doing his best to annihilate them,and thety accepted our hospitality, and laid the foundations of all our textile industries. We sheltered Mazzini when there was a price set upon his head, and we refused to give up Kossuth whenhe fled fromhis own country as apolitical exile. _

, I Are we to reverse all these glorious traditions of the past, and leave to the discretion of our police and our magistrates the question of who shall be admitted, or who shall be banished from the country? One section of the committee offered to vote for an Aliens Bill that would permit political martyrs, and refugees from tyranny and oppression' and exiles who had been guilty of nothing worse than honest poverty, and a desire for social and political reform, to come to this country. They were prepared to give power to the authorities to exclude known criminals, and traders in immorality, and dirty, diseased aliens who carry plagues and diseases with them everywhere. But the Government would neither compromise nor surrender any part of their bill, so there was a furious fight about it in committee. The Bill contained eleven clauses, consisting of two hundred and forty lines of printed matter. it was debated for seven- days, and only three lines of it were passed. Meanwhile thirteen pages of amendments were on the notice paper for con- sideration, and at that rate of progress it would have taken years to carry this Bill through the committee. So the Bill was dropped, and the angry legislators began falling outand blaming each other. The Attorney General asked, "Who killed Cock Robin?" and then he singled out Mr. Winston Churchill, M.P. for Oldham,as the grand assassin." The :junior member for Oldham was not likely to take this lying down, so be roundly accused the Attorney- General of producing a bill he did not want to pass,and that he dare not place on the statute book if he had the chance. lie compared this measure to those e-ipty Bottles and, dummy, packages that some chemists put in their shop windows. They are not for sale, or use, or consumption. They are only therolfor show, and this Aliens Bill was a bait for votes in the ,East End...of London. Then the member for Stepney lost his temper, and gave the show away by saying that thongh the Bill was dead the agitation for it would remain. And some wag made him worse mad than ever by asking him who found the money to pay for the agitation. Mr. T. W. Russell said the proceedings of the com- mittee were about as cheerful as an Irish wake. The Bill was dead, and its corpse would not keep long this hot weather, so they had better bury it at once, or it would stink worse than ever.

I hear Parliamentary candidates talk glibly enough about what fine things they will do when they get to the House of Commons, and how many measures of social reform they will carry. If they are lucky they may carry one solitary measure, like Mr. Shackleton, to a second reading, and then it will be hung up for the rest of the session. And that will be its fate every year till some friendly, sympathetic Government takes it up, and pilots it through. The fate of the Aliens Bill "Con- vinceff me that it is one of the hardest things in the world-to' pass any highly contentigus Measure, affecting only class interests, through Parliament. Those who doubt my word should try Mr. Shackleton. or they should try their hands at this business themselves. It is not so easy as it looks, T can assure you.

div.head: -..,-. A TRANSACTION IN CABBAGE PLANTS.
div.p: -..,-. A TRANSACTION IN CABBAGE PLANTS.
Action Against a Warrington Firm.
EXPERTS AT VARIANCE.

An interestinc, case to market gardeners was heard at the WarringtoeCounty Court on Thursday, before His Honour J. Bowen Rowlands K.C.—Alfred Melton, market gardener, Cadisbead, brought an action against Messrs. Thomas Pierpoint and Company, seed merchants Horsemarket-street, Warrington, to recover .R5O damages for breach of warranty. The defendant brought in a third party in the person of Thomas Walker, of Biggles- wade from whom the plants were obtained.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the plaintiff.—Mr. Cuthbert Smith. barrister, I,iverpool,(instructed by Mr. A. J. Willett) for the defendant.—Mr. George Passingham of Hitchen, represented Mr. Walker. Mr. Browne in stating' the plaintiff's case said the plaintiff was a market gardener in a small way of busi- ness at Cadishead, and he ordered from Messrs. Pier- point and Co. 15,000 cabbage plants kno;vn as Leeds Market and 2,000 Darley Dale. He had since ascer- tained that the plants supplied were not of the kind ordered, but of an inferior kind. The plants sent were for an early cabbage, whilst the Leeds Market and Darley Dale were a late cabbage. The plaintiff I planted the seedlings in the usual way but it was not until some months afterwards that he found out that the cabbages were of a different variety than that ordered. They were sent to the Man- chester market for sale, and realised a wretched price, some of them being sold for 2d. and 3d. a dozen, whereas ILeeds Market and Darley Dale cabbages should have fetched an average price of 9.1. or 10d. per dozen. Alfred Melton, market gardener at Caclishead, said that during the last ten years he had grown a large quantity of cabbages. He had always grown Leeds Market and Darley Dale cabbages which were late cabbages with large hearts. He ordered 15,000 Leeds Market and 2,000 Darley Dale from the defendants and afterwards found that they were of a poorer quality. The two small cabbages produced in Court were samples of those which had been produced. He also produced a sample of Leeds !Market and Darley Dale cabbages. These were a much larger cabbage and had larger hearts than those which he had been able to grow from Messrs. Pierpoint's plants.—Witness, in reply to Mr. Cuthbert Smith, said he made a complaint to defend- ant's clerk as soon as he found the cabbages were not as he had bargained for. That was not when he received e invoice threatening legal proceedings. / Andrew Warburton, farmer, and a grower of cabbages, said he knew the Leeds Market and Darley Dale plants and had grown the first-named for twelve years. He examined Mr. Melton's crop from time to time, and did not see a single Leeds Market or Darley Dale plant. On July 16th witness, through his agent, sold Leeds Market cabbages at 10d. a dozen, and on July 2nd at is 2d. He did not know that plaintiff only got 2d. a dozen for his. _

Frank Walton, farmer of Cadishead, stated that the plants sold to the plaintiff were not Darley Dale and Leeds Market cabbages but early Yorks. George Davies, fruit and produce salesman at Smith- field Market stated that the cabbages supplied by Mr. Melton were not Darley Dales and Leeds Market. He gave particulars of the prices obtained for the plaintiff's produce.—Cross-examined by Mr. Passingham : In his opinion the plants supplied were Early Offenhatn.

div.head: DEFENCE.
div.p: THE DEFENCE.
Mr. Cuthbert Smith then called witnesses for the defence.

William Yates (secretary for Frank Yates, seed mer- chant, Nottingham) said his firm supplied 2,000 market gardeners. The two small cabbages produced from the plaintiff's field were Leeds Market cabbage, but he accounted for their poor quality on the ground that they had been produced on poor land and had been short of manure and water.

Cross-axamined : He could swear they were Leeds Markets because of the large veins and the bluish-green tint. William S. Charnock. salesman in Manchester market said that the two small cabbages were the nearest ap- proach to Leeds Markets it was possible to get. He had visited the plaintiff's land and found that twb- thirds of the cabbages growing were of the Leeds Mar- ket variety. The land was not properly cultivated for the purposes of cabbages and that accounted for the small size. Cross-examined, Mr. Davies was a well- known salesman and had sold the cabbages well. Several other experts were called to prove that the cabbages grown by the plaintiff were from Leeds Mar- ket plants. On being called upon to name the two large cabbages produced in Court there was consider- able conflict of testimony. This led his Honour to re- mark! that if there was much more evidence of a like character he should hold that they were not cabbages at all. From what he could gather he must believe that one of them was a gigantic asparagus. (Laughter). 'Thomas Walker, of Biggleswade, stated that he sup- plied the plants to Messrs. Pierpoint and Co. What he supplied were Leeds Market plants. He had seen them growing on the plaintiff's land. They were very small because they had been grown on poor land. Frederick William Walters, traveller from Messrs. Pierpoint gave evidence as to forwarding the plants received from Mr. Walker's to the plaintiff. They were Leeds Market plants. Frederick Millard, foreman to Mr. Walker gave evi- dence as to forwarding the plants. Mr. Smith, in addressing the Court on behalf of the defendants, said whatever discrepancies there were in the evidence as to the cabbages produced in Court, all the witnesses for the defendant were agreed that the plaintiff had received Leeds Market plants but that he had not cultivated them properly. He had traced the origin of the plants and there was no doubt whatever but that the plaintiff had received Leeds Market plants as ordered. Mr. Passingham also addressed his Honour, laying stress on the long business career of Mr. Yates and Mr. Walker who were responsible for the seedlings.

div.head: HIS HONOUR'S DECISION.
div.p: HIS HONOUR'S DECISION.

His Honour, in giving judgment, said there had been a diversity of opinion and they had had the luxury of having three parties in a triangular fight. There were some circumstances on both sides which called for regrettable comment. The difficulty had been caused by the language used by the plaintiff in his letters and by his not making more energetic complaints, if such complaints were in reality well founded. To take the last first, he was of opinion that judgment must be in favour of the third party as far as they could be satisfied in this matter. No evidence had been called before him to justify him in coming to the conclusion that the third party had not performed the contract he was called upon to fulfil. There must be judgment for the third party with costs. The plaintiff had claimed various sums of money, and Mr. Browne as he usually did, had given the best explanation, namely that when the claim was first made sales had not taken place, and therefore the exact amount of loss could not be ascertained. It was an interesting thing to discover that the extent of the damages grew greater and greater as time went on and no one knew that if this action had not come on for some remote period, the damages might have reached a figure which would have pnzzled the arithmeticians. From circumstances either inherent in a cabbage or from the impossibility of concentrating their minds sufficiently upon the small specimens, he was of opinion on the evidence given that the plaintiff was entitled to recover. It was very much to be regretted that the suggestion made by the plaintiff in a letter to the defendants was not followed up in some way. in that letter the plaintiff wrote that there was not a Leeds Market or a Darley Dale among those that had been supplied. It was pointed out that inquiries were at once made. His Honour said that be thought inquiries were made only a le% days ago. His Honour proceeded to allude to a letter written by Mrs. Pierpoint in which she said "We are sold out of Leeds Market and Darley Dale plants, but are writing to another grower." In this scarcity of supply and in the confusion which might arise in the course of business which the defendants were carrying on, he was of opinion that they did not supply Darlev Dale or Leeds Market plants. except to a limited extent, which they had contracted to do. Therefore they were liable for such damages as flowed naturally from the breach of their contract. He thought the market price was fairly fixed at 9d. per dozen, and striking an average he thought the plaintiff was entitled to £2.2. He therefore gave judgment for the third party with costs against the defendant; judgment for the plaintiff on the claim against the defendant for £l2 and costs, and judgment for the defendant on the counterclaim of RS Ss. Id. for goods supplied and costs.

About half-past six o'clock on Wednesday evening a shocking accident occurred at the Green Lane Junction of the London and North-Western and Great Western Joint Railways, Birkenhead. From what can be gathered, it appears that a lamplighter named Turner in the employ of the company, was lighting the signal lamps along the line, when he attempted to cross the points. An express was approaching, and it is believed that the man saw it, but, thinking that it Would pass on another line, stood still, and the train dashed into him and practically decapitated him.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES- AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES- AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

A new and commendable departure was the Warring- ton eleven's match on Saturday with representatives of local junior organizations. Any efforts to stimulate interest in the sport and to bring to light exceptional talent are worthy of encouragement, and lam pleased to hear that the match is likely to become an annual event. Invitations had been forwarded to all the local clubs, but several of the best known ones could not find it convenient to send players. The team was picked from nine clubs and numbered eighteen, Mr. E. Pier- point, of the Warrington second eleven, undertaking the captaincy. Several of our local custodians of the peace figured in the ranks, and one at any rate distinguished , himself.

The juniors had first turn at the wicket, and were all dismissed for 58. Then the Warrington men went in, and having compiled 71 with only three wickets down declared their innings. The second effort of the juniors was productive of 126 for 6 wickets, and the match was therefore left drawn. As the score indicates, there was nothing remarkable in the first innings of the District team. The most successful batsman, J. Dargan, of Cros- field's, compiled 11, and P.C. Holland knocked up 10.

Several very creditable displays were witnessed in the second innings, J. Dargan showing that he is a batsman of no mean ability. The bowlers failed to disturb his pegs, and he carried out his bat after making 39. Another good performance was accomplished by E. Allen, of Walker's Brewery,who was responsible for 22 not out. H. Dutton (St. Helens Cable) and N. Nield (Fairfield) each ran up 16, and P.C. Holland again did good service with 11.

On the senior side, Alf Thewlfs' the ex-professional, attained the highest figures, making 25 not out. T. Wright placed 18 to his credit before he was bowled by P.C. Houghton, and R. Pierpoint scored 17 not out.

J. Dargan proved himself a capable bowler as well as batsman, capturing two wickets for 11 runs. The most successful bowler of the day was J. W. Bibby who acoounted for nine wickets at the small cost of 20 runs. E. A. Connor was also in fine form and took eight wickets for 35 runs. W. H. Podmore's capture was four for 80, and E. E. Woods was responsible for two forl7

With so many useful players doing duty at Arplev there were very few junior matches. Sankey Wire Mills journeyed to Glazebury, and made a draw of the engagement, their highest scorers being N. Cook (23) and Evans (18). R.Cook bowled with great effect,taking five wickets far 22 runs. For the home team Seddon (17) and Collier (13) did good service with the willow.

Latchford Baptists defeated Union Chapel, Manches- ter, on the Fallowfleld ground, by a margin of 16. St. Helens Cable Company triumphed over the" Guardian" eleven to the extent of 34. The only players to reach double numbers were G. Peacock (12) and W. Wright (11).

Moore and Daresbury had to admit defeat at the hands of Lostock Gralam, for whom Woods took six wickets for 14 runs. Stretton and Appleton disposed of Grappenhall second, their highest scorer being Ellison with 15.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

To--day sees the close of the Warrington and District league tourney, and opportunity may be taken to refer to the complete success which has attended the under- taking. From the very commencement the interest with which the games were entered into showed that the league was fulfilling a useful purpose. Rivalry has been keen but friendly, and some of the cream of War- rington's trundlers have met. The officials are deserv- ing of a meed of praise for the painstaking way in which they have discharged their duties. Mr. G. F. Freeman, as chairman of the committee, Mr. J. Earle, as hon. treasnrer, and Mr. Edward Taylor,ashon.secretary, have each rendered yeoman service, and have left no stone unturned to ensure the smooth working of the competition. It will be the wish of all enthusiasts that the league may have many prosperous seasons before it.

The championship was practically decided a fortnight ago' and the beautiful cup and gold medals will go to the Cemetery Club members who have displayed con- sistently good form throughout the season. The Bull's Head players have made a good fight, and thoroughly deserve the medals for the runners-up. At present the Cemetery Club have only two points lead, but to-day they have an opportunity of adding a couple if they can account for Brooklands on the Lovely-lane green.

There were three interesting matches on Saturday,anct in each case the home team was triumphant. Fearn: head entertained Penketh Park and ran out winners by 27 points. Some of the games were exceptionOly close. F. Swift of Penketh and W. Andrews, of Fearnhead ; J. Andrews of Fearnhead, and J. Wareham of Penketh; P. Croft of Fearnhead, and S. Shave of Penketh, were well matched, the first-named players securing the vic- tory by the odd point.

The Liberal Club have shown poor form this season, and that the wooden spoon will be their lot seems pretty well assured. To-day they have a last chance of placing themselves on an equality with Penketh, but as the match is at Fearnhead. the odds are against the visitors. Last Saturday Bull's Head severely trounced the Bewsey-street contingent winning ten of the twelve games. The keenest encounter was between H. Clare and H. Daintith, the first-named trundler who repre- sents the Bull's Head, being the victor by one point.

Brooklands had to admit defeat on the Horse and Jockey green, the home club running up a majority of 64. Two of tilt best contests were provided by R. Jefferson (Brooklands), and J. Simister (Horse and Jockey) ; R. Healey (Brooklands), and T. Harrison (Horse and Jockey), the first-mentioned players winning by a couple of points.

The following is the league table up-to-date : P. W. L. For Agst. Pts. Cemetery Bull's Head Fearnhead Horse and Jockey l4 .•• 7 ••• 7 ...2109 ...1875 ... 14 Chapel House Brooklands Penketh Liberal Club l3 ... 4 ... 9 _lBO2 _2003 ... 8
The matches to be played to-day are : Fearnhead v. Liberal Olub. Brooklands v. Cemetery.

The third annual bowling main plomoted by the employes of the Castle Rubber Company, Limited, War- rington, took place on Saturday, at the Bowling Green Hotel, Hollins Green, and a very enjoyable afternoon was spent. The firm very handsomely subscribed to the funds with the result that the prizes were considerably increased. Result rr, O'Brien ; 2, H. Fairbrother ; 3, R. Derbyshire ; 4, W. Bristowe; 5, T. Lally; 6, .T. Leigh; 7, G. Lea: 8, A. Field. A substantial tea was provided by the landlord which was followed by the cmstomary toasts, and a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Nevins for the manner in which he had catered.

The league individual merit championship has been keenly fought for, and to-day will witness the final effort. As matters at present stand A. Shaw, of Bull's Head: has the best record. He has played 14 games, and won 12,with a total of 202 points for and 134 against. J. Berry, who has still an opportunity of winning, has played 12 and won 11, .with 184 points for and 128 against. Berry will play for the Cemetery against Brooklands to-day, and if he bsats his opponent 15-2 he will be entitled to the championship of the league. Each player deserves every credit for his meritorious performance.

The Works handicap will be concluded on the King and Queen green to-day and 38 games are down for decision. At the close the medals and prizes will be presented by Mr. S. Taylor, the vice-president of the Association.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

Cranage was the Warrington club's destination on Saturday. Owing to the absence of a large number of members and the f(Ste at Walton, there was only a small turnout. The roads were in excellent condition and the ride across Rudheath, resplendent with autumn tints, was greatly enjoyed. After tea at the Swan Farm a stroll rdund the district was indulged in, Warrington being reached;about 9 o'clock after a very pleasant outing
Owing to the incessant downponr of rain Tuesday's run to Warburton had to be abandoned.

To-day's run is to Delamere via Frodsham and on Tuesday Bold will be the venue. , Picturesque Rostherne was visited by a dozen mem- bers of Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Club OR Saturday and the outing was successful and enjoyable.

div.head: Angling.
div.p: Angling.

Angling for course fish is now at Its height and so far as the season has advanced anglers generally have not had much reason to complain about lack of sport. The usual classes of course fish caught in theneighbour- hood have bitten well, canal fishing forming the princi- pal centre of attraction. J. BALL TAKES THE accounts under review. WORKING MEN, RATEPAYERS INTO HIS CONFIDENCE. , My interpretation of the duties of an elective auditor is to be considered as part of that municipal machine whose efficiency depends largely on the discriminating choice of the electors. Municipal development holds BY JOHN TAYLOR. , within itself the promise of a fairer and a happier day. Author of Search Lights on Laaa, Labour [To THE EDITOR OF THE EX4IIINER.I llt means better condition of labour, better homes, more ' " opportunities for pure and reasonable recreation and and Social Problems. Sir,—ln accordance with the circular issued on my pleasure for the mass of the people. Something has been behalf by the Committee_of the Independent Labour- done to make our town more habitable. Much remains Party (Warrington branch) in February last I have that will be rightly done only when all sections of the pleasure in submitting a report, as one of the Elective community realise the duties, privileges, and eoportuni- Auditors, on the accounts of the Warrington Corpora- ,ties of citizenship, and earnestly seeks ways and means to provide for all tion for the year ended March 31st, 1901. In taking nobler field of the faculties of man a fairer and a exercise. the unusual course (for Warrington) of issuing a report direct to the ratepayers, I recognise the general desire for greater detail- and fuller information as to , municipal expenditure to be legitimate and reasonable. The intention of the framers of the. Act which created the office of elective auditor was to provide a check against waste, extravagance, misuse of funds, and illegal and doubtful payments ; and high legal opinion is not lacking to show that a direct report to the general body of burgesses is eminently desirable, if not absolutely necessary, in the public interest. Since the days when the position was first instituted, municipal enterprize has developed tremendously. The rank and file of the electorate realize more and more that corporate work and schemes affect individual life very nearly. The multifarious activities of a modern town call for a high sense of civic duty and responsibility in our governors and administrators, but it is also requisite that those who take no active Ipart in local government shall display an intelligent interest and maintain a watchful and jealous eye on all public offices and appointments. Local circumstances have conduced to a keener interest in our town's affairs:- -As an elected representative, holding a public offide bY_the votes of a large number of my fellow townsmen, I submit a few points in the hope that, while deepening interest, they may _render criticism faller and more intelligent. The books and accounts of the Borough are in excellent order and it is evident that our accounting officials and their staffs take an honourable pride in the neatness and accuracy of their work. The methods adopted are, generally speaking, based on lines approved lijr authorities on accountantcy, and the general system is admirable. I made special enquiries as to cash transactions, including checking and pay- ment of wages, petty cash, etc., and find the checks imposed are such as make fraud difficult and reduce temptation to a minimum. Every facility has been afforded me to satisfy any doubts, suspicions or queries I have raised, and any documents or books necessary have been produced with courteous prompti- tude. The accounts of the Borough, published in due course contain much detail showing income, expendi- ture, l;alances, liabilities, etc., of each department and trading concern. There is no need, therefore, to burden this article with figures which are more accessible in other 'ways and I would refer those who delight in such things to the published accounts,where they may revel in figures to their heart's content. Several matters are, however, not so apparant in that form, and the following are items which have been suggested to me by an examination of the accounts. OUTSTANDING ACCOUNTS. , The joint report signed by my colleagues and MYseTl has already been published in the local press. Atten- tion was drawn to the large amount owing for goods and material supplied Airing the financial year, which had not been included in the accounts for that year. The bearing of this appears to have been misunderstood in some quarters,and a few words in explanation may be useful. The total amount referred to was £2,700 of which £1,113 was due to the Gas, Electricity and Water Departments, the balance of about £1,600, being due to various traders. Complaint was made some time ago that the estimates for the year had been exceeded by several of the Committees. When the £1,600, referred to is 'added, it is obvious that the estimate had been ex- ceeded to a greater extent than was apparent at the time the complaint was made. The other amount £1,113, is almost entirely due to the Gas and Electricity De- partments, the amount owing to the Water Department being small. The two trading concerns (Gas and Elec- tricity) take credit for the amount as part of their income for the year, but the corresponding debt is not shown in the other departments *for the same year. It also appears invidious that Corporation departments should press outside traders to send in their accounts while two of the municipal trading concerns are similarly in fault. IMPROPER PAYMENTS. In view of the recent agitation and enquiry, I kept a special look-out for any payments that might be con- sidered improper or unauthorised, but I could not trace a single item to any official, or any individual or private firm represented on the Town Council. EXPENSES OF DEPUTATIONS, OFFICIALS, ETC. Prominence has been given in various towns and cities to the extravagance of councillors and officials when engaged on public business. Much has been heard of public money being lavishly spent on expensive luncheons wines, and cigars. Such misuse of municipal funds has rightly been exposed and deplored. Whatever charms, hawever, "the beady bubble winking at the brim," or the flavour of a fine cigar, may or may not have had for gentlemenlwho travel on other Corporations' business, , the expenses in the case of our representatives seem reasonable and fair. The following examples are , samples of the whole :—Ship Canal case, railway fare, ' £2 13s. ; three days' hotel. £4 10s. ; cabs and telegrams, ss. 6d.; total, £7 Bs. Gd. April 6th and 7th, 1903, J. Lyon Whittle, journey to London attending High Court, Manchester Ship Canal case: Railway fares, telegrams land cabs, £3 45.; two days at 305., £3; total £6 45.. July 10th, 1903, T. Longdin, expenses of committee and self to Wallasey, £2 2s. 6d.; committee consisted of Alderman Heaton and Bennett, and Councillors Rogers, A. Peacock and Ellison. August 26th, 1903, R. W. Fmncomb, six attendances at Preston on Asylum Board business, January Ist to June 30th, 1903, at 13s. 6d., £4 is. The only occasion which might be considered in the nature of a " picnic "was the inspection of the water- works Delph-lane, Appleton &c. Invitations were issued to the members of the Council and to the principal officials to join the Water Committee in the ceremony of turning on the new water supply. I do not know how many persons took part,but the bill is as follows— whiskey, £1 Bs.; mineral waters, 10s. 9d.; cigars, £2 145.; conveyances, £3 15s.,total £7 7s. 9d. PURCHASES OF LAND AND BUILDINGS. Purchases of land and buildings for street improve- ments, tramway routes, &c., forma considerable item in the accounts. It would be invidious to .give details of price, Sic., especially as there is nothing in the accounts to show that any councillor was personally interested in the sales. No doubt the properties have been bought at their fair market value, but considering the age, position, and appearance of some of the lots purchased, via.—Dial-street,Rose-yard„Buttermarket-street, School brow, &c., one cannot help thinking that the market Value is not inherent in the 'property, but is partly enhanced value created by the necessities of a growing town. Taxation of land values, and indeed of all unearned increment, is a question municipalities need to press in season and out of season in self defence. There have been loud and deep complaints that rates are unduly high in Warrington. If, however, the local rates have become burdensome and the ordinary sources of revenue are being strained to bursting point, then the ratepayers of this Borough might usefully pay more attention to the question of land values and ensure•that all sections of the community pay their fair share of local taxation. GAS AND WATER ANNUITIES. One of the gratifying items in the Borough accounts is the profit of £lO,OOO on the Gas Works. This profit might be greater were not the revenue saddled with perpetual annuities to the extent of £2864 10s. which is equal to at least 11d. on every 1000 cubic feet of gas sold. These annuities represent part of the purchase money of the original gas undertaking, and have been paid for 27 years. They are irredeemable except at the wish of the holder and only then at 30 years' purchase. If the payments are made for another 27 years, the holder can still claim 30 more years in a lump sum be- fore be can be bought out. He may prefer not to sell out. He may therefore leave it to his heirs, and your grandchildren may pay to his grandchildren the per- petual annuity you now pay to him. Happy annuity that can imitate the brook and sing— , "For men ma 3 come and men may go But I go on for ever." Happy privilege of capital which not only rakes its toll from the present generation, but has power to tax generations still unborn. in the Warrington Corpora- tion Act, 1899, a clause was sought to empower the Cor- poration to compel sale at a certain date, but Parlia- mentary influence was powerful enough to have the cause deleted. Parliamentary hands would appear to be more concerned in safeguarding vested interest than in promoting the public weal. This question of the gas works will sound like ancient history to many, but if we suffer now from the apathy of a former generation, the point of these remarks lies in the fact that watch- ful criticism from the general body of ratepayers will go far to render similar burdens impossible in future. The water department annuities have in the course of years been bought out until the figure now stands at £1,042. These are also redeemable at the handsome rate of 30 years' purchase. They are comparatively short lived, having about 17 more years to run, as per the Act mentioned above. CHARACTER OF AUDIT. The accounts of this Borough are not subjected to any audit except that conducted by the Mayor's Auditor, appointed yearly, and two elective auditors, elected yearly by ballot. In view of the increasing volume and complexity of municipal accounts, many boroughs engage professional auditors, the elective auditors being an additional safeguard from a judicial point of view. The Borough audit in Warrington is largely professional, but in addition to satisfying myself that the entries

rington Anglers' Association was duly decided in the waters of the Bridgewater Canal at Thelwall on Satur- day last. There was a record entry of over 140 competi- tors, and arrangements were superintended by Mr. Knight. A good contest resulted in Mr. H. Moores proving successful with a weight of just over a pound. The gold medal is presented by Mr. J. Lyon Whittle. The second match of the season in connection with the Latchford Angling Society was fished at Grappenhall on Saturday last,thirty-six members competing. Messrs. J. W. Starkey, T. Craven and Harry Taylor (president), conducted arrangements and all proceeded satisfactorily. Fishing was not of the briskest, though a successful match resulted.—lst, G. Taylor, 6oz. 3drs. ; 2nd, J. Jones ; 3rd, W. Hamilton ; 4th, A. Handles; sth, W. H. Shakeshaft ; 6th, A. Gorton; 7th, IV. Starkey and Bth,, - A. Holland. The next match takes place at Northwich and the prize distribution will be undertaken on Mon- day evening next at the • club headquarters. the Brook. Inn, Latchford. The members of the Black Bear Angling Society , visited Agden Bridge on Saturday last to fish the third ' contest of the season and the drive thereto was much enjoyed. Excellent arrangements had been made by the club secretary, Mr. Sam. Grindley, and though perhaps catches were not of the best, yet all the prizes were won. Result :-Ist, T. Nixon, 7ozs. 15drs. ; 2nd, Robert Taylor; 3rd, J. Brown ; 4th, J. Mairs • sth, A. Bate ; 6th, J. Clarke; 7th, S. Grindley; and Bth, \V. Burton. The prizes were distributed on Monday even- ing last. -- -- Anglers who are holders of licences for fishing the Bridgewater Canal are reminded that to-day (Saturday) is the last day on which entrances can be accepted for the Challenge Shield and Championship Competition in connection with the Worsley Canal Fishery Board. Entries may be made with Mr. P. Knight. hon. secre- tary of the IV. A. A., and the contest takes place ou Saturday afternoon next, one section at London Bridge, Stockton Heath, and the other at Worsley. Anglers who fish the Bridgewater Canal are requested to note that fishing is only allowable from the tow-path side. Water Polo. Two interesting watches were down for decision at the Corporation baths on Tuesday, and there was a good attendance. In the first place, the second team tried conclusions with Birkenhead, and a keen tussle was witnessed. During the first half the visitors had the best of matters,and Holt registered two goals. Turner and Allen tried hard to place Warrington in a better position, but at half-time Southport were leading by two to nil.On resuniing,Warrington displayed better Torn], and W. Warren scored easily from a penalty. IV. Allen equalised with along shot, and although the home team tried hard to gain the lead, the match which was a League fixture resulted in a draw. The first team met Southport in a friendly match and gave a decidedly good account of themselves. The visitors lacked the assistance of Battersby and Radcliffe, tip Warringtonians being at full st-ongth. Southport dlifended the deep end,and Warringtua soon showed that they meant to make a good fight. Play had only been in progress about a minute, when IV. Sutton passed to Peers who scored easily. The efforts of the sand grounders to break away were futile, and a second goal for Warrington soon followed. NV. Ashton secured about midway and sent in a shot which the visitors' custodian only partially cleared. Peers was lying ia wait, and put the ball through. Sutton and C. Ashton scored before the interval which arrived with Warring- ton ahead by 4 goals to nil. On resuming, Warrington again took up the attack,and Sutton scored No. 5. Some unpleasantness now occurred with the result that the Southport captain withdrew his team, and the game' ended. In a squadron race Warrington defeated Southport by' a length. Under the auspices of the Liverpool and District League, the St. Helens and Wigan water poloists met on Tuesday, at the St. Helens Corporation Baths, before' a good attendance. St. Helens played without Sharrock, Turner, and Lawrenson—Barr, Thornley, mid Manning being included in the team. Swift opened The score for Wigan, Nevison adding a second and a third. Halftime- Wigan 3, St. Helens 0. Restarting play, Satindeis score for Wigan, and a fifth came from Swift. Saunders next • scored, St. Helens being shockingly overplayed. Final • Wigan 6 goals, St. Helens nothing. -- Football. , The Warrington men are sparing no trouble to get themselves fit for the opening of the season next wee"' Therephave been representative turn-outs to the prac- tices held last Saturday and Thursday evenings. On Thursday practically all the first and" A "team players ' ' were on view. Hallam and Harris being the onll notable absentees. The three new forwards, Shit 0 Preston and Belton all took their places in the pack I°.J n°,? gave a very promising exhibition. Together scit;`_ Boardman they made a very formidable front rafl. quartette, and the club officials are confident that tha have got a sat of scrim-onagers who will not be bustled with the ball by any team they may Ine.A. It is gratifying also to learn that the backs are show- ing all their old-time dash and speed. In fact it is the general opinion that the three-quarter line has got more pace in it than ever. Fish has trained steadily during the last month and he is to-day running in a style which augurs well for the season's matches. On Thursday he got a couple of very fine ties, in the course of a keen game in which neither seniors nor juniors gave anything. away. Practice matches are unfortunately full of danger- Last season Harris was incapacitated with a brok0l! collar-bone sustained in practice, which kept him out 01. the team for the first two months. Last Saturday, Short, the promising " A " team right wing was eonall unlucky for he got his shoulder dislocated. On Thar?" day it was feared that Dickenson was badly hurt in, a rush for the line, but he came out with nothing than a bruising and some loosened front teeth. This quite sufficient to be going on with, and I hope the resu of the players will keep out of harm's way until there are points at stake. The match with Leigh,on Saturday seems certain t; take a lot of the home enthusiasts to Mather-lane, an,l there is plenty of confidence that Warrington repeat their last season's success. They should cartain':: prove their superiority over any fifteen that Leigh es" put in the field. The important transfer of"Jaek"F'reston from Swinton to Warrington was completed on Saturday, and tber the " wire-pullers !' thus se,curK the services of one of best forwards in, Lancashire.
